hypotheses.label: positive dimension
hypotheses.note: The ambient dimension is at least one; the constant does not otherwise depend on it.

hypotheses.label: centred law
hypotheses.note: Every linear functional of the sampling law has mean zero.

hypotheses.label: identity covariance
hypotheses.note: The covariance form is the Euclidean inner product.

hypotheses.label: finite third moment
hypotheses.note: The Lyapunov quantity $\beta$; the only feature of the sampling law entering the bound.

formalizationNotes: The point of the ball version is that *all three* constants feeding it are dimension-free: the spherical-shell anti-concentration constant for the standard Gaussian (obtained from a uniform bound on the chi density with no Stirling asymptotics), the third-derivative constant of a smoothed radial indicator, and the Cameron–Martin tilt-remainder constant. The exponent $1/2$ is the same as in the convex-set version and is a strict improvement over the elementary $1/4$; the sharp $\beta/\sqrt n$ rate is not obtained. Sets are taken in the form $\{\|z\|^2 \le t\}$, i.e. centred balls only — no statement is made about off-centre balls.

reference.formal: V. Bentkus, "On the dependence of the Berry–Esseen bound on dimension", *Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference* **113** (2003), 385–402.
reference.biblio: Over balls the multivariate Berry–Esseen problem is easier than over general convex sets, and Bentkus (2003) records a dimension-free constant there. The formalized statement reproduces the dimension-freeness but not the rate: the exponent is $1/2$ rather than $1$, which is what the elementary Lindeberg-plus-Cameron–Martin route yields without a self-improving induction.

title: Riemann–Lebesgue lemma, uniformly over a totally bounded family
informal: For an integrable $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ write $\widehat f(s) = \int f(x)\,e^{isx}\,dx$ for its oscillatory integral. The Riemann–Lebesgue lemma says that $\widehat f(s) \to 0$ as $|s| \to \infty$ for each fixed $f$. Let now $S$ be a set of indices and $(f_i)_{i \in S}$ a family of functions, each integrable, which is totally bounded in $L^{1}$ — for every $\delta > 0$ there is a finite subset $J \subseteq S$ such that each $f_i$ is within $L^{1}$-distance $\delta$ of some $f_j$ with $j \in J$. Then for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a compact set outside of which $$\sup_{i \in S}\;\bigl|\widehat{f_i}(s)\bigr| \;\le\; \varepsilon .$$ Uniformity is genuinely a consequence of total boundedness and does not hold without it: the translates $f(\cdot - a)$, $a \in \mathbb{R}$, all have the same transform modulus, and no single function's transform decays uniformly along a family that is not relatively compact.
summary: Oscillatory integrals of a family of integrable functions tend to zero uniformly over the family as the frequency leaves every compact set, provided the family is totally bounded in $L^1$.
leanSignature:
theorem eventually_norm_fourierOsc_le_of_totallyBounded (f : ι → ℝ → ℂ) (S : Set ι)
    (hf : ∀ i ∈ S, Integrable (f i))
    (hnet : ∀ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ → ∃ J : Finset ι, ↑J ⊆ S ∧
      ∀ i ∈ S, ∃ j ∈ J, (∫ x : ℝ, ‖f i x - f j x‖) ≤ δ)
    {ε : ℝ} (hε : 0 < ε) :
    ∀ᶠ s in Filter.cocompact ℝ, ∀ i ∈ S, ‖fourierOsc (f i) s‖ ≤ ε

hypotheses.label: integrable family
hypotheses.note: Every member of the family is in $L^1$, so its oscillatory integral is defined.

hypotheses.label: finite $L^1$ nets
hypotheses.note: Total boundedness in $L^1$, stated as the existence of finite $\delta$-nets indexed by the family itself.

formalizationNotes: The whole content is the two-line estimate $|\widehat{f_i}(s)| \le |\widehat{f_j}(s)| + \|f_i - f_j\|_{L^1}$ with $j$ ranging over a finite net; total boundedness is exactly the hypothesis that makes the finitely many Riemann–Lebesgue "eventually"s intersect to a single one. The $\varepsilon$-net hypothesis is stated as a finite set of *indices* rather than of $L^1$ elements, which is the form a finite subcover of a compact parameter set produces, and the $L^1$ distance is written as an honest integral rather than through the $L^p$ quotient by almost-everywhere equality; nothing is lost and no lifting into the quotient is needed.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer, Cham, 2022.
reference.biblio: The Riemann–Lebesgue lemma itself is classical. The uniform version over a totally bounded family is the technical device needed to verify a *multivariate* Cramér condition — H. Cramér's (1937) condition that the characteristic function be bounded away from modulus one at large frequencies — for a law carried by a curve, where the family is the set of one-dimensional projections indexed by a compact sphere of directions. Cramér's condition is what licences Edgeworth expansions and higher-order bootstrap accuracy in Lehmann and Romano (2022, Ch. 16).

title: Cramér-type decay of a quadratic-phase oscillatory integral
informal: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ be integrable. Then for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a radius $R > 0$ such that $$\left|\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(y)\,e^{\,i(t_0 y + t_1 y^{2})}\,dy\right| \;\le\; \varepsilon \qquad \text{whenever } |t_0| + |t_1| \ge R .$$ This is exactly the cocompact decay that a multivariate Cramér condition for a law carried by the parabola $y \mapsto (y, y^{2})$ demands, and it holds with no hypothesis on $f$ beyond integrability. The two frequency regimes are handled differently: for bounded $|t_1|$ the family of quadratic twists is totally bounded in $L^{1}$ and the uniform Riemann–Lebesgue lemma applies, while for large $|t_1|$ — uniformly in $t_0$ — one squares the integral and uses the autocorrelation identity, which moves the oscillation into the *frequency* of an ordinary Fourier transform and leaves $t_0$ inside a unimodular factor.
summary: For any integrable density the oscillatory integral with a quadratic phase becomes arbitrarily small once the sum of the absolute values of the two frequency coefficients is large.

hypotheses.label: integrable density
hypotheses.note: The only hypothesis: $f \in L^1(\mathbb{R})$. In particular no smoothness, decay or absolute continuity is assumed.

formalizationNotes: The large-$|t_1|$ regime is *not* a Riemann–Lebesgue statement — the quadratic twists $y \mapsto e^{it_1 y^2} f(y)$ are not relatively compact in $L^1$ over an unbounded set of $t_1$ — and is instead proved through the autocorrelation identity, avoiding any van der Corput estimate and any smoothness hypothesis on $f$. The statement is a purely existential bound: no rate in $|t_0| + |t_1|$ is claimed.

reference.formal: H. Cramér, *Random Variables and Probability Distributions*, Cambridge Tracts in Mathematics **36**, Cambridge University Press, 1937.
reference.biblio: H. Cramér (1937) introduced the condition $\limsup_{|t|\to\infty}|\varphi(t)| < 1$ on a characteristic function as the hypothesis under which Edgeworth expansions are valid; its multivariate analogue for a law carried by a curve reduces, after projecting, to the decay of oscillatory integrals with a polynomial phase. What is formalized is the quadratic case in full generality (integrable density, no smoothness), which is what a law on a parabola — the joint law of a variable and its square, as in studentized statistics — requires.

title: Exact variance of a linear statistic under sampling without replacement
informal: Assign $m$ of $n$ labelled items to the first group, all $\binom{n}{m}$ splits being equally likely, and let $W_i = \mathbf{1}\{i \text{ is in the first group}\}$ be the inclusion indicators. These are exchangeable Bernoulli$(m/n)$ variables, negatively correlated because $\sum_i W_i = m$. Assume the split exists, $m \le n$, and that there are at least two items, $n \ge 2$. Then for any deterministic coefficients $c_1, \ldots, c_n$, writing $\bar c = n^{-1}\sum_i c_i$, $$\operatorname{Var}\Bigl(\sum_i c_i W_i\Bigr) \;=\; \frac{m(n-m)}{n(n-1)}\sum_i (c_i - \bar c)^{2}.$$ Both degenerate splits $m = 0$ and $m = n$ give variance zero, as they must. Consequently the group average $m^{-1}\sum_i c_i W_i$ has variance at most $\tfrac{2}{m}\cdot n^{-1}\sum_i (c_i - \bar c)^2$, an $O(1/m)$ bound which is what drives the negligibility of individual summands in the permutation central limit theorem.
summary: The variance of a linear statistic in the inclusion indicators of a simple random sample without replacement equals the finite-population factor times the centred sum of squares of the coefficients.
leanSignature:
theorem var_linear {n m : ℕ}
    (hm : m ≤ n)
    (hn : 2 ≤ n) (c : Fin n → ℝ) :
    expect (fun s : SubsetsOfCard n m =>
        ((∑ i, c i * weight i s)
          - expect (fun s' : SubsetsOfCard n m => ∑ i, c i * weight i s')) ^ 2)
      = ((m : ℝ) * ((n : ℝ) - m)) / ((n : ℝ) * ((n : ℝ) - 1))
          * ∑ i, (c i - (n : ℝ)⁻¹ * ∑ j, c j) ^ 2

hypotheses.label: the split exists
hypotheses.note: The sample size does not exceed the population size; otherwise the sample space is empty.

hypotheses.label: at least two items
hypotheses.note: The factor $n-1$ is a denominator, so the degenerate case $n \le 1$ must be excluded.

formalizationNotes: Randomness is carried by the finite-set model — the sample space is the collection of $m$-element subsets, uniformly weighted — rather than by a random permutation, because every identity is then a counting statement about how many subsets contain a given index or pair of indices. Two conventions are worth flagging: the expectation operator is a normalized counting average, which returns the junk value $0$ when the sample space is empty, so every identity carries the hypothesis $m \le n$ — for $m > n$ there are no $m$-element subsets and both sides would report that convention rather than the intended moments, and all subtraction is performed in the reals, never as truncated natural subtraction, which would silently change the identity at $m = 0$.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer, Cham, 2022.
reference.biblio: These are the classical moments of the hypergeometric sampling scheme, presented in Lehmann and Romano (2022, §12.2) as the arithmetic backbone of permutation inference: every linear statistic of a two-sample permutation test is of the form $\sum_i c_i W_i$ for a coefficient vector built from the pooled data. The finite-population correction factor $m(n-m)/(n(n-1))$ is what distinguishes sampling without replacement from the binomial case, and the $O(1/m)$ bound on the group average is the input to Hoeffding's (1951) combinatorial central limit theorem.

title: Pólya's theorem: pointwise convergence of distribution functions to a continuous limit is uniform
informal: Let $F_1, F_2, \ldots$ and $F$ be real functions on $\mathbb{R}$. Assume each $F_n$ is nondecreasing and is a distribution function in the sense that it tends to $0$ at $-\infty$ and to $1$ at $+\infty$; assume the limit $F$ has the same tail limits and is moreover continuous; and assume $F_n(x) \to F(x)$ for every $x$. Then the convergence is uniform: $$\sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} \bigl|F_n(x) - F(x)\bigr| \;\longrightarrow\; 0 .$$ This is the bridge from convergence in distribution to "the approximation is uniform in the argument", which every calibration argument — critical values, $p$-values, bootstrap thresholds — needs before passing from a pointwise limit law to a statement about the level actually attained.
summary: If distribution functions converge pointwise to a continuous distribution function, the convergence is uniform on the whole line.
leanSignature:
theorem tendstoUniformly_of_monotone_of_continuous {Fn : ℕ → ℝ → ℝ} {F : ℝ → ℝ}
    (hmono : ∀ n, Monotone (Fn n))
    (hFn_atBot : ∀ n, Tendsto (Fn n) atBot (𝓝 0))
    (hFn_atTop : ∀ n, Tendsto (Fn n) atTop (𝓝 1))
    (hFcont : Continuous F)
    (hF_atBot : Tendsto F atBot (𝓝 0))
    (hF_atTop : Tendsto F atTop (𝓝 1))
    (hconv : ∀ x : ℝ, Tendsto (fun n => Fn n x) atTop (𝓝 (F x))) :
    TendstoUniformly Fn F atTop

hypotheses.label: monotone approximants
hypotheses.note: Each approximating function is nondecreasing; monotonicity of the limit is not assumed but derived.

hypotheses.label: approximant tail limits
hypotheses.note: Genuinely needed, not cosmetic: without them $F_n = F - n\mathbf{1}_{(-\infty,-n)}$ is a counterexample.

hypotheses.label: continuous limit
hypotheses.note: The only place continuity is used is in choosing a finite grid on which the limit increments are small.

hypotheses.label: pointwise convergence
hypotheses.note: Convergence is assumed only pointwise; uniformity is the conclusion.

formalizationNotes: Monotonicity of the limit is *not* a hypothesis: it is forced by monotonicity of the approximants together with pointwise convergence, and is derived in the proof. The tail limits of the approximants, by contrast, are genuinely needed — the sequence $F_n = F - n\,\mathbf{1}_{(-\infty,-n)}$ is nondecreasing and converges pointwise to a continuous distribution function while the supremum distance diverges. The statement is purely about real functions, with no measure theory: it applies to any family of distribution functions, however produced.

reference.formal: G. Pólya, "Über den zentralen Grenzwertsatz der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung und das Momentenproblem", *Mathematische Zeitschrift* **8** (1920), 171–181.
reference.biblio: The theorem is due to G. Pólya (1920), where it is used to upgrade the central limit theorem from a pointwise to a uniform approximation statement. Lehmann and Romano (2022, §11.2) record it as the standard tool for turning weak convergence into a uniform-in-the-argument approximation, which is what any statement about the attained level of a test requires. The formalization is faithful, with the limit's monotonicity derived rather than assumed.

title: Halmos–Savage equivalent countable mixture
informal: Let $\{P_\theta : \theta \in \Theta\}$ be a family of probability measures on a measurable space, and suppose the family is dominated by a $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$, i.e. $P_\theta \ll \mu$ for every $\theta$. Then there exist parameters $\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots$ and strictly positive weights $c_1, c_2, \ldots$ summing to $1$ such that the countable mixture $$\lambda \;=\; \sum_{i} c_i\, P_{\theta_i}$$ dominates every member of the family, $P_\theta \ll \lambda$ for all $\theta$, and has exactly the common null sets of the family: for every set $A$, $$\lambda(A) = 0 \iff P_\theta(A) = 0 \text{ for every } \theta .$$ The point is that $\lambda$ is built *from the family itself*, so a density with respect to $\lambda$ is automatically a legitimate statistical object, whereas densities against an arbitrary dominating measure are not. Every later step in the theory of sufficiency for dominated families — the factorization criterion, minimal sufficiency, the likelihood-ratio construction — is run against this $\lambda$.
summary: A family of probability measures dominated by a $\sigma$-finite measure admits a countable mixture of its own members that is equivalent to the whole family.
leanSignature:
theorem exists_equivalent_countable_mixture {Θ 𝓧 : Type*} [MeasurableSpace 𝓧]
    [Nonempty Θ]
    (P : Θ → Measure 𝓧)
    [∀ θ, IsProbabilityMeasure (P θ)]
    (μ : Measure 𝓧)
    [SigmaFinite μ]
    (hdom : ∀ θ, P θ ≪ μ) :
    ∃ (θs : ℕ → Θ) (c : ℕ → ℝ≥0∞) (lam : Measure 𝓧),
      lam = Measure.sum (fun i => c i • P (θs i)) ∧
      (∀ i, 0 < c i) ∧ (∑' i, c i) = 1 ∧
      (∀ θ, P θ ≪ lam) ∧
      ∀ A : Set 𝓧, (∀ θ, P θ A = 0) ↔ lam A = 0

hypotheses.label: dominated family
hypotheses.note: Every member is absolutely continuous with respect to a fixed $\sigma$-finite reference measure; this is the definition of a dominated family and the lemma is false without $\sigma$-finiteness.

formalizationNotes: The null-set equivalence is stated for an *arbitrary* set, with no measurability hypothesis. This is both safe and strictly stronger: the countable-sum vanishing criterion holds without measurability, and absolute continuity is itself defined by an implication between outer-measure values of arbitrary sets, so callers holding only a measurable set lose nothing. Domination is carried as an explicit hypothesis against an explicit reference measure rather than packaged into a structure, so the lemma applies verbatim to families dominated by a measure produced in the middle of another proof. The index type is assumed inhabited, which lets a genuinely finite selection be padded by repetition; repeating an index only merges weights for the same member and changes neither the null sets nor absolute continuity.

reference.formal: P. R. Halmos and L. J. Savage, "Application of the Radon–Nikodym theorem to the theory of sufficient statistics", *Annals of Mathematical Statistics* **20** (1949), 225–241.
reference.biblio: The lemma and the equivalent-mixture device are due to P. R. Halmos and L. J. Savage (1949), who introduced them precisely in order to prove the factorization criterion for sufficiency in dominated families: without replacing the arbitrary dominating measure by a mixture of members of the family, densities need not behave measurably in the parameter. Lehmann and Romano (2022, §2.6) use it in the same way for Theorem 2.6.2. The formalized statement is the existence half, with the null-set equivalence strengthened to arbitrary (not necessarily measurable) sets.

title: Measurable selection of minimizers of a parametrized convex scan
informal: Let $f(\omega, \cdot)$ be a family of functions of a real "scan" variable with values in $[0, \infty]$, indexed by a parameter $\omega$ in a measurable space, and assume the family is jointly measurable in the pair. Assume that for every $\omega$ the function $f(\omega, \cdot)$ is convex, lower semicontinuous, coercive — it tends to $+\infty$ as the scan variable leaves every compact set — and is finite at the origin. Then there is a *measurable* map $\omega \mapsto u(\omega)$ with $$f\bigl(\omega, u(\omega)\bigr) \;=\; \inf_{v \in \mathbb{R}} f(\omega, v) \qquad \text{for every } \omega .$$ This is the brick that makes "minimize the conditional risk pointwise, then read the answer off as an estimator" legitimate: a pointwise minimizer must be a measurable function of the conditioning variable before it can be called an estimator at all.
summary: A jointly measurable family of convex, lower-semicontinuous, coercive functions of a real variable, each finite at the origin, admits a measurable selection of minimizers.
leanSignature:
theorem exists_measurable_argmin_of_convex_of_finite {Ω : Type*} [MeasurableSpace Ω]
    {f : Ω → ℝ → ℝ≥0∞} (hf : Measurable (Function.uncurry f))
    (hlsc : ∀ ω, LowerSemicontinuous (f ω))
    (hconv : ∀ ω, ConvexOn ℝ≥0 Set.univ (f ω))
    (hcoer : ∀ ω, Tendsto (f ω) (cocompact ℝ) (𝓝 (⊤ : ℝ≥0∞)))
    (hf0 : ∀ ω, f ω 0 < ⊤) :
    ∃ u : Ω → ℝ, Measurable u ∧ ∀ ω, f ω (u ω) = ⨅ v : ℝ, f ω v

hypotheses.label: jointly measurable
hypotheses.note: Measurability in the pair (parameter, scan variable), not merely in each separately.

hypotheses.label: lower semicontinuous
hypotheses.note: Weaker than continuity; the weakening is what an unbounded convex loss forces, since the objective may jump to $+\infty$.

hypotheses.label: convex in the scan
hypotheses.note: Convexity of each member; combined with one finiteness point it makes the rational-relaxed-sublevel construction valid.

hypotheses.label: coercive
hypotheses.note: The objective blows up off compact sets, which forces the minimum to be attained.

hypotheses.label: finite at the origin
hypotheses.note: One finiteness point; without it a convex lower-semicontinuous objective can be finite only at a single irrational point, where the minimum is invisible to a countable rational scan and the construction breaks.

formalizationNotes: Continuity is not weakened to plain lower semicontinuity, because the selection is built from rational-relaxed sublevel sets: for a merely lower-semicontinuous convex objective whose finiteness domain is a single irrational point the minimum is invisible to the rationals, so the infimum over the rationals differs from the true infimum and the construction no longer returns a minimizer. Convexity together with the single finiteness point at the origin excludes exactly that configuration. The selection is the *leftmost* minimizer, so it is canonical. Two Lean-side conventions: convexity is taken with nonnegative-real coefficients, which for $[0,\infty]$-valued functions of a real variable is the usual midpoint-convexity condition and is the only predicate that typechecks; and coercivity is stated as convergence to $+\infty$ along the cocompact filter, not "at infinity" in the extended-order sense, which for $[0,\infty]$-valued functions would degenerate to "equals $+\infty$ off a compact set". An almost-everywhere variant, in which the finiteness point is only required for almost every parameter, is proved alongside and is what the conditional-risk consumers use.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer, New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Measurable selection of minimizers is the silent hypothesis in every construction of a minimum-risk equivariant or Bayes estimator: Lehmann and Casella (1998, §3.1, Theorem 1.10 and Corollary 1.11) minimize a conditional risk pointwise in the conditioning variable and then treat the minimizer as an estimator. The general theory is the Kuratowski–Ryll-Nardzewski measurable selection theorem; what is proved here is the elementary special case sufficient for convex losses on a one-dimensional scan, obtained by selecting the leftmost minimizer and testing relaxed sublevel sets on the rationals.

title: Randomized test (critical function)
informal: A **randomized test**, or *critical function*, for a statistical model on a sample space $\mathcal{X}$ is a measurable function $\varphi : \mathcal{X} \to [0,1]$: on observing $x$ the null hypothesis is rejected with probability $\varphi(x)$ and accepted with probability $1 - \varphi(x)$. Nonrandomized tests are the special case in which $\varphi$ takes only the values $0$ and $1$, that is $\varphi = \mathbf{1}_R$ for a rejection region $R \subseteq \mathcal{X}$. Against a model $\{P_\theta : \theta \in \Theta\}$ the **power function** of $\varphi$ is $$ \beta_\varphi(\theta) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_\theta \varphi(X) \;=\; \int \varphi \, dP_\theta , $$ the test has **level** $\alpha$ on a null set $\Theta_0$ when $\beta_\varphi(\theta) \le \alpha$ for every $\theta \in \Theta_0$, and its **size** is $\sup_{\theta \in \Theta_0} \beta_\varphi(\theta)$. The whole optimality theory of Chapter 3 is a comparison of power functions inside this class.
summary: A randomized test is a measurable function on the sample space with values in the unit interval, giving the probability with which each observation leads to rejection.
leanSignature:
def IsCriticalFn (φ : 𝓧 → ℝ) : Prop :=
  Measurable φ ∧ ∀ x, φ x ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The randomized-test formulation, the power function, and the programme of maximizing power subject to a bound on the size are due to Neyman and Pearson (1933). The formalization keeps the predicates unbundled — measurability and the range condition form one predicate, the level condition another — so that theorems can widen or narrow the competitor class explicitly rather than through a fixed bundled structure.

formalizationNotes: Powers are real Bochner integrals: for probability measures and $0 \le \varphi \le 1$ they are automatically finite, so no extended-real bookkeeping is needed at the definition layer. Level, size, uniform optimality, unbiasedness, similarity and Neyman structure are all defined in the same file in terms of this predicate and the power function.

title: Uniformly most powerful test
summary: A test is uniformly most powerful at level α when it has level α on the null set and is at least as powerful as every other level-α test at every alternative.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The optimality criterion is that of Neyman and Pearson (1933); the uniform version, and the recognition that it is attainable only for special problems (one-sided hypotheses under a monotone likelihood ratio, and two-sided hypotheses in a one-parameter exponential family), is the organizing theme of Chapter 3 of the reference text. In the formalization the competitor class is quantified explicitly, so weakening it (for instance to unbiased competitors, giving the UMP-unbiased notion) is a visible change of statement.

formalizationNotes: Unbiasedness, UMP-unbiasedness, similarity and Neyman structure are defined alongside in the same file, each as a separate predicate over the same critical-function class; nothing is bundled into a structure, so a theorem's competitor class is always readable off its statement.

title: Validity of the p-value of a nested family of rejection regions
informal: Let $\{R_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in \mathbb{R}}$ be a family of rejection regions in the sample space which is nested in the significance level, so that $R_\alpha \subseteq R_{\alpha'}$ whenever $\alpha \le \alpha'$, for which no observation is rejected at a negative significance level and every observation is rejected at some level strictly below one. Define the **p-value** of an observation $x$ as the smallest level at which it is rejected, $$ \hat p(x) \;=\; \inf\{\alpha : x \in R_\alpha\} . $$ If each region is valid at its own level, in the sense that $\mathbb{P}_\theta(R_\alpha) \le \alpha$ for every $0 < \alpha < 1$ and every null parameter $\theta$, then $\hat p$ is **super-uniform** under every null distribution: $$ \mathbb{P}_\theta\{\hat p(X) \le u\} \;\le\; u \qquad \text{for all } u \ge 0 \text{ and all } \theta \in \Theta_0 . $$ Consequently, rejecting when $\hat p(X) \le \alpha$ is a test of level $\alpha$.
summary: The p-value obtained from a nested family of valid rejection regions is super-uniform under every null distribution.
leanSignature:
theorem superUniform_nestedPValue (P : Θ → Measure 𝓧) [∀ θ, IsProbabilityMeasure (P θ)]
    (Θ₀ : Set Θ) {R : ℝ → Set 𝓧}
    (hmono : Monotone R)
    (hR_neg : ∀ α : ℝ, α < 0 → R α = ∅)
    (hR_exh : ∀ x : 𝓧, ∃ α < 1, x ∈ R α)
    (hvalid : ∀ α : ℝ, 0 < α → α < 1 → ∀ θ ∈ Θ₀, P θ (R α) ≤ ENNReal.ofReal α) :
    ∀ θ ∈ Θ₀, SuperUniform (nestedPValue R) (P θ)

hypotheses.label: nested regions
hypotheses.note: The rejection regions increase with the significance level, so rejecting at a smaller level is a stronger verdict.

hypotheses.label: no negative-level rejection
hypotheses.note: Regions at negative levels are empty; this makes the set of rejecting levels bounded below, so the infimum is not junk.

hypotheses.label: exhaustive family
hypotheses.note: Every observation is rejected at some level below one, so the set of rejecting levels is nonempty.

hypotheses.label: valid regions
hypotheses.note: Each region has null probability at most its own level, uniformly over the null set.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: Significance levels attained by the data go back to Fisher (1925); the systematic treatment of the p-value as a random variable, and of its null distribution, is due to Bahadur (1960), while the underlying nested family of rejection regions is the Neyman–Pearson (1933) construction. The formalization proves the inequality (super-uniformity) rather than the exact-uniformity statement available when the regions have exactly their nominal size, and states the conclusion through the same super-uniformity predicate used by the multiple-testing results, so p-values produced here feed the false-discovery-rate theorems unchanged.

formalizationNotes: The p-value is the literal infimum, so the two non-degeneracy conditions are carried explicitly: without them the junk value of an infimum over an empty or unbounded-below set would be $0$ and would destroy super-uniformity (take all regions empty). Measurability of the regions is *not* assumed for super-uniformity — the argument only compares measures of nested sets — and reappears only where an integral is formed, in the companion statement that the p-value test has level $\alpha$. Only the inequality direction is formalized; exact validity of the regions would give the exact-uniform conclusion by the same argument.

title: Test inversion produces confidence sets
informal: Suppose that for each parameter value $\theta$ we are given a measurable acceptance region $A(\theta) \subseteq \mathcal{X}$, and that the nonrandomized test that rejects the simple hypothesis $H(\theta)$ off $A(\theta)$ has level $\alpha$, i.e. $\mathbb{P}_\theta\{X \notin A(\theta)\} \le \alpha$, where $\alpha \ge 0$. Then the inverted family $$ S(x) \;=\; \{\theta : x \in A(\theta)\} $$ of parameter values not rejected on observing $x$ is a family of confidence sets at confidence level $1 - \alpha$: $$ \mathbb{P}_\theta\{\theta \in S(X)\} \;\ge\; 1 - \alpha \qquad \text{for every } \theta . $$ The converse inversion also holds: the slices of any confidence family at level $\gamma$ are acceptance regions of tests of level $1 - \gamma$.
summary: Inverting a family of level-α tests, one for each parameter value, yields a family of confidence sets at confidence level 1 − α.

    (hα : 0 ≤ α)
    (hmeas : ∀ θ, MeasurableSet (A θ))
    (hlevel : ∀ θ, IsLevel P {θ} (acceptanceTest (A θ)) α) :
    IsConfidenceFamily P (confidenceSet A) (1 - α)

hypotheses.label: nonnegative level
hypotheses.note: The significance level is nonnegative; for negative α the coverage statement is vacuous.

hypotheses.label: measurable regions
hypotheses.note: Each acceptance region is measurable, so that the associated indicator really is a test.

hypotheses.label: level-α tests
hypotheses.note: For every θ, the test with acceptance region A(θ) has level α against the simple hypothesis H(θ).

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: Confidence sets, the confidence level, and the inversion of a family of tests are due to Neyman (1937). The formalization states coverage in the extended nonnegative reals, which keeps the definition free of real-valued conversion side conditions and makes a negative confidence level vacuous rather than junk; the converse direction (confidence sets produce tests) is stated separately in the same file, so the duality is available in both directions.

formalizationNotes: Measurability of the acceptance regions is a Lean-side requirement, not a weakening of the book: a critical function must be measurable for its power to be defined. The acceptance region enters through the nonrandomized test given by the indicator of its complement, so the book's level condition becomes a level statement about that test.

title: Optimality transfers along the test/confidence duality
informal: Suppose that the significance level satisfies $\alpha \ge 0$ and $\alpha \le 1$, that each acceptance region $A(\theta_0)$ is measurable, and that for every null value $\theta_0$ the test with acceptance region $A(\theta_0)$ is uniformly most powerful at level $\alpha$ for $H(\theta_0)$ against the alternatives $K(\theta_0)$. Then the inverted family $S(x) = \{\theta : x \in A(\theta)\}$ is **uniformly most accurate** at confidence level $1 - \alpha$: it has confidence level $1 - \alpha$, and for every competing confidence family $S'$ of the same level, every $\theta_0$, and every $\theta \in K(\theta_0)$, $$ \mathbb{P}_\theta\{\theta_0 \in S(X)\} \;\le\; \mathbb{P}_\theta\{\theta_0 \in S'(X)\} . $$ That is, $S$ covers each parameter value other than the true one with the smallest possible probability, uniformly over the parameters at which the covered value is not the true one.
summary: Inverting a family of uniformly most powerful level-α tests gives a uniformly most accurate family of confidence sets at level 1 − α.

hypotheses.note: The significance level is nonnegative.

hypotheses.label: level at most one
hypotheses.note: The significance level is at most one, so the confidence level 1 − α is nonnegative.

hypotheses.label: measurable regions
hypotheses.note: Each acceptance region is measurable, so the inverted family has measurable slices.

hypotheses.label: UMP tests
hypotheses.note: For each null value the corresponding test is uniformly most powerful at level α against its alternative set.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The accuracy criterion for confidence sets and its link with the power of the underlying tests are due to Neyman (1937), resting on the optimality theory of Neyman and Pearson (1933). The formalization quantifies only over competitor families whose slices are measurable — the argument inverts a competitor into a genuine test, and coverage of a non-measurable family is not a probability statement in the first place.

formalizationNotes: Only the one-sided framing is stated: for each null value the competitor class is the tests of $H(\theta_0)$ against $K(\theta_0)$, and the conclusion compares the probabilities of covering $\theta_0$ at parameter points of $K(\theta_0)$. The specialization to one-sided confidence *bounds* under a monotone likelihood ratio is a separate statement (see the uniformly most accurate lower bound).

title: Neyman–Pearson fundamental lemma: existence
informal: Let $P_0$ and $P_1$ be probability measures on a sample space, with $P_0$ having density $p_0$ with respect to a $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$ and $P_1$ having density $p_1$ with respect to the same $\mu$. For any level $0 \le \alpha \le 1$ there exist a threshold $C \in [0, \infty]$ and a boundary weight $\gamma \in [0,1]$ such that the **likelihood-ratio test** $$ \varphi(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} 1, & p_1(x) > C\, p_0(x), \\ \gamma, & p_1(x) = C\, p_0(x), \\ 0, & p_1(x) < C\, p_0(x), \end{cases} $$ has size **exactly** $\alpha$ under the null, $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}\varphi = \alpha$, and is most powerful at level $\alpha$ for testing $P_0$ against $P_1$: every critical function $\psi$ with $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}\psi \le \alpha$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}\psi \le \mathbb{E}_{P_1}\varphi$.
summary: For every level there exist a threshold and a boundary randomization for which the likelihood-ratio test has exactly that size and is most powerful.
leanSignature:
theorem exists_mostPowerful
    (μ : Measure 𝓧) [SigmaFinite μ]
    (P₀ P₁ : Measure 𝓧) [IsProbabilityMeasure P₀] [IsProbabilityMeasure P₁]
    {p₀ p₁ : 𝓧 → ℝ}
    (h₀ : HasDensity μ p₀ P₀)
    (h₁ : HasDensity μ p₁ P₁)
    {α : ℝ} (hα : α ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1) :
    ∃ (C : ℝ≥0∞) (γ : ℝ), γ ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1 ∧
      powerAgainst P₀ (npTest p₀ p₁ C γ) = α ∧
      IsMostPowerful P₀ P₁ α (npTest p₀ p₁ C γ)

hypotheses.label: null density
hypotheses.note: The null distribution possesses a nonnegative measurable density with respect to the dominating measure.

hypotheses.label: alternative density
hypotheses.note: The alternative distribution possesses a density with respect to the same dominating measure; taking μ = P₀ + P₁ always works.

hypotheses.label: level in [0,1]
hypotheses.note: The nominal level is a free choice in the closed unit interval; both endpoints are covered.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The lemma, the randomized-test formulation and the existence/sufficiency/necessity trichotomy are due to Neyman and Pearson (1933), with the systematic treatment of boundary randomization in Neyman and Pearson (1936); measure-theoretic formulations under an arbitrary dominating measure were given by Dantzig and Wald (1951). The formalization proves the full trichotomy: existence with exact size (this statement), sufficiency of the likelihood-ratio shape, and its necessity almost everywhere.

formalizationNotes: The threshold is an *extended* nonnegative real. This is what makes the corner $\alpha = 0$ available ($C = \infty$, rejecting only on a null set) and turns the convention $0 \cdot \infty = 0$, used exactly at that corner, into ambient arithmetic rather than a side convention; the comparison is therefore made between extended nonnegative reals and the ratio $p_1/p_0$ is never formed. Both endpoints $\alpha \in \{0,1\}$ are covered, the second by $C = 0$ and $\gamma = 1$.

title: Neyman–Pearson fundamental lemma: necessity of the likelihood-ratio shape
informal: Let $P_0$ have density $p_0$ and $P_1$ have density $p_1$ with respect to a $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$, and let $\varphi$ be a most powerful test at level $\alpha$ for $P_0$ against $P_1$. Then there is a threshold $C \in [0,\infty]$ for which $\varphi$ has the likelihood-ratio shape almost everywhere with respect to $\mu$: $\varphi = 1$ a.e. on $\{p_1 > C p_0\}$ and $\varphi = 0$ a.e. on $\{p_1 < C p_0\}$, with no constraint on the boundary set $\{p_1 = C p_0\}$. Moreover $\varphi$ has size exactly $\alpha$, $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}\varphi = \alpha$, **unless** there already exists a test of size strictly less than $\alpha$ whose power against $P_1$ equals $1$.
summary: Every most powerful level-α test has likelihood-ratio shape almost everywhere, and has size exactly α unless a smaller-size test already has power one.

theorem npTest_necessity
    (μ : Measure 𝓧) [SigmaFinite μ]

    (h₀ : HasDensity μ p₀ P₀)
    (h₁ : HasDensity μ p₁ P₁)
    (hφ : IsMostPowerful P₀ P₁ α φ) :
    (∃ C : ℝ≥0∞, HasNPShape μ p₀ p₁ C φ) ∧
      ((¬ ∃ ψ, IsCriticalFn ψ ∧ powerAgainst P₀ ψ < α ∧ powerAgainst P₁ ψ = 1) →
        powerAgainst P₀ φ = α)

hypotheses.label: null density
hypotheses.note: The null distribution has a density with respect to the dominating measure.

hypotheses.label: alternative density
hypotheses.note: The alternative distribution has a density with respect to the same dominating measure.

hypotheses.label: most powerful test
hypotheses.note: The property being reverse-engineered: φ maximizes power against the alternative among all level-α critical functions.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The necessity half of the fundamental lemma is Neyman and Pearson (1933); the measure-theoretic form, in which the shape is only claimed almost everywhere and the exact-size clause carries its escape hypothesis, follows Dantzig and Wald (1951). The formalization transcribes both clauses exactly as stated: nothing is claimed on the boundary set, and the exact-size conclusion is guarded by its escape hypothesis rather than asserted unconditionally.

formalizationNotes: The escape clause is genuine and is stated as a hypothesis of the second conjunct only: when a test of size below $\alpha$ already attains power $1$, a most powerful test need not exhaust the level. The threshold ranges over the extended nonnegative reals, so the degenerate regimes $C = 0$ and $C = \infty$ are both handled inside the statement rather than excluded.

title: Strict unbiasedness of the most powerful test
informal: Let $P_0$ have density $p_0$ and $P_1$ have density $p_1$ with respect to a $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$, fix a level $0 < \alpha < 1$, and let $\varphi$ be most powerful at level $\alpha$ for testing $P_0$ against $P_1$. If the null and the alternative are different distributions, $P_0 \ne P_1$, then $$ \mathbb{E}_{P_1}\varphi \;>\; \alpha : $$ the most powerful test is *strictly unbiased*, its power exceeding its level. In the excluded degenerate case $P_0 = P_1$ every most powerful test has power exactly $\alpha$, so the two statements together settle the power of a most powerful test in all cases.
summary: For a nondegenerate level, the power of a most powerful test strictly exceeds the level unless the null and the alternative are the same distribution.

hypotheses.label: alternative density
hypotheses.note: The alternative distribution has a density with respect to the same dominating measure.

hypotheses.note: φ maximizes power against the alternative among all level-α critical functions.

hypotheses.note: The two distributions differ; this is the stated exception of the classical corollary.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The corollary is Neyman and Pearson's (1933) observation that the fundamental lemma automatically delivers an unbiased test, since the constant test $\varphi \equiv \alpha$ is a level-$\alpha$ competitor with power $\alpha$. The formalization also states the degenerate case honestly as a separate result: when the two distributions coincide, every most powerful test has power exactly equal to the level, so the strict inequality genuinely requires the exception.

formalizationNotes: The endpoints $\alpha \in \{0,1\}$ are excluded because the strict inequality cannot hold there. The companion statement for the excluded case ($P_0 = P_1$ forces power exactly $\alpha$) is proved in the same file, so no case is left implicit.

title: Generalized fundamental lemma: existence and necessity of the multipliers
informal: Let $f_1, \dots, f_{m+1}$ be measurable and $\mu$-integrable functions on the sample space, and consider the class of critical functions obeying the $m$ side conditions $\int \varphi f_i \, d\mu = c_i$ for $i = 1, \dots, m$, the objective being to maximize $\int \varphi f_{m+1} \, d\mu$. Suppose the constraint vector $(c_1, \dots, c_m)$ is an interior point of the attainable-moment set $M = \{(\int \varphi f_1 d\mu, \dots, \int \varphi f_m d\mu) : \varphi \text{ a critical function}\}$. Then there exist multipliers $k_1, \dots, k_m$ such that 1. some critical function satisfies the side conditions and has the **multiplier shape** $$ \varphi(x) = 1 \text{ where } f_{m+1}(x) > \sum_i k_i f_i(x), \qquad \varphi(x) = 0 \text{ where } f_{m+1}(x) < \sum_i k_i f_i(x) ; $$ 2. **every** maximizer in the constraint class has that same shape almost everywhere with respect to $\mu$, for the *same* multipliers. The attainable-moment set is itself convex and closed.
summary: At an inner point of the attainable-moment set there are undetermined multipliers realized by some optimal test, and every maximizer is forced to have the corresponding multiplier shape.
leanSignature:
theorem exists_multipliers_of_max {m : ℕ}

    (f : Fin (m + 1) → 𝓧 → ℝ)

    (hint : ∀ i, Integrable (f i) μ)
    {c : Fin m → ℝ}
    (hc : c ∈ interior (momentSet μ fun i => f i.castSucc)) :
    ∃ k : Fin m → ℝ,
      (∃ φ, IsCriticalFn φ ∧ (∀ i, ∫ x, φ x * f i.castSucc x ∂μ = c i) ∧
        HasMultiplierShape μ f k φ) ∧
      ∀ φ, IsCriticalFn φ → (∀ i, ∫ x, φ x * f i.castSucc x ∂μ = c i) →
        (∀ ψ, IsCriticalFn ψ → (∀ i, ∫ x, ψ x * f i.castSucc x ∂μ = c i) →
          ∫ x, ψ x * f (Fin.last m) x ∂μ ≤ ∫ x, φ x * f (Fin.last m) x ∂μ) →
        HasMultiplierShape μ f k φ

hypotheses.note: Each of the m+1 functions of the problem is measurable, so the moments are meaningful.

hypotheses.label: integrable data
hypotheses.note: Each of the m+1 functions is integrable with respect to the dominating measure — the printed hypothesis.

hypotheses.label: inner point
hypotheses.note: The constraint vector lies in the interior of the attainable-moment set; on the boundary the multiplier characterization genuinely fails.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The extension of the fundamental lemma to several side conditions is due to Neyman and Pearson (1936); its definitive measure-theoretic form, including the analysis of what happens when the inner-point condition fails, is due to Dantzig and Wald (1951). The formalization bundles both halves of the inner-point clause under a single existential over the multipliers, so that the multipliers exhibited by the supporting hyperplane are literally the ones every maximizer must use; splitting them would silently weaken the result.

formalizationNotes: The classical statement is set on a Euclidean sample space, the only role of that assumption being to support weak compactness of the class of critical functions; the formalization works over an arbitrary measurable space with a $\sigma$-finite dominating measure, which is a strict generalization. The multiplier shape is stated almost everywhere rather than pointwise, which strengthens the sufficiency direction and makes this necessity statement land exactly on the book's conclusion. The inner-point hypothesis is transcribed as membership in the *ambient* interior; upgrading it to the weaker relative-interior hypothesis is a documented gap.

title: A test with prescribed sizes and strictly larger power
informal: Let $P_1, \dots, P_{m+1}$ be probability measures with densities $p_1, \dots, p_{m+1}$ with respect to a $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$, and let the level satisfy $\alpha > 0$ and $\alpha < 1$. Then exactly one of the following holds: 1. $p_{m+1}$ is almost everywhere a linear combination of the others, i.e. there are constants $k_1, \dots, k_m$ with $p_{m+1} = \sum_{i} k_i p_i$ almost everywhere with respect to $\mu$; or 2. there is a critical function $\varphi$ with $\mathbb{E}_{P_i}\varphi = \alpha$ for every $i = 1, \dots, m$ and $\mathbb{E}_{P_{m+1}}\varphi > \alpha$. In words: unless the alternative is degenerately tied to the null distributions, one can always keep the size at $\alpha$ against all of them while doing strictly better than chance against the alternative.
summary: Given m + 1 densities and a nondegenerate level, either the last density is almost everywhere a linear combination of the others, or there is a test of size exactly α against each of the first m whose power against the last strictly exceeds α.

hypotheses.label: level below one
hypotheses.note: The level is strictly below one; at α = 1 the strict inequality fails.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.

title: Reduction of a composite null to a simple one
informal: To test the composite hypothesis $H : \{P_\theta, \theta \in \omega\}$ against a simple alternative $G$, replace $H$ by the **simple** hypothesis $H_\Lambda$ whose density is the mixture $h_\Lambda(x) = \int_\omega f_\theta(x) \, d\Lambda(\theta)$ against a prior $\Lambda$. Assume the family is jointly measurable in the parameter and the observation — which is what makes the mixture a genuine density — and that the prior is carried by $\omega$, $\Lambda(\omega) = 1$. If $\varphi$ is most powerful at level $\alpha \ge 0$ for testing the mixture $H_\Lambda$ against $G$ and, in addition, $\varphi$ keeps level $\alpha$ against every member of the composite null, $\mathbb{E}_\theta \varphi \le \alpha$ for all $\theta \in \omega$, then $\varphi$ is most powerful at level $\alpha$ for the original composite problem: every critical function $\psi$ of level $\alpha$ on $\omega$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}_G \psi \le \mathbb{E}_G \varphi$. Uniqueness transfers as well.
summary: A most powerful test of the mixed hypothesis that happens to keep its level against every member of the composite null is most powerful for the composite problem.

reference.biblio: Reducing a composite hypothesis by averaging its members against a weight function goes back to Wald, and the notion of a least favorable prior is central to Wald (1950); the existence theory and the transfer results formalized here are due to Lehmann (1952), resting on the optimality of the likelihood-ratio test of Neyman and Pearson (1933). The formalization carries the prior as a measure on the whole parameter space together with the condition that it charges $\omega$ fully, rather than as a measure on a subtype, so that the power function and the level predicate remain usable verbatim.

title: The prior is least favorable
informal: Keep the mixture set-up of the previous statement: the composite null $\{P_\theta, \theta \in \omega\}$, a simple alternative $G$, a jointly measurable family of densities and a prior $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda(\omega) = 1$. Write $\beta(\Lambda)$ for the largest power against $G$ available to a test of level $\alpha \ge 0$ for the mixed hypothesis $H_\Lambda$. If some test $\varphi$ is most powerful at level $\alpha$ for the mixed problem and that test keeps level $\alpha$ against every member of the composite null, then $\Lambda$ is **least favorable**: $$ \beta(\Lambda) \;\le\; \beta(\Lambda') \qquad \text{for every prior } \Lambda' \text{ carried by } \omega . $$ No prior over $\omega$ makes less power available; equivalently, $\Lambda$ makes the testing problem as hard as it can be.
summary: A prior whose mixed-problem optimum keeps its level against the whole composite null minimizes the power available to level-α tests, i.e. it is least favorable.

hypotheses.label: optimal for the mixture
hypotheses.note: φ is most powerful at level α for the simple problem obtained by mixing the null over the prior.

hypotheses.label: level on the whole null
hypotheses.note: That optimum keeps size at most α against every member of the composite null.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The concept of a least favorable distribution is Wald's (1950); the characterization formalized here — that a prior whose mixed optimum is feasible for the composite problem is least favorable — is due to Lehmann (1952). The maximum attainable power is defined as a supremum over level-$\alpha$ competitors; for a nonnegative level that set contains the constant test $\varphi \equiv \alpha$ and is bounded above by one, so it is a genuine supremum rather than a junk value.

For a negative level the competitor set would be empty and the supremum would take its junk value; all statements therefore carry $\alpha \ge 0$.

title: Monotone likelihood ratio
informal:
Let $\{p_\theta : \theta \in \Theta\}$ be a family of densities on a sample space, with $\Theta$ ordered, and let $T$ be a real-valued statistic. The family has **monotone likelihood ratio (MLR)** in $T$ when, for every pair $\theta < \theta'$, the ratio $p_{\theta'}/p_\theta$ is a nondecreasing function of $T$. Division-free — and this is the form used throughout — the condition reads
$$ T(x) \le T(y) \ \text{ and } \ \theta < \theta' \quad \Longrightarrow \quad p_{\theta'}(x)\, p_\theta(y) \;\le\; p_\theta(x)\, p_{\theta'}(y) , $$
that is, total positivity of order two in the pair (parameter, statistic). The one-parameter exponential family with a strictly increasing natural parametrization has monotone likelihood ratio in its natural statistic, and this is the standing hypothesis of the one-sided optimality theory.
summary: A family of densities on an ordered parameter set has monotone likelihood ratio in a statistic when the ratio of any two of its members is a nondecreasing function of that statistic.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The monotone-likelihood-ratio condition and the resulting one-sided optimal tests are due to Karlin and Rubin (1956), with antecedents in the binomial and hypergeometric analyses of Neyman and Pearson (1936); total positivity is systematized in Karlin's later monograph. The formalization records the cross-product (total positivity) form, which avoids division junk entirely and is exactly what the Neyman–Pearson-style arguments consume.

formalizationNotes: The definition deliberately omits the classical non-degeneracy clause that $P_\theta \ne P_{\theta'}$ for $\theta < \theta'$. That clause is irrelevant for existence and optimality of the one-sided test, but it is exactly what makes the power function *strictly* increasing (a constant family satisfies the cross-product condition vacuously); it is therefore carried as an explicit hypothesis of the strict-monotonicity result and of the confidence-bound corollary, and nowhere else. Only a preorder on the parameter set is needed for the definition; the one-sided testing theorems assume a linear order.

title: UMP one-sided test under a monotone likelihood ratio
informal: Let $\{P_\theta : \theta \in \mathbb{R}\}$ be a family of probability measures with densities $p_\theta$ with respect to a $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$, let $T$ be a measurable real statistic, and assume the family has monotone likelihood ratio in $T$. Fix a null boundary $\theta_0$ and a level $0 < \alpha < 1$. Then there exist a critical value $C$ and a boundary weight $\gamma \in [0,1]$ such that the one-sided test $$ \varphi(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} 1, & T(x) > C, \\ \gamma, & T(x) = C, \\ 0, & T(x) < C, \end{cases} $$ has size exactly $\alpha$ at $\theta_0$, $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}\varphi = \alpha$, and is **uniformly most powerful** at level $\alpha$ for testing $H : \theta \le \theta_0$ against $K : \theta > \theta_0$: it has level $\alpha$ on the whole null and beats every level-$\alpha$ competitor at every alternative simultaneously. The power function of such a test is nondecreasing in $\theta$, and strictly increasing wherever it is neither $0$ nor $1$ provided distinct parameter values give distinct distributions.
summary: For a family with monotone likelihood ratio in a statistic T, the test rejecting for large T is uniformly most powerful for a one-sided hypothesis.

    (μ : Measure 𝓧) [SigmaFinite μ]

    (p : ℝ → 𝓧 → ℝ) (hp : ∀ θ, HasDensity μ (p θ) (P θ))

    ∃ C γ : ℝ, γ ∈ Set.Icc (0 : ℝ) 1 ∧

      IsUMP P (Set.Iic θ₀) (Set.Ioi θ₀) α (oneSidedTest T C γ)

hypotheses.note: Every member of the family has a density with respect to the common σ-finite dominating measure.

hypotheses.label: measurable statistic
hypotheses.note: The statistic in which the likelihood ratio is monotone is measurable.

hypotheses.label: monotone likelihood ratio
hypotheses.note: For θ < θ′ the ratio of densities is a nondecreasing function of the statistic — the whole content of the setup.

hypotheses.label: level strictly inside (0,1)
hypotheses.note: The level is strictly between 0 and 1; at the endpoints the exact-size requirement cannot be met by a one-sided test with a real critical value.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: Monotone likelihood ratio and the resulting uniformly most powerful one-sided tests are due to Karlin and Rubin (1956); the one-parameter exponential-family case and the underlying optimality argument go back to Neyman and Pearson (1936). The formalization derives the uniform statement from the simple-versus-simple fundamental lemma together with monotonicity of the power function, which is itself obtained from a correlation identity for monotone statistics under a monotone likelihood ratio.

At the endpoints the exact-size clause is unattainable by a one-sided test with a *real* critical value whenever the statistic is essentially unbounded in the relevant tail: for the normal location family with $T$ the identity the upper tail probability is positive for every real threshold, so no such test has size exactly $0$. The critical value here is a real number, not an extended one: it is a level of the statistic, not a likelihood-ratio threshold. The strict-monotonicity companion additionally assumes that distinct parameters give distinct laws, the clause the cross-product definition of monotone likelihood ratio omits.

title: One-sided tests form an essentially complete class
informal: Consider the two-decision problem in which accepting the null at $\theta$ costs $L_0(\theta)$ and rejecting it costs $L_1(\theta)$, so a test $\varphi$ has risk $R(\theta, \varphi) = \beta_\varphi(\theta) L_1(\theta) + (1 - \beta_\varphi(\theta)) L_0(\theta)$. Let the model have densities with respect to a $\sigma$-finite measure and monotone likelihood ratio in a statistic $T$, and let the losses be monotone about $\theta_0$: rejecting costs strictly more than accepting for every $\theta < \theta_0$ and strictly less for every $\theta > \theta_0$. Then the one-sided tests form an **essentially complete class**: for every test $\psi$ whose size at $\theta_0$ lies strictly between $0$ and $1$ there are a critical value $C$ and a boundary weight $\gamma \in [0,1]$ with $$ R\bigl(\theta, \varphi_{C,\gamma}\bigr) \;\le\; R(\theta, \psi) \qquad \text{for every } \theta . $$
summary: Under a monotone likelihood ratio and monotone losses, every test is matched or beaten in risk, uniformly in the parameter, by a one-sided test.

title: UMP one-sided test in a one-parameter exponential family
informal: Let the model be a one-parameter exponential family with densities $p_\theta(x) = \exp\{\eta(\theta) T(x) - A(\eta(\theta))\}$ with respect to a $\sigma$-finite reference measure, where the parametrization $\theta \mapsto \eta(\theta)$ is strictly increasing, the model is exactly this canonical family read through $\eta$, and every parameter value is mapped into the natural parameter set, so that each member is a genuine probability measure. Fix a null boundary $\theta_0$ and a level $0 < \alpha < 1$. Then there are a critical value $C$ and a boundary weight $\gamma \in [0,1]$ for which the test rejecting when $T > C$, with randomization $\gamma$ when $T = C$, has size exactly $\alpha$ at $\theta_0$ and is uniformly most powerful at level $\alpha$ for $H : \theta \le \theta_0$ against $K : \theta > \theta_0$. The reason is that such a family has monotone likelihood ratio in $T$, since for $\theta < \theta'$ the log-ratio $(\eta(\theta') - \eta(\theta)) T(x)$ is increasing in $T(x)$.
summary: In a one-parameter exponential family with strictly increasing natural parametrization, the test rejecting for large values of the natural statistic is UMP for a one-sided hypothesis.

title: Stochastic ordering is equivalent to a monotone coupling
informal:
Let $\mu_0$ and $\mu_1$ be probability measures on the real line, with distribution functions $F_0$ and $F_1$. Then
$$ F_1(x) \le F_0(x) \ \text{ for all } x \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \exists\, V,\ f_0 \le f_1 \text{ nondecreasing with } f_0(V) \sim \mu_0, \ f_1(V) \sim \mu_1 . $$
That is, $\mu_1$ puts less mass on every lower ray precisely when both laws can be realized simultaneously on one probability space as nondecreasing functions of a single random variable, one everywhere below the other. The realization is explicit: take $V$ uniform on $(0,1)$ and $f_i$ the quantile function of $F_i$, which is nondecreasing and satisfies $f_i(y) \le x$ if and only if $y \le F_i(x)$; the ordering of the distribution functions then transfers pointwise to the ordering of the quantiles. This is the coupling behind the monotonicity of the power function in families with monotone likelihood ratio.
summary: Two laws on the real line are stochastically ordered exactly when they can be realized as two ordered nondecreasing functions of a single random variable.
leanSignature:
theorem cdf_le_iff_exists_monotone_coupling
    (μ₀ μ₁ : Measure ℝ) [IsProbabilityMeasure μ₀] [IsProbabilityMeasure μ₁] :
    (∀ x : ℝ, (μ₁ (Set.Iic x)).toReal ≤ (μ₀ (Set.Iic x)).toReal) ↔
      ∃ (ν : Measure ℝ) (_ : IsProbabilityMeasure ν) (f₀ f₁ : ℝ → ℝ),
        Monotone f₀ ∧ Monotone f₁ ∧ (∀ v, f₀ v ≤ f₁ v) ∧
          ν.map f₀ = μ₀ ∧ ν.map f₁ = μ₁

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The equivalence between stochastic ordering and the existence of a monotone coupling is due to Lehmann (1955); it is the one-dimensional case of the coupling theorem of Strassen (1965). Its use for families with monotone likelihood ratio is systematized by Karlin and Rubin (1956). The formalization writes distribution functions directly as the measure of a lower ray, so the statement is about the measures themselves and needs no compatibility lemma.

formalizationNotes: Measurability of the two coupling maps is not part of the conclusion because it follows from monotonicity, so the pushforwards are automatically defined. A constructive companion statement in the same file pins the coupling variable to the uniform law on the unit interval; there the monotonicity and the domination are asserted on the open interval $(0,1)$ only. The restriction to $(0,1)$ is needed on both counts: no globally monotone map pushes a compactly supported law onto a full-support one, and at the endpoint level $1$, where the quantile function takes its junk value, the two quantiles need not be ordered. The version stated here recovers the global monotone form by reading the quantiles through an increasing reparametrization of the line onto $(0,1)$.

title: UMP test of a two-sided hypothesis in an exponential family
informal: Let the model be a one-parameter exponential family with natural statistic $T$, a strictly increasing parametrization $\theta \mapsto \eta(\theta)$, presented canonically through that parametrization and with every parameter value inside the natural parameter set. Fix two boundaries $\theta_1 < \theta_2$ and a level $0 < \alpha < 1$, and assume no single level of the statistic carries null probability $\alpha$ or more, i.e. $\mathbb{P}_{\theta_1}\{T = t\} < \alpha$ for every $t$. Then there exist constants $C_1 < C_2$ and boundary weights $\gamma_1, \gamma_2 \in [0,1]$ for which the test $$ \varphi(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} 1, & C_1 < T(x) < C_2, \\ \gamma_i, & T(x) = C_i, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}, \end{cases} $$ satisfies the two size conditions $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_1}\varphi = \mathbb{E}_{\theta_2}\varphi = \alpha$ and is uniformly most powerful at level $\alpha$ for testing $H : \theta \le \theta_1 \text{ or } \theta \ge \theta_2$ against $K : \theta_1 < \theta < \theta_2$. Outside $[\theta_1, \theta_2]$ the same test *minimizes* the rejection probability among all tests meeting the two size conditions.
summary: In a one-parameter exponential family there is a uniformly most powerful test of the hypothesis that the parameter lies outside an interval, rejecting on a bounded interval of the natural statistic.

title: Uniformly most accurate one-sided confidence bound
informal: Let $\{P_\theta : \theta \in \mathbb{R}\}$ have densities with respect to a $\sigma$-finite measure and monotone likelihood ratio in a measurable statistic $T$. Write $F_\theta(t) = \mathbb{P}_\theta\{T \le t\}$ and assume $F_\theta(t)$ is continuous in $t$ for each fixed $\theta$ (it is also assumed continuous in $\theta$ for each fixed $t$, as in the printed statement) and distinct parameter values give distinct distributions. Fix a level $0 < \alpha < 1$ and assume the defining equation is solvable at every level of the statistic, i.e. for each $t$ there is a $\theta$ with $F_\theta(t) = 1 - \alpha$. Then there is a measurable lower bound $\underline{\theta}(x)$ such that the family of half-lines $[\underline{\theta}(x), \infty)$ is a **uniformly most accurate** family of confidence sets at level $1 - \alpha$: it covers each value $\theta_0$ other than the true one with the smallest possible probability, uniformly over the parameters $\theta > \theta_0$. Moreover $\underline{\theta}(x)$ is characterized as the unique solution of $$ F_\theta\bigl(T(x)\bigr) \;=\; 1 - \alpha . $$
summary: Inverting the UMP one-sided tests of a family with monotone likelihood ratio produces a uniformly most accurate lower confidence bound, characterized as the unique root of the equation F_θ(T(x)) = 1 − α.

title: Boundary Optimality Implies UMP Unbiasedness
informal: Consider testing a null set $\Theta_0$ against an alternative set $\Theta_1$ at a level $\alpha$ with $0 \le \alpha \le 1$, and suppose every randomized test has a power function that is continuous in the parameter. Write $\omega_B = \overline{\Theta_0} \cap \overline{\Theta_1}$ for the common boundary of the two sets, that is, the parameter points that are points or limit points of both. Let $\varphi_0$ be a randomized test. If $\varphi_0$ has level $\alpha$ on the null set, so that $\mathbb{E}_\theta[\varphi_0] \le \alpha$ for every $\theta \in \Theta_0$, if $\varphi_0$ is similar of size $\alpha$ on the boundary, that is $\mathbb{E}_\theta[\varphi_0] = \alpha$ for every $\theta \in \omega_B$, and if $\varphi_0$ is at least as powerful on $\Theta_1$ as every randomized test that is similar of size $\alpha$ on $\omega_B$, then $\varphi_0$ is uniformly most powerful unbiased at level $\alpha$: it is unbiased of level $\alpha$, and $\mathbb{E}_\theta[\psi] \le \mathbb{E}_\theta[\varphi_0]$ for every $\theta \in \Theta_1$ and every unbiased level-$\alpha$ test $\psi$. The mechanism has two halves. Continuity of the power function propagates the inequality $\mathbb{E}_\theta[\psi] \le \alpha$ from $\Theta_0$ to its closure and the inequality $\alpha \le \mathbb{E}_\theta[\psi]$ from $\Theta_1$ to its closure, so every unbiased level-$\alpha$ test is similar on $\omega_B$ and the boundary-similar class contains the unbiased class. Conversely, the constant test $\varphi \equiv \alpha$ is itself boundary-similar, and comparing $\varphi_0$ with it shows that $\varphi_0$ is unbiased.
summary: If every power function is continuous, a level-α test that is optimal among the tests similar on the common boundary of the null and alternative sets is uniformly most powerful unbiased.

title: Continuity of the Power Function of an Exponential Family
informal: Let $\{P_\eta\}$ be an exponential family on a finite-dimensional real inner product space of natural parameters, with natural statistic $T$, reference measure $\nu$, and members given by the tilted densities proportional to $e^{\langle \eta, T(x)\rangle}$; let $\mathcal{N}$ denote the natural parameter set, the set of $\eta$ for which $e^{\langle \eta, T(x)\rangle}$ is $\nu$-integrable. If $\varphi$ is a randomized test, that is, a measurable function of the observation with values in $[0,1]$, then the power function $$ \eta \;\longmapsto\; \mathbb{E}_\eta[\varphi] \;=\; \frac{\int \varphi(x)\, e^{\langle \eta, T(x)\rangle}\, d\nu(x)}{\int e^{\langle \eta, T(x)\rangle}\, d\nu(x)} $$ is continuous at every point of the interior of $\mathcal{N}$. This is the regularity input that licenses the boundary device for unbiased testing: numerator and denominator are both differentiable, hence continuous, on the interior of the corresponding natural parameter sets, and the bound $|\varphi| \le 1$ places $\mathcal{N}$ inside the $\varphi$-weighted natural parameter set. The denominator is strictly positive there unless the reference measure vanishes, in which case every member is the zero measure and the power is identically $0$.
summary: The power function of any randomized test against a finite-dimensional exponential family is continuous on the interior of the natural parameter set.

title: Similar Tests Have Neyman Structure under Bounded Completeness
informal: Let $\{P_\theta\}$ be a family of probability measures on the sample space, let $\omega$ be a set of boundary parameters, and let $T$ be a measurable statistic. Let $Q$ be a Markov kernel on the range of $T$, playing the role of the conditional distribution of the observation given $T = t$, and assume $T$ is sufficient for the boundary family, in the disintegration form that for every $\theta \in \omega$ the joint law of the pair $(T(X), X)$ under $P_\theta$ is the law of $T$ under $P_\theta$ composed with $Q$. Assume further that the family of laws of $T$ indexed by $\omega$ is boundedly complete: any bounded measurable function of $t$ whose mean vanishes under every one of those laws is almost everywhere zero. Then every randomized test $\varphi$ that is similar of size $\alpha$ on $\omega$, that is $\mathbb{E}_\theta[\varphi] = \alpha$ for every $\theta \in \omega$ has *Neyman structure* with respect to $T$: for every $\theta \in \omega$ and almost every $t$ under the law of $T$, $$ \int \varphi \, dQ_t \;=\; \alpha . $$ Disintegrating the similarity equation along $T$ turns it into the statement that the bounded measurable function $t \mapsto \int \varphi \, dQ_t - \alpha$ has zero mean under every boundary law, and bounded completeness forces that function to vanish. This is the reduction that replaces the search for optimal similar tests by a family of one-dimensional conditional Neyman–Pearson problems, one on each surface $T = t$.
summary: If the family of laws of a sufficient statistic is boundedly complete, every similar test of size α has conditional size α given that statistic.

    ∀ θ ∈ ω, HasNeymanStructure T Q (statLaw P T θ) α φ

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.

The Lean statement is the forward half of the book's Theorem 4.3.2, with sufficiency transcribed in the graph (disintegration) form, which is what the proof consumes.

title: Neyman Structure for All Similar Tests Implies Bounded Completeness
informal: Keep the setting of the previous result: a family $\{P_\theta\}$ of probability measures, a boundary set $\omega$, a measurable statistic $T$, and a Markov kernel $Q$ on the range of $T$ with $T$ sufficient for the boundary family, in the sense that for every $\theta \in \omega$ the joint law of $(T(X), X)$ is the law of $T$ composed with $Q$. Suppose the level satisfies $\alpha > 0$ and $\alpha < 1$, and suppose every randomized test that is similar of size $\alpha$ on $\omega$ has Neyman structure with respect to $T$, that is, conditional size $\alpha$ given $T = t$ for almost every $t$ under every boundary law. Then the family of laws of $T$ indexed by $\omega$ is boundedly complete. The argument perturbs the constant test: given a bounded measurable $f$ with zero mean under every boundary law of $T$, the test $\varphi = c\,f(T(\cdot)) + \alpha$ is a randomized test for $c = \min(\alpha, 1-\alpha)/M$ with $M$ a positive bound for $|f|$, and it is similar of size $\alpha$. Its assumed Neyman structure forces the conditional average of $f \circ T$ to vanish almost everywhere, and testing the disintegration identity against a bounded weight identifies that conditional average with $f$ itself. Together the two facts give $f = 0$ almost everywhere.
summary: Conversely, if every similar test of size α has Neyman structure with respect to a sufficient statistic, the family of laws of that statistic is boundedly complete.

title: Conditioning Eliminates the Nuisance Parameters
informal: Let the observation have a multiparameter exponential family distribution whose sufficient statistic splits into a real coordinate $U$ carrying the parameter of interest $\theta$ and a coordinate $T$, in a finite-dimensional inner product space, carrying the nuisance parameters $\vartheta$. Assume $U$ is measurable and $T$ is measurable, and assume the joint law of the pair $(U, T)$ is canonical on the parameter set $\Omega$, that is, for every $(\theta,\vartheta) \in \Omega$ it has density $$ C(\theta,\vartheta)\, \exp\bigl(\theta u + \langle \vartheta, t \rangle\bigr) $$ with respect to one fixed parameter-free measure $\nu$ on the range of the pair. Then there are a family of base measures $\nu_t$ on the line, depending only on $t$, and normalizing constants $C_t(\theta)$, depending only on $t$ and $\theta$ — in particular **not** on the nuisance parameters — such that for every parameter of $\Omega$ and almost every $t$ under the law of $T$, the conditional distribution of $U$ given $T = t$ has density $$ C_t(\theta)\, e^{\theta u} $$ with respect to $\nu_t$. Conditionally on $T = t$ the model is therefore a one-parameter exponential family in $\theta$ with natural statistic $u$, and the nuisance parameters have disappeared. Every test built on this conditional family has a nuisance-free conditional size, so the one-parameter optimality theory applies surface by surface.
summary: In a canonical multiparameter exponential family, the conditional law of the interest statistic given the nuisance statistic is a one-parameter exponential family whose base measure and normalizer do not involve the nuisance parameters.

title: UMP Unbiased Test of a Point Null in a One-Parameter Exponential Family
informal: Let $\{P_\theta\}$ be a one-parameter exponential family with natural statistic $T$ and densities $dP_\theta = C(\theta)\, e^{\theta T(x)}\, d\nu(x)$, and let $\Xi$ be a set of parameter values inside the interior of the natural parameter set, with the model agreeing with the canonical family at every $\theta \in \Xi$ and $\Xi$ open. Fix $\theta_0 \in \Xi$ and a level $0 < \alpha < 1$. Let $\varphi$ be a randomized test with critical values $C_1 \le C_2$ such that $\varphi$ rejects whenever $T < C_1$ or $T > C_2$, $\varphi$ accepts whenever $C_1 < T < C_2$, and $\varphi$ takes the constant randomization values $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ on $\{T = C_1\}$ and $\{T = C_2\}$. Suppose the constants satisfy **both** side conditions: the size condition $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}[\varphi] = \alpha$, and the derivative condition $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}[T\varphi] = \alpha\, \mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}[T]$. Then $\varphi$ is uniformly most powerful unbiased at level $\alpha$ for testing $H : \theta = \theta_0$ against $K : \theta \neq \theta_0$, $\theta \in \Xi$. The second condition is not decoration. Unbiasedness forces the power function to have a minimum at $\theta_0$, and differentiating the power of an exponential family under the integral sign turns the vanishing of the derivative at $\theta_0$ into exactly $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}[T\varphi] - \mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}[T]\,\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}[\varphi] = 0$, which combines with the size equation to give the displayed form. Neither equation may be dropped.
summary: For a point null in a one-parameter exponential family, the test rejecting outside an interval in the natural statistic is UMP unbiased once its constants satisfy the size and the derivative conditions.

informal: Let $\{P_\theta\}$ be a one-parameter exponential family with natural statistic $T$ and densities $dP_\theta = C(\theta)\, e^{\theta T(x)}\, d\nu(x)$, and let $\Xi$ be a set of parameter values inside the interior of the natural parameter set, with the model agreeing with the canonical family at every $\theta \in \Xi$ and $\Xi$ open. Fix $\theta_1 < \theta_2$ in $\Xi$ and a level $0 < \alpha < 1$. Let $\varphi$ be a randomized test with critical values $C_1 \le C_2$ such that $\varphi$ rejects whenever $T < C_1$ or $T > C_2$, $\varphi$ accepts whenever $C_1 < T < C_2$, and $\varphi$ takes the constant randomization values $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_2$ at the two critical values. If $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_1}[\varphi] = \alpha$ and $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_2}[\varphi] = \alpha$, then $\varphi$ is uniformly most powerful unbiased at level $\alpha$ for testing $$ H : \theta_1 \le \theta \le \theta_2 \qquad\text{against}\qquad K : \theta < \theta_1 \ \text{ or }\ \theta > \theta_2 , \qquad \theta \in \Xi. $$ Here the boundary of the testing problem consists of the two endpoints, and unbiasedness together with continuity of the power function forces similarity there; so the two size equations replace the size-plus-derivative pair of the point-null problem. That the test also has level $\alpha$ at interior points of the null interval is a consequence, not an assumption: it follows from the variation-diminishing property of the exponential kernel, since the difference $\varphi - \alpha$ and a suitable combination $a e^{\theta_1 t} + b e^{\theta_2 t} - e^{\vartheta t}$ change sign at exactly the same two points.

title: UMP Unbiased One-Sided Test for a Multiparameter Exponential Family
informal: Let the observation have a multiparameter exponential family distribution whose sufficient statistic is a pair $(U, T)$, with $U$ real carrying the parameter of interest $\theta$ and $T$ carrying the nuisance parameters $\vartheta$ in a finite-dimensional space, and assume the joint law of $(U, T)$ is canonical on the parameter set $\Omega$, with density $C(\theta,\vartheta)\exp(\theta u + \langle \vartheta, t\rangle)$ against a fixed measure. Assume $(U, T)$ is sufficient in the operative sense that every randomized test of the observation is matched, in power at every parameter of $\Omega$, by a randomized test of the pair alone. Assume $\Omega$ is convex and $\Omega$ is not contained in any proper affine subspace, and that $\Omega$ reaches strictly below and strictly above the null value $\theta_0$. Let $C_0$ and $\gamma_0$ be measurable functions of $t$ with $\gamma_0(t) \in [0,1]$ for every $t$, and let $\varphi$ be the conditional one-sided test that, on the surface $T = t$, rejects when $U > C_0(t)$, randomizes with probability $\gamma_0(t)$ when $U = C_0(t)$, and accepts otherwise. If at every parameter of $\Omega$ whose interest coordinate equals $\theta_0$ the conditional size given $T = t$ is $\alpha$ for almost every $t$, then $\varphi$ is uniformly most powerful unbiased at level $\alpha$ for testing $$ H : \theta \le \theta_0 \qquad\text{against}\qquad K : \theta > \theta_0 $$ within $\Omega$, for any level $0 < \alpha < 1$.
