formalizationNotes: **Two hypotheses are added relative to the transcribed statement, for independent reasons, and both are visible in the signature.** First, the transcription did not carry the book's standing convention that the observation *is* the sufficient statistic: the canonical hypothesis constrains only the law of the pair $(U, T)$, while uniform most powerful unbiasedness quantifies over all randomized tests of the sample space, so with a constant pair the remaining hypotheses say nothing about the model and the optimality conclusion is out of reach; the file records that configuration formally. The added sufficiency-reduction hypothesis restores the convention and is vacuously true in the book's own setting, where the sample space is the range of the pair. Second, the book's 'not contained in a linear space of dimension less than $k+1$' is read as an *affine* flat: the weaker linear-span condition does not suffice, since a convex set with full linear span can have a single-point boundary surface, leaving the completeness step without a full-dimensional slice. Two further instance hypotheses — Borel measurable structure and finite dimensionality of the nuisance space — are what make the canonical exponent measurable and the boundary slice full-dimensional. The conditional size conditions are imposed almost everywhere rather than everywhere, which is the weaker hypothesis and all the averaging identity consumes.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The construction of UMP unbiased tests for multiparameter exponential families by conditioning on the sufficient statistic for the nuisance parameters is due to Neyman and Pearson (1936) and Neyman (1937); the completeness theory that carries similar tests to tests with Neyman structure is due to Lehmann and Scheffé (1950). The book packages the four resulting tests as Theorem 4.4.1; the Lean statement proves the one-sided case with the sufficiency and affine-nondegeneracy amendments described above, both certified necessary by explicit counterexamples.

title: UMP Unbiased Test of a Point Null for a Multiparameter Exponential Family
informal: Keep the canonical multiparameter setting: a sufficient statistic pair $(U, T)$ with $U$ real carrying the parameter of interest $\theta$, and the joint law of $(U, T)$ canonical on the parameter set $\Omega$, with density $C(\theta,\vartheta)\exp(\theta u + \langle \vartheta, t\rangle)$ against a fixed measure. Assume $(U, T)$ is sufficient, in the sense that every randomized test of the observation is matched in power at every parameter of $\Omega$ by a randomized test of the pair, that $\Omega$ is convex and that $\Omega$ is not contained in any proper affine subspace, and that $\Omega$ reaches strictly below and strictly above the null value $\theta_0$. Let $C_1(t) \le C_2(t)$ and $\gamma_1(t), \gamma_2(t) \in [0,1]$ be measurable functions of the nuisance statistic, and let $\varphi$ be the conditional test that, on the surface $T = t$, rejects when $U < C_1(t)$ or $U > C_2(t)$, randomizes with probabilities $\gamma_1(t), \gamma_2(t)$ at the two endpoints, and accepts strictly inside. If, at every parameter of $\Omega$ whose interest coordinate equals $\theta_0$ and for almost every $t$, the conditional size satisfies $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}[\varphi \mid T = t] = \alpha$ and the conditional derivative condition $\mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}[U\varphi \mid T = t] = \alpha\, \mathbb{E}_{\theta_0}[U \mid T = t]$ holds, then $\varphi$ is uniformly most powerful unbiased at level $\alpha$ for testing $H : \theta = \theta_0$ against $K : \theta \neq \theta_0$ within $\Omega$, for any level $0 < \alpha < 1$. The second condition is what unbiasedness contributes: the conditional power function has a minimum at $\theta_0$, and its vanishing derivative there is exactly the displayed first-moment equation. It may not be dropped.

Both conditional side conditions are imposed almost everywhere with respect to the law of the nuisance statistic, at every parameter of the boundary surface; by the nuisance-independence of the conditional law this is no stronger than imposing them at one such parameter. The two-sided alternative is handled in one stroke because the separating object is the secant, or on a degenerate fibre the tangent, of an exponential, and convexity is blind to the sign of the exponent.

The Lean statement carries the sufficiency and affine-nondegeneracy amendments and states both conditional side conditions explicitly, the derivative condition being the analytic content of unbiasedness.

title: Family-Preserving Transformations Form a Group
informal: Call a bimeasurable bijection $g$ of the sample space *family-preserving* for a model $\{P_\theta\}$ when the law of $g(X)$ is again a member of the family: there is an induced map $\bar g$ of the parameter space *onto* itself with $$ P_\theta\{ g(X) \in A \} \;=\; P_{\bar g \theta}\{ X \in A \} $$ for every measurable set $A$. If the model is identifiable, that is, distinct parameters index distinct distributions, then the family-preserving transformations form a subgroup of the group of all permutations of the sample space: they contain the identity, are closed under composition, and are closed under inversion. The induced maps compose accordingly, $\overline{g' g} = \bar g' \, \bar g$ and $\overline{g^{-1}} = \bar g^{\,-1}$. Consequently any class of transformations leaving a testing problem invariant may be enlarged to a group of such transformations without loss, which is what makes the invariance reduction a group-theoretic device.
summary: For an identifiable model the bimeasurable bijections that preserve the family form a subgroup of the permutation group of the sample space.
leanSignature:
def familyPreservingSubgroup (P : Θ → Measure 𝓧) (hP : Function.Injective P) :
    Subgroup (Equiv.Perm 𝓧)

hypotheses.label: identifiability
hypotheses.note: Distinct parameters index distinct distributions, which is what makes the induced parameter map injective.

formalizationNotes: Preservation is defined set-theoretically: the induced parameter map is packaged existentially together with the surjectivity demanded of it (the 'onto' half of parameter preservation), rather than being bundled as a bijection. Injectivity of the induced map is deliberately **not** part of the definition — it is a consequence of identifiability, proved separately — which keeps the definition honest about what preservation alone delivers. This is why the subgroup construction carries the identifiability hypothesis explicitly: without it, closure under inversion is not available.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: Invariance as a systematic reduction principle for testing problems is due to Hunt and Stein (1946) and Stein (1956), developed in Lehmann's lecture tradition of the 1950s; the orbit and maximal-invariant calculus is treated systematically by Hall, Wijsman and Ghosh (1965). The book's Lemma 6.1.1 records that the family-preserving transformations form a group; the Lean version constructs the subgroup explicitly and isolates identifiability as the hypothesis that closure under inversion requires.

title: Invariant Tests Are the Measurable Functions of a Maximal Invariant
informal: Let a group $G$ act on the sample space, and let $M$ be a maximal invariant for the action: it is constant along each orbit, and it takes equal values only at points of a common orbit. Points on a common orbit are indistinguishable by an invariant test, so at the level of sets an invariant test is automatically a function of $M$; upgrading that factor to a *measurable* function requires a structural assumption. Suppose a complementary measurable coordinate $Y$ is given for which $x \mapsto (M(x), Y(x))$ is a measurable embedding — one-to-one onto a measurable subset of the product, with measurable inverse, and suppose this coordinate map is onto the whole product. Then for a real function $\varphi$ on the sample space: $$ \varphi \ \text{is measurable and invariant} \iff \varphi = h \circ M \ \text{for some measurable } h. $$ The standard instance is the sample space $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{0\}$ with $G$ the scalings, $M(x) = x/\|x\|$ and $Y(x) = \|x\|$.
summary: Under a measurable coordinate assumption, a test is measurable and invariant exactly when it is a measurable function of a maximal invariant.

    (hsurj : Function.Surjective fun x => (M x, Y x))

The purely set-level factorization, which needs no structural assumption at all, is available separately in the same file.

title: Stepwise Maximal Invariants
informal: Let a group $G$ act on the sample space and let $D$ and $E$ be subgroups with $D$ and $E$ together generating $G$. Let $s$ be a maximal invariant for the subgroup $D$, and suppose the action of $E$ descends along $s$: equal values of $s$ are carried to equal values of $s$ by every element of $E$, so that each $e \in E$ induces a transformation $e^{*}$ of the range of $s$ by $e^{*}(s(x)) = s(ex)$. If $t$ is invariant under the induced group, that is $t(s(ex)) = t(s(x))$ for every $e \in E$ and every $x$, and $t$ separates the orbits of the induced group, that is $t(s(x_1)) = t(s(x_2))$ implies $s(x_2) = s(e x_1)$ for some $e \in E$, then $t \circ s$ is a maximal invariant for the whole group $G$. A maximal invariant may therefore be computed in stages: reduce first by one subgroup, then by the action the second subgroup induces on the reduced data. This is how the maximal invariants of the classical linear-model problems are built.
summary: A maximal invariant for a group generated by two subgroups can be computed in two stages, first for one subgroup and then for the induced action of the other.

The invariance half of the conclusion is obtained by observing that the set of group elements leaving the composite unchanged is a subgroup containing both generators.

The book states it as Theorem 6.2.2; the Lean statement transcribes the induced group's maximal-invariance condition pointwise through the first-stage statistic rather than constructing the induced group as an object.

title: UMP Invariant Test under a Finite Group with Transitive Induced Action
informal: Let a **finite** group $G$ act on the sample space with an induced action on the parameter space, and suppose the model intertwines the two actions, so that the law of $gX$ under $P_\theta$ is $P_{g\theta}$. Suppose the model is dominated by a $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$ with measurable nonnegative densities $p_\theta$ and that $\mu$ is itself invariant under the group. Assume the null class $\Theta_0$ and the alternative class $\Theta_1$ are stable under the induced action, that the induced action is transitive on $\Theta_0$, and that the induced action is transitive on $\Theta_1$. Fix representatives $\theta_0 \in \Theta_0$ and $\theta_1 \in \Theta_1$ and write $$ \bar p_\theta(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} p_\theta(g x) $$ for the orbit average of a density. Let $\varphi$ be an invariant randomized test that rejects wherever $\bar p_{\theta_1} > k\, \bar p_{\theta_0}$ and accepts wherever $\bar p_{\theta_1} < k\, \bar p_{\theta_0}$. If $\varphi$ has size exactly $\alpha$ at the null representative, then $\varphi$ is uniformly most powerful among invariant level-$\alpha$ tests. The reason is that an invariant test has the same power at every parameter of an induced orbit, so transitivity collapses the composite-versus-composite problem to a simple-versus-simple one, and the Neyman–Pearson lemma applied to the pair of orbit-averaged densities produces the optimal invariant test. The displayed ratio does not depend on which representatives are chosen.
summary: When a finite group acts transitively on the null and on the alternative classes, the Neyman–Pearson test for the orbit-averaged densities is UMP invariant.

title: Almost Invariant Tests Are Equivalent to Invariant Ones
informal: A function is **almost invariant** with respect to a measure $\mu$ when, for each group element separately, it is unchanged along the action outside a $\mu$-null set, the exceptional set being allowed to depend on the group element. This is strictly weaker than invariance in general, and it is the class that appears naturally when invariance is compared with unbiasedness or reached through a sufficiency reduction. Let a group $G$ act jointly measurably on the sample space — the pair map $(g, x) \mapsto g x$ being measurable on the product — and let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure on the sample space. Suppose the group carries a $\sigma$-finite measure $\nu$ which is not the zero measure and whose null sets are stable under right translation, so that $\nu(B) = 0$ implies $\nu(Bg) = 0$ for every group element $g$. Then every measurable function $\varphi$ that is almost invariant with respect to $\mu$ agrees $\mu$-almost everywhere with a measurable function that is genuinely invariant. The right-translation condition holds in particular for a right-invariant measure, whose existence is guaranteed for a large class of groups by Haar theory, but the weaker null-set form is what the argument needs and is often easier to check directly. The mechanism is a Fubini argument on the product of sample space and group, followed by averaging over the group.
summary: If the group carries a nonzero σ-finite measure whose null sets survive right translation, every measurable almost invariant function agrees almost everywhere with a genuinely invariant one.

formalizationNotes: Non-degeneracy of the group measure is stated explicitly; the averaging step normalizes it to a probability measure, which is impossible for the zero measure, and the source leaves this implicit. The normalization is carried out inside the proof: a $\sigma$-finite measure carries an everywhere-positive integrable density, hence is equivalent to a finite one, and only null sets enter the hypotheses. Because the function need not be integrable, the averaging is performed in the bounded chart $\arctan$ and read back through $\tan$; the invariant representative is the *essential value* of the orbit function, which is genuinely invariant — not merely invariant almost everywhere — because right translation preserves both the property of being essentially constant along an orbit and the value of that constant. title: Invariant Power Function versus Almost Invariant Test
informal: Restricting attention to invariant tests departs from comparing tests purely by their power functions, so it is natural to ask what invariance means at the level of power functions. One implication is immediate: an almost invariant test has a power function invariant under the induced parameter action. The converse fails in general, but holds once the problem has been reduced to a statistic whose family of laws is boundedly complete. Let $T$ be a statistic, let the group act on its range and on the parameter space, and suppose the family of laws of $T$ is boundedly complete: a bounded measurable function with zero mean under every one of those laws vanishes almost everywhere, the reduced problem is invariant, that is, the law of $T$ under the parameter $g\theta$ is the image under $g$ of its law under $\theta$, and the group acts on the range of $T$ by measurable maps. Then for a randomized test $\psi$ of the statistic: $$ \mathbb{E}_{g\theta}[\psi] = \mathbb{E}_\theta[\psi] \ \text{ for all } g, \theta \iff \psi \ \text{is almost invariant under every law of } T. $$ This is what makes almost invariance, rather than invariance, the right class to work with.
summary: For a boundedly complete family of laws of a statistic, a test of that statistic has invariant power function exactly when it is almost invariant.

title: Unbiasedness and Invariance Coincide when the Unbiased Test Is Unique
informal: Unbiasedness and invariance are logically independent optimality restrictions: each succeeds on problems where the other does not. Where both deliver a uniformly most powerful member, however, the two answers agree, and this is not accidental. Consider an invariant testing problem: the model intertwines the actions on the sample space and the parameter space, the null class is preserved by the induced action, and the alternative class is preserved by it. Let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure equivalent to the family, and let the level satisfy $0 \le \alpha \le 1$. If $\varphi^{*}$ is uniformly most powerful unbiased at level $\alpha$ and the UMP unbiased test is unique up to sets of measure zero, then any test $\varphi$ that is uniformly most powerful among almost invariant level-$\alpha$ tests satisfies $\varphi = \varphi^{*}$ almost everywhere — and the UMP almost invariant test is itself unique up to null sets. The reason is a symmetry of the unbiased class. Because the induced action permutes the null and alternative classes, a test is unbiased of level $\alpha$ exactly when each of its translates is; so every translate of $\varphi^{*}$ is again UMP unbiased, and uniqueness collapses them onto $\varphi^{*}$, which is therefore almost invariant. The UMP almost invariant test is then at least as powerful as $\varphi^{*}$; conversely it is itself unbiased, by comparison with the invariant constant test $\varphi \equiv \alpha$, hence dominated by $\varphi^{*}$. Equality of the two power functions plus uniqueness finishes the argument.
summary: In an invariant problem with an essentially unique UMP unbiased test, that test and the UMP almost invariant test agree almost everywhere.

title: Convex Acceptance Regions Are Admissible in an Exponential Family
informal: Optimality within a restricted class does not by itself make a test admissible: a uniformly most powerful invariant test can be beaten uniformly by a test that is not invariant. For exponential families the classical route to admissibility is convexity of the acceptance region. Work on the natural-statistic scale of an exponential family in $s$ real natural parameters, and let $\varphi_0$ be the nonrandomized test that rejects exactly outside a set $A_0$. Assume the null class lies inside the natural parameter set and the alternative class lies inside it as well, both nonempty and disjoint; assume $A_0$ is closed and $A_0$ is convex; and assume the ray condition: whenever an open half-space $\{t : \langle a, t\rangle > c\}$ misses $A_0$, the alternative class contains a point $\theta^{*}$ and scalars $\lambda_n \to \infty$ with $\theta^{*} + \lambda_n a$ in the alternative class for every $n$. Then $\varphi_0$ is **d-admissible**: any randomized test whose power is at least that of $\varphi_0$ everywhere on the alternatives and at most that of $\varphi_0$ everywhere on the null has the same power function as $\varphi_0$ throughout. The mechanism is geometric. A competitor protruding from a closed convex set can be separated from it by a hyperplane; pushing the natural parameter to infinity along the direction of that hyperplane makes the protruding part dominate the likelihood, so the competitor would have to be *strictly* worse somewhere on the alternatives.
summary: In an exponential family, a nonrandomized test whose acceptance region is closed and convex is d-admissible against any alternative class satisfying the ray condition.

title: A Unique Bayes Test Is Admissible
informal: A general decision-theoretic route to admissibility is to exhibit a procedure as the **unique Bayes solution** of some prior problem. For testing, the prior problem is a pair of priors — one carried by the null class, one by the alternative class — under $0$–$1$ loss. Let the model be dominated by a $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$, with densities $f_\theta(x)$ that are nonnegative and jointly measurable in the parameter and the observation, and suppose the support $\{x : f_\theta(x) > 0\}$ does not depend on $\theta$. Let $\Lambda_0$ and $\Lambda_1$ be prior probability measures on the parameter space with $\Lambda_0$ carried by the null class and $\Lambda_1$ carried by the alternative class, and form the mixture densities $$ h_i(x) \;=\; \int f_\theta(x)\, d\Lambda_i(\theta), \qquad i = 0, 1 . $$ Consider the nonrandomized Bayes test that rejects exactly where $h_1 \ge k\,h_0$. If the Bayes boundary $\{x : h_1(x) = k\,h_0(x)\}$ is $\mu$-null, then this test is **d-admissible** for testing the null class against the alternative class: any randomized test at least as powerful on the alternatives and no more powerful on the null has the same power function. The test is a Neyman–Pearson test for the simple problem $h_0$ versus $h_1$; a null boundary makes that test unique, and uniqueness upgrades directly to admissibility of the original test.
summary: The nonrandomized Bayes test for a pair of priors under 0–1 loss is d-admissible whenever its boundary set is null.

title: The Sign-Change Identity for Tests of Symmetry
informal: Tests of the hypothesis that a distribution is symmetric about the origin are usually built from the ranks of the absolute observations together with the signs, and are calibrated under the assumption that the observations are an independent sample from continuous distributions symmetric about the origin. That assumption is often the doubtful part of the model — the observations may be gathered under different experimental conditions and need be neither identically distributed nor independent. Let $\varphi$ be a randomized test of $N$ real observations, and suppose $\varphi$ has mean $\alpha$ under every product of continuous distributions symmetric about the origin — that is, whenever the coordinates are independent with atomless marginals each unchanged by sign reversal. Let $Q$ be a joint law of the $N$ observations which is unchanged by all $2^N$ coordinatewise sign changes and which assigns probability zero to every Lebesgue-null set. Then $\varphi$ has mean $\alpha$ under $Q$ as well. So the calibration survives the loss of both independence and identical distribution. In the paired-comparison design the sign-change invariance is guaranteed by construction, since the treatment is assigned at random within each pair; the stated significance level is therefore exactly right regardless of how the pairs differ from one another. The mechanism is that the calibration forces the average of $\varphi$ over the $2^N$ sign patterns to equal $\alpha$ almost everywhere, while sign-change invariance of $Q$ makes the conditional distribution of the signs given the absolute values uniform over those patterns.
summary: A test calibrated on independent continuous symmetric samples keeps its level under every absolutely continuous joint law invariant under coordinatewise sign changes.

formalizationNotes: **Two hypotheses of the printed identity are adjusted.** The calibration hypothesis pins the sign-average to $\alpha$ only off a set that is null for every *non-atomic* law, and a sign-change invariant law may sit entirely on that set: with one observation, level $0$, the test the indicator of the origin and the joint law a Dirac mass at the origin, every printed hypothesis holds while the two integrals differ. The file records that configuration formally, together with a second one carrying no zeros and no ties. Absolute continuity of the joint law is therefore **required**, and it is exactly what rules atomic configurations of this kind out. Separately, the calibration class is widened from the independent identically distributed products to the merely independent ones. This second change is not forced: keeping the narrower class would require a completeness statement for order statistics from non-atomic laws, whose standard proof is an inclusion–exclusion over $N^N$ terms, whereas with independent marginals the same conclusion is one application of the product structure. Once the class is widened, the permutation-symmetry hypothesis of the printed statement is no longer needed and is dropped, so the identity holds for every randomized test.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: Randomization within matched pairs as the source of exact significance levels for sign and signed-rank procedures goes back to Fisher (1935), and the one-sample signed-rank statistic to Wilcoxon (1945). The observation that a symmetric rank test retains its level under any sign-change-invariant joint law, dispensing with both independence and identical distribution, belongs to the non-parametric program of Lehmann and Stein (1949). The Lean statement is the book's Lemma 6.10.1 with two documented amendments — a forced absolute-continuity assumption on the joint law, and a calibration class of independent but not necessarily identically distributed samples — both adjustments, and the situations that motivate them, documented in the same file.

title: Uniformly Most Accurate Equivariant Confidence Sets
informal: The duality between tests and confidence sets — the parameter $\theta$ lies in $S(x)$ exactly when $x$ lies in the acceptance region $A(\theta)$ — carries the invariance reduction across to interval estimation. A group acting on the data induces an action on the parameter space and hence on *sets* of parameters, and a confidence family is **equivariant** when transforming the data transforms the confidence statement in the matching way, so that the statement does not depend on the coordinate system. Let $A(\theta)$ be a family of acceptance regions with dual confidence family $S(x) = \{\theta : x \in A(\theta)\}$. Suppose the confidence family is equivariant, that is, applying the induced parameter action to $S(x)$ produces $S(gx)$, it has confidence level $1 - \alpha$, every acceptance region is measurable, and for each parameter value $\theta$ the nonrandomized test rejecting off $A(\theta)$ is uniformly most powerful at level $\alpha$ for testing $\theta' = \theta$ among the tests invariant under the transformations that fix $\theta$. Then the confidence family is **uniformly most accurate equivariant** at level $1 - \alpha$: among all equivariant families at that level, it minimizes the probability of covering each parameter value other than the true one.
summary: If each acceptance region is the UMP invariant test of its own parameter value, the dual equivariant confidence family is uniformly most accurate among equivariant families.

hypotheses.label: equivariant confidence family
hypotheses.note: Transforming the data transforms the confidence set by the induced parameter action.

hypotheses.label: confidence level
hypotheses.note: The family covers the true parameter with probability at least the stated level.

hypotheses.label: measurable acceptance regions
hypotheses.note: Each acceptance region is measurable, so that it can be read as a test.

hypotheses.label: UMP invariant acceptance regions
hypotheses.note: Each acceptance region is the UMP level-α test of its own parameter value among tests invariant under its stabilizer.

formalizationNotes: The source's group of transformations leaving the hypothesis $\theta' = \theta$ invariant is replaced here by the **stabilizer** of $\theta$, which is the largest such group, so the statement specializes to every group the source allows. The competitors are quantified over families with **measurable slices**, matching the sibling definition of uniform accuracy: without it the optimality transfer is not even expressible, since the argument inverts a competitor into a test that must be a critical function, and the coverage of a family with non-measurable slices is not a probability statement in the first place. Uniform accuracy is stated as the source defines it, by minimizing the probability of covering each value other than the true one. The dictionary between equivariant confidence families and equivariant acceptance regions is proved separately in the same file, in both directions; stabilizer-invariance of the acceptance regions alone is *not* enough to recover equivariance of the confidence family.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The duality between families of tests and confidence sets is due to Neyman (1937). Equivariance of confidence sets and the transfer of invariance optimality across the duality belong to the invariance program of Hunt and Stein (1946) and Stein (1956), as developed in Lehmann's lecture tradition; the relation between invariance and sufficiency in this setting is treated by Hall, Wijsman and Ghosh (1965). The book's Lemma 6.11.1 states both halves; the Lean version proves the dictionary in both directions and the optimality transfer, using the stabilizer in place of an arbitrary group fixing the parameter.

title: Consistency of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test
informal: Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be real-valued observations, let $F_0$ be a fully specified null distribution function, and let $\hat F_n$ be the empirical distribution function of the first $n$ observations. The Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic is $$ T_n \;=\; \sup_{t \in \mathbb{R}} \sqrt{n}\,\bigl|\hat F_n(t) - F_0(t)\bigr| \;=\; \sqrt{n}\, d_K(\hat F_n, F_0), $$ where $d_K$ denotes the sup (Kolmogorov) distance between distribution functions, and the test rejects when $T_n$ exceeds the calibrated critical value $s_\alpha = \sqrt{16 \log(4/\alpha)}$. Assume that the nominal level is a nondegenerate probability, $0 < \alpha < 1$, that the observations are independent and identically distributed with common sampling law $P$ whose distribution function is $F$, that $F_0$ is the distribution function of the null law, and that the alternative genuinely differs from the null, in the sense that $d_K(F, F_0) = \sup_t |F(t) - F_0(t)| > 0$. Then the power of the test tends to one, $$ \mathbb{P}\{T_n > s_\alpha\} \;\longrightarrow\; 1 \qquad (n \to \infty). $$
summary: Against any fixed alternative at positive Kolmogorov distance from the null, the power of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test tends to one.

hypotheses.label: nondegenerate level
hypotheses.note: The nominal level $\alpha$ lies strictly between $0$ and $1$.

hypotheses.label: independent observations
hypotheses.note: The coordinates of the sample are jointly independent.

hypotheses.label: common sampling law
hypotheses.note: Every observation has the same law $P$, whose distribution function is $F$.

hypotheses.label: positive Kolmogorov distance
hypotheses.note: The alternative is separated from the null in the sup distance; this is what makes the separation $\sqrt n\, d_K(F,F_0)$ diverge.

formalizationNotes: Documented calibration deviation: the critical value is not the $1-\alpha$ quantile of the null law of $T_n$ but the constant $s_\alpha=\sqrt{16\log(4/\alpha)}$ obtained by solving $4e^{-s^2/16}=\alpha$, the envelope of the repository's uniform Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz deviation brick. Three consequences, all recorded in the source file: the critical value does not depend on $n$, so the companion level statement (`ks_dkw_level`) is nonasymptotic and no appeal to the Kolmogorov limit law $\mathbb P\{T_n>d\}\to 2\sum_{k\ge1}(-1)^{k+1}e^{-2k^2d^2}$ is made; no continuity assumption on $F_0$ is needed anywhere; and the constants are conservative (the sharp tail is $2e^{-2d^2}$, the brick delivers $4e^{-d^2/16}$), so the calibrated test is conservative rather than exact. The theorem is derived as the constant selection of the triangular-array statement `ks_uniform_power`, the diverging separation being $\varepsilon_n=\sqrt n\,d_K(F,F_0)$. Measurability of the uncountable supremum defining $T_n$ is derived once, from right continuity of the distribution functions, rather than assumed.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The statistic and its limiting distribution are due to Kolmogorov (1933), with the further distribution theory developed by Smirnov (1948); the elementary consistency argument transcribed here goes back to Massey (1950). The book calibrates the test by the $1-\alpha$ quantile of the null law of $T_n$ and proves consistency from the Glivenko–Cantelli theorem together with convergence of the quantiles; the formalization instead calibrates through the uniform deviation inequality of Dvoretzky, Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956), whose sharp constant is due to Massart (1990), so that the critical value is an explicit constant and the level statement is nonasymptotic. What is formalized is therefore the same theorem for a slightly conservative critical value: the power against any fixed $F$ with $d_K(F,F_0)>0$ tends to one, with no continuity assumption on $F_0$.

title: Uniform power of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test over shrinking alternatives
informal: Consider a triangular array of experiments: at stage $n$ the sample $X_{n,1},\dots,X_{n,n}$ is drawn from a law with distribution function $F_n$, and the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test of the fixed null $F_0$ rejects when $T_n = \sqrt n\, d_K(\hat F_n, F_0)$ exceeds the calibrated critical value $s_\alpha$. Assume the nominal level is a nondegenerate probability, $0 < \alpha < 1$, that at every stage the observations are independent and identically distributed, that the stage-$n$ alternative is separated from the null by $\sqrt{n}\, d_K(F_n, F_0) \ge \varepsilon_n$, and that the separation diverges, $\varepsilon_n \to \infty$. Then the power tends to one, $$ \mathbb{P}\{T_n > s_\alpha\} \;\longrightarrow\; 1 . $$ Equivalently: the power of the test converges to one uniformly over the classes of alternatives $\{F : \sqrt n\, d_K(F, F_0) \ge \varepsilon_n\}$. Behind it lies the nonasymptotic bound $\mathbb{P}\{T_n > s_\alpha\} \ge 1 - 4\exp\bigl(-(\varepsilon - s_\alpha)^2/16\bigr)$ valid whenever $\sqrt n\, d_K(F,F_0) \ge \varepsilon > s_\alpha$.
summary: The power of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test tends to one uniformly over alternatives separated from the null by more than $\varepsilon_n/\sqrt n$ whenever $\varepsilon_n \to \infty$.

hypotheses.note: The nominal level $\alpha$ lies strictly between $0$ and $1$.

hypotheses.label: stagewise i.i.d. sample
hypotheses.note: At each sample size the observations are jointly independent with a common stage-$n$ law.

hypotheses.label: separation at stage $n$
hypotheses.note: The stage-$n$ alternative lies at Kolmogorov distance at least $\varepsilon_n/\sqrt n$ from the null.

hypotheses.label: diverging separation
hypotheses.note: The separation sequence $\varepsilon_n$ tends to infinity, which is what forces the power to one.

formalizationNotes: Stated in sequence (triangular-array) form rather than as an infimum of powers over the class $\{F : \sqrt n\, d_K(F,F_0)\ge\varepsilon_n\}$: the two are equivalent for a family of powers bounded in $[0,1]$, and the sequence form is what types, since each stage carries its own sampling law and its own sample of size $n$. The critical value is the DKW-calibrated constant $s_\alpha=\sqrt{16\log(4/\alpha)}$ (see the note on `ks_consistent`), so the nonasymptotic power bound carries the constants $4$ and $(\varepsilon-s_\alpha)^2/16$ in place of the classical sharp $2$ and $2(\varepsilon-s_\alpha)^2$; the classical step “the quantiles converge to a finite limit” disappears because the critical value does not depend on $n$. No continuity of $F_0$ is assumed.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The uniform-power statement is the quantitative companion of Kolmogorov's (1933) limit theorem; the deviation inequality that drives it is due to Dvoretzky, Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956), with the sharp constant obtained by Massart (1990). The book derives the power bound from the limit law plus a separate deviation step; here both the level and the power bound come from one and the same uniform inequality evaluated at two ends, which is why the formalized constants are those of the deviation brick rather than the sharp ones.

title: The Kolmogorov–Smirnov test has no power at $o(n^{-1/2})$
informal: Consider again a triangular array in which the stage-$n$ sample is drawn from a law with distribution function $F_n$, and the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test of the fixed null $F_0$ rejects when $T_n > s_\alpha$. Assume the nominal level is a nondegenerate probability, $0 < \alpha < 1$, that at every stage the observations are independent and identically distributed, and that the alternatives approach the null faster than $n^{-1/2}$, that is $\sqrt n\, d_K(F_n, F_0) \to 0$. Then $$ \limsup_{n \to \infty} \; \mathbb{P}\{T_n > s_\alpha\} \;\le\; \alpha : $$ the test cannot distinguish sequences of alternatives at Kolmogorov distance $o(n^{-1/2})$ from the null, so $n^{-1/2}$ is the exact resolution of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. More generally, if $\sqrt n\, d_K(F_n,F_0) \to \delta$ with $\delta < s_\alpha$, then the limiting power is at most $4\exp\bigl(-(s_\alpha-\delta)^2/16\bigr)$.
summary: Against alternatives approaching the null faster than $n^{-1/2}$ in Kolmogorov distance, the limiting power of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test is at most the nominal level.

The book states the result for the quantile-calibrated test; the formalization proves it for the DKW-calibrated test, where the triangle inequality $d_K(\hat F_n,F_0)\le d_K(\hat F_n,F_n)+d_K(F_n,F_0)$ plus the uniform deviation bound give the conclusion with no loss in the constant.

title: Pearson's chi-squared statistic: the null limiting distribution
informal: In $n$ independent trials, each resulting in one of $k+1$ outcomes, let $Y_j$ denote the number of trials falling in cell $j$ and let $$ Q_n \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{k+1} \frac{(Y_j - n\pi_j)^2}{n\pi_j} $$ be Pearson's chi-squared statistic for the simple null hypothesis that cell $j$ has probability $\pi_j$. Assume there is at least one degree of freedom, $k \ge 1$, that the null cell probabilities are strictly positive, i.e. an interior point of the simplex and sum to one, that at every stage the trials are independent and identically distributed, and that the null hypothesis holds, so that a single trial falls in cell $j$ with probability $\pi_j$. Then $Q_n$ converges in distribution to the chi-squared law with $k$ degrees of freedom, $$ Q_n \;\Longrightarrow\; \chi^2_k . $$ The degrees of freedom are one fewer than the number of cells because the counts satisfy the linear constraint $\sum_j Y_j = n$, so only $k$ of the centred and scaled cell frequencies are free.
summary: Under a simple multinomial null, Pearson's chi-squared statistic converges in distribution to the chi-squared law with one degree of freedom fewer than the number of cells.

hypotheses.label: at least one degree of freedom
hypotheses.note: The chi-squared law with zero degrees of freedom is degenerate, so $k\ge1$ is required.

hypotheses.label: interior null probabilities
hypotheses.note: Every null cell probability is strictly positive; the statistic divides by $n\pi_j$ and the limiting covariance matrix is singular otherwise.

hypotheses.label: probability vector
hypotheses.note: The null cell probabilities sum to one.

hypotheses.label: independent trials
hypotheses.note: At each sample size the trials are jointly independent with a common law.

hypotheses.label: simple null hypothesis
hypotheses.note: The cell probabilities of the sampling law are exactly $\pi_1,\dots,\pi_{k+1}$.

formalizationNotes: The statistic is defined directly on categorical observations taking values in a $(k+1)$-element set rather than on a multinomial random vector: the cell counts are then genuine functions of the sample, the multinomial law is a consequence of independence rather than an assumption, and independence enters exactly as in the other sampling models of the area. Cell probabilities are recorded through the law of a single observation, which keeps the null and the local alternatives in one format. Degenerate cells ($\pi_j=0$) or an empty sample make the corresponding summand a division by zero, i.e. the junk value $0$; every statement carries the interior-point hypothesis. The proof is the multivariate central limit theorem for the vector of the first $k$ centred cell frequencies followed by the continuous mapping theorem for the quadratic form with the inverse covariance matrix; the algebraic identity that this quadratic form equals $Q_n$ (which reintroduces the $(k+1)$-st cell through a Sherman–Morrison inverse) is the only combinatorial step.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The statistic and the chi-squared approximation to its null distribution are due to Pearson (1900). The book's Theorem 16.3.1 is stated for the simple null hypothesis and proved by the multivariate central limit theorem; the formalization follows that route verbatim, with the degrees of freedom $k$ arising from the linear constraint on the cell counts, and adds the interior-point requirement $\pi_j>0$ explicitly, since without it the limiting covariance matrix is singular and the statistic itself divides by zero.

title: Pearson's statistic under local alternatives: the noncentral chi-squared limit
informal: Keep the setting of Pearson's statistic $Q_n$ for the simple null $p = \pi$, but let the true cell probabilities move towards the null at the parametric rate, $$ p^{(n)}_j \;=\; \pi_j + \frac{h_j}{\sqrt n}, \qquad j = 1, \dots, k+1 . $$ Assume the null cell probabilities are strictly positive and sum to one, that the local shifts sum to zero, so that the perturbed vector is again a probability vector, that at every stage the trials are independent and identically distributed, and that at stage $n$ a single trial falls in cell $j$ with probability $\pi_j + h_j/\sqrt n$. Then $$ Q_n \;\Longrightarrow\; \chi^2_k(\lambda), \qquad \lambda \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{k+1} \frac{h_j^2}{\pi_j}, $$ the noncentral chi-squared law with $k$ degrees of freedom and noncentrality parameter $\lambda$. The noncentrality is the squared length of the local shift measured in the multinomial information metric, which is why it governs the local power of the chi-squared test.
summary: Along local alternatives $\pi_j + h_j n^{-1/2}$, Pearson's statistic converges in distribution to a noncentral chi-squared law with noncentrality $\sum_j h_j^2/\pi_j$.

The noncentrality parameter of the limiting law is passed through the positive-part coercion, which is the identity here because the interior-point hypothesis makes $\sum_j h_j^2/\pi_j$ nonnegative. The companion theorem `pearsonQ_local_power_nondegenerate` turns this limit into a power statement: if some $h_j\ne0$ the power of the chi-squared test converges to a limit strictly between $\alpha$ and $1$; and `pearsonQ_consistent` gives power tending to one against any fixed alternative $p\ne\pi$.

title: Pearson's chi-squared test is asymptotically maximin
informal: For the multinomial goodness-of-fit problem with simple null $p = \pi$, consider the shrinking families of alternatives $p = \pi + h/\sqrt n$ whose standardized distance $$ \lambda(h) \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{k+1} \frac{h_j^2}{\pi_j} $$ from the null is at least $b^2$, whose shifts are centred ($\sum_j h_j = 0$), and which keep $\pi + h/\sqrt n$ a probability vector. Assume the family has positive radius, $b > 0$, that the critical value $c$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of the chi-squared law with $k$ degrees of freedom, that the null cell probabilities are strictly positive, that under every local parameter the trials are independent and identically distributed, and that under the local parameter $h$ a single trial falls in cell $j$ with probability $\pi_j + h_j/\sqrt n$. Then the minimum power of Pearson's test, which rejects when $Q_n > c$, converges over that family to $$ \mathbb{P}\bigl\{\chi^2_k(b^2) > c\bigr\}, $$ and no sequence of tests based on the sample whose power at the null tends to $\alpha$ can exceed that value in the limit. Pearson's chi-squared test is therefore asymptotically maximin against these local alternatives; the worst case is asymptotically attained on the inner boundary $\lambda(h) = b^2$, the noncentral chi-squared tail being increasing in the noncentrality parameter.
summary: Over the local multinomial alternatives at standardized distance at least $b$ from the null, Pearson's test attains the maximal limiting minimum power among all sample-based tests of asymptotic level $\alpha$.

formalizationNotes: Adjusted hypothesis: in the optimality half the competing tests are required to be *based on the sample*, i.e. each is a measurable function of the observations. The restriction is needed because the local experiments are abstract data, and without it nothing prevents them from encoding the local parameter $h$ in a coordinate of the sample space that the observations do not see; the source file records a two-cell instance of exactly that, where a competitor reading the hidden coordinate attains asymptotic minimum power $1$. The restriction appears inside the second conjunct of the conclusion rather than as a top-level hypothesis. Pearson's test enters as the nonrandomized critical function $\mathbf{1}\{Q_n>c\}$, so it is a competitor in the same class as the tests quantified over. The upper-bound half is the multinomial instance of the Gaussian-shift transfer lemma `asymptotic_maximin_upper_bound`; the attainment half runs on a whitened score vector built from an orthonormal system in $L^2(\pi)$, where Parseval identifies $Q_n$ with a squared norm and $\lambda(h)$ with the squared norm of the drift. That the worst case is $\lambda=b^2$ uses only stochastic monotonicity of the noncentral chi-squared tail, not the sharper monotone likelihood ratio.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The statistic is Pearson's (1900). Its optimality among tests of asymptotic level $\alpha$, in the maximin sense over shrinking families of local alternatives, follows the least-favourable mixture program of Neyman and Pearson (1933) and Wald (1945), transported to the local limit experiment of Le Cam (1960). The book states the result for the shell $\{h : \lambda(h)\ge b^2\}$; the formalization proves both halves for the sample-size-dependent shell that also requires $\pi+h/\sqrt n$ to be a probability vector, and adds the sample-measurability restriction on competitors, which the optimality half requires.

title: Chi-squared power decreases in the number of degrees of freedom
informal: Let $$ M(k,h) \;=\; \mathbb{P}\bigl\{\chi^2_k(h^2) > c_k\bigr\} $$ be the limiting power of the chi-squared test with $k$ degrees of freedom against a local alternative at standardized distance $|h|$ from the null, where $c_k$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of the central chi-squared law with $k$ degrees of freedom, for every $k \ge 1$ — so that $M(k,0) = \alpha$ — and the nominal level is a nondegenerate probability, $0 < \alpha < 1$. Then $M(\cdot, h)$ is nonincreasing in the number of degrees of freedom, and strictly decreasing when $h \ne 0$: $$ 1 \le k_1 \le k_2 \;\Longrightarrow\; M(k_2, h) \le M(k_1, h), $$ with strict inequality when $k_1 < k_2$ and $h \ne 0$. Spending degrees of freedom on directions in which the alternative does not move costs power; this is the quantitative reason why the number of cells of a chi-squared test cannot be increased for free.
summary: For a fixed noncentrality, the power of the level-$\alpha$ chi-squared test is nonincreasing in the degrees of freedom, and strictly decreasing whenever the noncentrality is positive.

title: Asymptotic maximin upper bound for multisided local alternatives
informal: Let $\{Q_{n,h}\}$ be a triangular array of local experiments indexed by a local parameter $h \in \mathbb{R}^k$ — in the applications, the law of a sample of size $n$ under $\theta_0 + h n^{-1/2}$ — standardized so that the information matrix is the identity, and let $\varphi_n$ be any sequence of randomized tests. Assume the sphere of alternatives has positive radius $b$, that the critical value $c$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of the chi-squared law with $k$ degrees of freedom, that the tests are asymptotically of level $\alpha$, i.e. their power at the null tends to $\alpha$, that the centring statistics $Z_n$ converge in distribution to the standard Gaussian law $N(0, I_k)$ under the null experiment, that the log-likelihood ratio of $Q_{n,h}$ against $Q_{n,0}$ admits the quadratic expansion $\langle h, Z_n\rangle - \tfrac12\|h\|^2$ uniformly over the sphere $\|h\| = b$, with remainder dominated by an envelope that is negligible in probability under the null, and that the families of alternatives eventually contain that sphere. Then $$ \limsup_{n\to\infty}\; \inf_{h \in S_n} \; \mathbb{E}_{Q_{n,h}}[\varphi_n] \;\le\; \mathbb{P}\bigl\{\chi^2_k(b^2) > c\bigr\}. $$ The bound is proved by the least-favourable mixture route: the minimum power over the alternatives is at most the power against the uniform mixture over the sphere, the Neyman–Pearson lemma bounds the latter by the power of the likelihood-ratio test, and the sphere-averaged limiting likelihood ratio is a monotone function of $\|x\|$, so that the limiting Neyman–Pearson test *is* the chi-squared test.
summary: In an asymptotically normal array of local experiments, no test sequence of asymptotic level $\alpha$ can exceed the noncentral chi-squared value in minimum power over a sphere of local alternatives.

formalizationNotes: Two amendments to the frozen statement, both forced and both strengthenings for the consumers. First, the conclusion is quantified over any family of alternatives containing the least-favourable sphere, rather than over the single shell $\{h : h^\top I h \ge b^2\}$: that shell is a strict superset of both consumers' families (the smooth test uses a bounded shell $b\le\|h\|\le B$, the multinomial one carries an extra sample-size dependent positivity constraint), and an infimum over a subset is larger, so the frozen conclusion transfers to neither. Second, the information matrix is standardized to the identity; the general positive definite case is the reparametrization $\eta = I^{1/2}h$, performed by the consumer on its own shell. Two further generalizations are free and needed: the sample space may vary with $n$, and the shell condition is only required eventually. Two hypotheses are honest regularity requirements of the mixture argument rather than restrictions: joint measurability of the log-likelihood field (without it the mixture likelihood ratio is not a random variable), and uniformity of the LAN remainder over the sphere — the pointwise-in-$h$ remainder does not imply it, and the mixture step genuinely needs it. The mixing measure is not constructed by hand but realized as the law of the direction of a standard Gaussian vector rescaled to length $b$; the accompanying `sphereAverage_lr_monotone` shows the sphere-averaged likelihood ratio is a monotone function of the norm.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The maximin principle for tests and the least-favourable mixture device are due to Neyman and Pearson (1933) and Wald (1945); the rotation-invariant mixture that produces the chi-squared test as a maximin procedure in the Gaussian shift experiment, and the reduction of local testing problems to that experiment, are due to Le Cam (1960). The book uses this argument twice, for Pearson's test in §16.3 and for the smooth test in §16.4; the formalization isolates it once, as a statement about an asymptotically normal array of local experiments, and both goodness-of-fit maximin theorems are instances of it.

title: Neyman's smooth test is asymptotically maximin
informal: To test a fully specified null law $P_0$ on an arbitrary sample space, embed it in the $k$-parameter exponential family of densities $$ p_\theta(x) \;=\; C_k(\theta)\exp\Bigl(\sum_{j=1}^{k}\theta_j\,\psi_j(x)\Bigr) $$ relative to $P_0$, and test $\theta = 0$ with Neyman's smooth statistic $$ S_n \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{k} Z_{n,j}^2, \qquad Z_{n,j} \;=\; n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi_j(X_i), $$ rejecting when $S_n > c$. Assume the shell of alternatives has positive inner radius $b$ and a finite outer radius $B > b$, that the critical value $c$ is the $1-\alpha$ quantile of the chi-squared law with $k$ degrees of freedom, that the score functions $\psi_1,\dots,\psi_k$ are orthonormal in $L^2(P_0)$ and orthogonal to the constants, i.e. have mean zero under $P_0$, that the null value $\theta = 0$ is an interior point of the natural parameter set, and that under the local parameter $h$ the observations are an independent sample from $p_{h n^{-1/2}}$. Then the minimum power of the smooth test over the local alternatives $\theta = h n^{-1/2}$ with $b \le \|h\| \le B$ converges to $$ \mathbb{P}\bigl\{\chi^2_k(b^2) > c\bigr\}, $$ and no sequence of sample-based tests of asymptotic level $\alpha$ does better in the limit. The worst case is asymptotically attained on the inner boundary $\|h\| = b$.
summary: Over the local alternatives $b \le \|h\| \le B$ of the embedding exponential family, Neyman's smooth test attains the maximal limiting minimum power among all sample-based tests of asymptotic level $\alpha$.

It is needed because the local experiment is abstract data and may encode $\|h\|$ in a coordinate the observations do not see, which a competitor reading that coordinate can exploit; the source file records such a local experiment. title: Neyman's smooth test with a growing number of score directions
informal: For a fixed number $k$ of score directions the smooth test is consistent only against alternatives that move one of the first $k$ scores. Letting $k$ grow with the sample size removes that restriction, at the price of a different limit theory: since $\chi^2_k \approx N(k, 2k)$ for large $k$, the chi-squared approximation is replaced by a normal one. Assume the score functions are orthonormal in $L^2(P_0)$ and orthogonal to the constants, that their third absolute moments are finite and uniformly bounded, $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}|\psi_j(X)|^3 \le B$ for every $j$, and that the number of directions diverges, $k_n \to \infty$, but slowly enough that $k_n^3/n \to 0$. Then, under the null hypothesis that the observations are an independent sample from $P_0$, $$ \frac{S_{n,k_n} - k_n}{(2k_n)^{1/2}} \;\Longrightarrow\; N(0,1), $$ so that the test rejecting when that ratio exceeds the standard normal upper-$\alpha$ quantile is asymptotically of level $\alpha$.
summary: If the number of score directions grows with $k_n^3/n \to 0$, the standardized smooth statistic is asymptotically standard normal under the null.

The absence of a dimensional factor in the constant is what makes the growth condition as weak as $k_n^3/n\to0$; the convex-set bound, whose constant carries a factor $k^{1/4}$, would force the strictly stronger $k_n^{7/2}/n\to0$. title: Limit law of an efficient estimator under local alternatives
informal: Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be independent observations from a model $\{P_\theta\}$ that is differentiable in quadratic mean at $\theta_0$ with score $\tilde\eta_{\theta_0}$, given by densities with respect to a dominating measure, and whose Fisher information matrix $I(\theta_0)$ is nonsingular. Let $\hat\theta_n$ be an asymptotically linear (efficient) estimator sequence at $\theta_0$, i.e. one satisfying $\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n - \theta_0) = I^{-1}(\theta_0) Z_n + o_P(1)$ under $P^n_{\theta_0}$, where $$ Z_n \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i \le n} \tilde\eta_{\theta_0}(X_i) $$ is the normalized score. The expansion is assumed *only at $\theta_0$*. Then for every local alternative sequence $\theta_n = \theta_0 + h_n/\sqrt n$ with $h_n \to h$, under $P^n_{\theta_n}$, $$ \sqrt{n}\,(\hat\theta_n - \theta_n) \;\rightsquigarrow\; N\bigl(0, I^{-1}(\theta_0)\bigr), $$ the same law as under $\theta_0$; equivalently $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n - \theta_0) \rightsquigarrow N(h, I^{-1}(\theta_0))$. This weak robustness of the limiting law under perturbations of size $n^{-1/2}$ is what makes such estimator sequences the backbone of asymptotic testing theory.
summary: An asymptotically linear estimator sequence, recentred at a local alternative, has the same Gaussian limit law there as it has at the null.

The proof route is contiguity of the local experiments plus Le Cam's third lemma applied to the pair (linearized estimator, log-likelihood ratio), followed by the Cramér–Wold device; the fixed-direction case is proved for the full sequence, with no subsequence extraction, because asymptotic linearity identifies the joint limit outright, and the moving direction $h_n$ is replaced by its limit through an $n$-fold Hellinger estimate obtained by tensorising the per-sample residual. The file is free of unproved content. title: The normalized score vector under local alternatives
informal: Let the model be differentiable in quadratic mean at $\theta_0$ with score $\tilde\eta_{\theta_0}$, given by densities with respect to a dominating measure, and with nonsingular Fisher information matrix $I(\theta_0)$. Under $P^n_{\theta_0}$ the normalized score $$ Z_n \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i\le n}\tilde\eta_{\theta_0}(X_i) $$ is asymptotically $N(0, I(\theta_0))$. Then along a local alternative sequence $\theta_n = \theta_0 + h_n/\sqrt n$ with $h_n \to h$, the limit is the *same Gaussian, shifted by* $I(\theta_0)h$: $$ Z_n \;\rightsquigarrow\; N\bigl(I(\theta_0)h,\; I(\theta_0)\bigr) \qquad \text{under } P^n_{\theta_n}. $$ The alternative moves the mean of the limiting law while leaving the covariance unchanged, which is exactly what makes the local power of the score test computable.
summary: Along local alternatives the normalized score vector converges to the same Gaussian law as under the null, shifted in mean by the information matrix applied to the local direction.

title: The Rao score statistic is asymptotically chi-squared
informal: Test the simple null $\theta = \theta_0$ in an i.i.d. model with $k$-dimensional parameter, using the Rao score statistic $$ R_n \;=\; Z_n^{\top}\, I^{-1}(\theta_0)\, Z_n, \qquad Z_n \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i\le n}\tilde\eta_{\theta_0}(X_i), $$ a quadratic form in the normalized score that uses no estimator of the parameter at all. Assume the model is a family of densities with respect to a dominating measure, that it is differentiable in quadratic mean at $\theta_0$ with score $\tilde\eta_{\theta_0}$, and that the Fisher information matrix $I(\theta_0)$ is positive definite. Then, under $P^n_{\theta_0}$, $$ R_n \;\rightsquigarrow\; \chi^2_k . $$ Consequently the score test rejecting when $R_n$ exceeds the $1-\alpha$ quantile of $\chi^2_k$ is asymptotically of level $\alpha$.
summary: Under the simple null, the Rao score statistic converges in distribution to the chi-squared law with as many degrees of freedom as parameters.

title: Asymptotic equivalence of the Wald, score and likelihood ratio statistics
informal: Three statistics test the same simple null $\theta = \theta_0$ in an i.i.d. quadratic mean differentiable model: the Wald statistic $W_n = n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)^{\top} I(\theta_0)(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)$, the Rao score statistic $R_n = Z_n^{\top} I^{-1}(\theta_0) Z_n$, and the likelihood ratio statistic $2\log \Lambda_n = 2[\ell_n(\hat\theta_n) - \ell_n(\theta_0)]$. Assume the model is differentiable in quadratic mean at $\theta_0$ with score $\tilde\eta_{\theta_0}$, that the Fisher information $I(\theta_0)$ is positive definite, that $\hat\theta_n$ is an efficient (asymptotically linear) estimator sequence, and, for the likelihood ratio half, that there is an envelope function $M$ with finite mean under $P_{\theta_0}$ satisfying the two-point second-order bound $\bigl|\log(p_\theta(x)/p_{\theta_0}(x)) - \log(p_{\theta'}(x)/p_{\theta_0}(x)) - \langle\theta-\theta', \tilde\eta_{\theta_0}(x)\rangle\bigr| \le M(x)(\|\theta-\theta_0\| + \|\theta'-\theta_0\|)\|\theta-\theta'\|$ for all $\theta, \theta'$ in a neighbourhood of $\theta_0$ and all sample points $x$. Then, under $P^n_{\theta_0}$, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $$ \mathbb{P}\{|W_n - R_n| \ge \varepsilon\} \to 0 \quad\text{and}\quad \mathbb{P}\{|2\log\Lambda_n - R_n| \ge \varepsilon\} \to 0 . $$ The three tests therefore reject the same data sets with probability tending to one, and each statistic converges in distribution to $\chi^2_k$.
summary: Under the simple null, the Wald and likelihood ratio statistics each differ from the Rao score statistic by a quantity tending to zero in probability.

title: Wilks' theorem for an affine composite null
informal: Let the null hypothesis restrict $\theta$ to an affine subspace $a + \operatorname{range} B$ of the $k$-dimensional parameter space — equivalently, $A(\theta - a) = 0$ for a matrix $A$ of full rank $p$ — where the chart $B$ is injective and the codimension is the difference of dimensions, $m + p = k$ with $p \ge 1$. Let $\hat\theta_n$ be an efficient estimator sequence in the full model and $\hat\beta_n$ an efficient estimator sequence in the restricted model $\beta \mapsto P_{a + B\beta}$, and form $$ 2\log\Lambda_n \;=\; 2\bigl[\ell_n(\hat\theta_n) - \ell_n(a + B\hat\beta_n)\bigr]. $$ Assume the model is differentiable in quadratic mean at a null point $\theta_0 = a + B\beta_0$ with positive definite information, that the two-point second-order envelope condition holds on a neighbourhood of $\theta_0$ with an integrable envelope, and that no parameter value kills a sample point that $\theta_0$ keeps. Then, under $P^n_{\theta_0}$, $$ 2\log\Lambda_n \;\rightsquigarrow\; \chi^2_p : $$ the degrees of freedom count the restrictions, i.e. the dimension of the full parameter space minus that of the null.
summary: For a null restricting the parameter to an affine subspace of codimension $p$, the likelihood ratio statistic converges in distribution to the chi-squared law with $p$ degrees of freedom.

formalizationNotes: The composite null is presented as an affine subspace given by a chart rather than by constraint equations, which lets the restricted model be an honest parametric family in the chart, so that “efficient estimator assuming the null” is the *same* predicate applied to the restricted model rather than an unverified formula for its influence function; differentiability in quadratic mean, the score and the information matrix all transport along the chart, the restricted score being the adjoint image of the full one. The smooth constraint version (null $\{\theta : g(\theta)=0\}$ with a continuously differentiable $g$ of full-rank Jacobian) is not stated separately: at $\theta_0$ it is this statement in the chart supplied by the implicit function theorem, with the same $p$ degrees of freedom. Two adjustments are recorded on the declaration: the common-support hypothesis, without which the splitting of the affine likelihood ratio does not hold at the points where a density vanishes and the ratio takes its junk value, and the two-point envelope condition. Joint measurability of the densities in parameter and sample point is required for the statistic to be a measurable function of the sample.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The chi-squared limit of the likelihood ratio statistic for a composite null is Wilks' (1938) theorem; the companion Wald (1943) formulation tests the same restrictions through the estimator. The modern proof under quadratic-mean differentiability and contiguity is due to Le Cam (1960, 1970). The book states the result for a null given either by linear restrictions or by smooth constraints; the formalization proves the affine case in a chart of the null subspace — which is the same statement — and identifies the affine likelihood ratio with the difference of two simple-null score statistics, whence the $p$ degrees of freedom.

title: Uniform local asymptotic normality over bounded directions
informal: The quadratic expansion of the log-likelihood ratio $$ \log L_{n,h} \;=\; \langle h, Z_n\rangle - \tfrac12\langle h, I(\theta_0)h\rangle + o_P(1), \qquad L_{n,h} = \frac{L_n(\theta_0 + h/\sqrt n)}{L_n(\theta_0)}, $$ holds under quadratic mean differentiability for each *fixed* direction $h$. Arguments that substitute a *random* direction — most importantly $\hat h_n = \sqrt n(\hat\theta_n - \theta_0)$ in the analysis of the likelihood ratio statistic — need the remainder to be small uniformly over $\|h\| \le c$. Assume the model is differentiable in quadratic mean at $\theta_0$ with score $\tilde\eta_{\theta_0}$, that there is an envelope $M$ with finite mean under $P_{\theta_0}$ satisfying the two-point second-order bound $\bigl|\log(p_\theta(x)/p_{\theta_0}(x)) - \log(p_{\theta'}(x)/p_{\theta_0}(x)) - \langle\theta-\theta', \tilde\eta_{\theta_0}(x)\rangle\bigr| \le M(x)(\|\theta-\theta_0\|+\|\theta'-\theta_0\|)\|\theta-\theta'\|$ for all $\theta, \theta'$ in a neighbourhood of $\theta_0$ and all sample points $x$, and fix a radius $c > 0$. Then, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, the probability under $P^n_{\theta_0}$ that *some* direction with $\|h\| \le c$ has remainder at least $\varepsilon$ tends to zero; equivalently $$ \epsilon_{n,c} \;=\; \sup_{\|h\|\le c}\Bigl|\log L_{n,h} - \bigl[\langle h, Z_n\rangle - \tfrac12\langle h, I(\theta_0)h\rangle\bigr]\Bigr| \;\xrightarrow{\;P\;}\; 0 . $$
summary: Under quadratic mean differentiability and a two-point second-order envelope condition, the remainder of the quadratic log-likelihood expansion is small uniformly over every bounded set of local directions.

hypotheses.label: quadratic mean differentiability
hypotheses.note: Differentiability in quadratic mean at $\theta_0$ with the stated score; it gives the expansion for each fixed direction.

hypotheses.label: integrable envelope
hypotheses.note: The envelope has finite mean under the single-observation law at $\theta_0$; only its mean is used, through Markov's inequality — no law of large numbers is needed.

hypotheses.label: two-point second-order envelope
hypotheses.note: Amended from the printed one-point condition, which does not suffice: it is the increments of the remainder, not its size at each point, that a random direction probes.

hypotheses.label: radius of directions
hypotheses.note: Uniformity is claimed over the closed ball of radius $c$ in the local parameter.

formalizationNotes: Documented adjustment of the envelope condition. The source's condition is one-point, $|\log p_\theta(x)-\log p_{\theta_0}(x)-\langle\theta-\theta_0,\tilde\eta_{\theta_0}(x)\rangle|\le M(x)\|\theta-\theta_0\|^2$, and it does not by itself give the uniform statement; the source file records the configuration it leaves open, a model on $[0,1]$ whose densities carry a perturbation $\exp(|\theta-\theta_0|^2(2\cdot\mathbf{1}_{A_{|\theta-\theta_0|}}-1))$ indexed by finite sets $A_s$ chosen so that for each $n$ some direction with $\|h\|\le c$ picks out the observed sample. Every fixed direction then has vanishing remainder almost surely, as it must, while at a data-dependent direction the remainder is at least $2c^2 n/(n+1)$, so the probability in the conclusion tends to one. The two-point form used here is the weakest strengthening that covers this: taking $\theta'=\theta_0$ returns the printed condition verbatim, it follows from an integrable bound on the second derivative of the log-density, and it is exactly what makes the remainder class stochastically equicontinuous. The supremum over an uncountable ball is avoided at statement level: instead of asserting that a possibly non-measurable supremum converges in probability, the statement bounds the (outer) measure of the event that some admissible direction has remainder at least $\varepsilon$, which is equivalent when quantified over all $\varepsilon>0$ and needs no measurable-selection argument. The proof is a net argument: the two-point envelope makes the remainder Lipschitz in $h$ with a random constant that is bounded in probability, and a finite net of the compact ball reduces uniformity to finitely many fixed-direction statements.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The quadratic expansion of the log-likelihood ratio and the local asymptotic normality framework are due to Le Cam (1960), with the quadratic-mean differentiability hypothesis introduced in Le Cam (1970). Uniform-in-direction control of the remainder is the technical device by which the classical likelihood ratio theory of Wilks (1938) is recovered without third-derivative conditions. The book states the expansion for fixed directions and uses it at a random one; the formalization isolates the uniform version, shows that the printed hypotheses do not imply it, and proves it under the two-point strengthening.

title: The Randomization Hypothesis
informal: Let $\mathbf{G}$ be a finite group of transformations acting on the sample space $\mathcal{X}$, and let $P$ be a candidate null distribution of the data $X$. The randomization hypothesis holds for $P$ when the law of the data is unchanged by every element of the group: for each $g \in \mathbf{G}$ the transformed observation $gX$ has the same distribution as $X$, that is, the image of $P$ under the map $x \mapsto gx$ is again $P$. Only the null law is required to be invariant; nothing at all is assumed about the distribution of the data under an alternative. Two standard instances are the group of the $2^n$ sign changes $x \mapsto (\pm x_1, \ldots, \pm x_n)$, for which the hypothesis says that the observations are symmetric about $0$, and the group of the $N!$ permutations of the coordinates of a pooled sample, for which it says that the pooled observations are exchangeable.
summary: The null distribution of the data is invariant under every element of a finite group of transformations of the sample space.
leanSignature:
def RandomizationHypothesis (P : Measure 𝓧) : Prop :=
  ∀ g : G, P.map (g • ·) = P
formalizationNotes: Stated for an arbitrary finite group acting on an arbitrary measurable space; invariance is expressed as equality of the pushforward measure with the original one. Measurability of the individual transformations is deliberately not built into the definition — it is carried as an explicit hypothesis wherever it is needed, because the group action is user-supplied data rather than something the setup forces.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: Randomization tests originate with R. A. Fisher (1935) and E. J. G. Pitman (1937); the group-theoretic formulation used here, in which a finite group of transformations leaves the null law invariant, is due to E. L. Lehmann and C. Stein (1949). The reference text isolates the invariance requirement as the defining condition of the whole construction, and the formalization follows it literally: invariance of $P$ under each element of the group, with no requirement whatsoever on the alternative.

title: The Randomization Test
informal: Fix a finite group $\mathbf{G}$ of transformations of the sample space, write $M = |\mathbf{G}|$, and let $T$ be an arbitrary real-valued test statistic. Given an observed data point $x$, order the $M$ values $T(gx)$, $g \in \mathbf{G}$, taken by the statistic over the orbit of $x$ as $$ T^{(1)}(x) \le T^{(2)}(x) \le \cdots \le T^{(M)}(x) , $$ and put $k = M - \lfloor M\alpha \rfloor$, so that $T^{(k)}(x)$ is the critical orbit order statistic. Write $M^{+}(x)$ for the number of group elements with $T(gx) > T^{(k)}(x)$ and $M^{0}(x)$ for the number with $T(gx) = T^{(k)}(x)$, and set $$ a(x) \;=\; \frac{M\alpha - M^{+}(x)}{M^{0}(x)} . $$ The randomization test is the critical function $\varphi$ that rejects when $T(x) > T^{(k)}(x)$, rejects with probability $a(x)$ when $T(x) = T^{(k)}(x)$, and accepts when $T(x) < T^{(k)}(x)$. The boundary weight is chosen so that $M^{+}(x) + a(x)\,M^{0}(x) = M\alpha$ exactly, which is what lets the construction calibrate without any integrality assumption on $M\alpha$.
summary: The level-$\alpha$ randomization test, which compares the observed statistic with the order statistics of its values over the orbit and randomizes on the boundary.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def randTest (T : 𝓧 → ℝ) (α : ℝ) (x : 𝓧) : ℝ :=
  if randCritValue G T α x < T x then 1
  else if T x = randCritValue G T α x then randGamma G T α x
  else 0
formalizationNotes: All constructions are total. Out-of-range orbit order statistics return $0$, and the boundary weight's denominator $M^{0}(x)$ is at least $1$ whenever the observed statistic equals the critical value (the identity element of the group always contributes), so the $0/0$ corner is unreachable in every statement that uses the test. That the resulting value always lies in $[0,1]$ — i.e. that this really is a critical function — is proved from the orbit identity rather than assumed.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The construction is Fisher's (1935) randomization test in the group-theoretic form of E. L. Lehmann and C. Stein (1949), with the boundary randomization that makes the level exact for arbitrary $M\alpha$. M. Dwass (1957) showed that a random subset of the group may be used in place of the whole group. The formalization transcribes the reference text's definition, including the ordering of the orbit values and the critical index $k = M - \lfloor M\alpha\rfloor$; it is defined for an arbitrary statistic, with no distributional input.

title: Exact Finite-Sample Level of the Randomization Test
informal: Let $\mathbf{G}$ be a finite group of transformations of the sample space, $M = |\mathbf{G}|$, and let $\varphi$ be the randomization test at nominal level $\alpha$ built from a real-valued statistic $T$. Assume that the statistic $T$ is measurable, that each transformation $x \mapsto gx$ is measurable, and that the null law $P$ is invariant under every element of the group. If the nominal level satisfies $\alpha > 0$ and $\alpha < 1$, then the test has size exactly $\alpha$, $$ \mathbb{E}_P[\varphi(X)] \;=\; \alpha , $$ at every finite sample size. The proof is the averaging argument: for every data point $x$ and every statistic one has the counting identity $\sum_{g \in \mathbf{G}} \varphi(gx) = M\alpha$, and integrating it against $P$ while using invariance to replace each $\mathbb{E}_P[\varphi(gX)]$ by $\mathbb{E}_P[\varphi(X)]$ gives the conclusion. In particular nothing is assumed about $T$ beyond measurability, and $M\alpha$ need not be an integer.
summary: Under the randomization hypothesis the randomization test built from any statistic has size exactly $\alpha$ at every finite sample size.

    {α : ℝ}
    (hα₀ : 0 < α) (hα₁ : α < 1) :
    powerAgainst P (randTest G T α) = α

hypotheses.label: level below one
hypotheses.note: Together with positivity this keeps the critical index inside the range of the orbit order statistics.

formalizationNotes: No integrality condition on $M\alpha$ appears anywhere: the boundary weight is defined so that the orbit sum equals $M\alpha$ exactly. The level restriction $0 < \alpha < 1$ is needed only to keep the critical index in the range $\{1, \dots, M\}$, so that the critical value stays off the junk branch of the order-statistic definition, and to guarantee that the boundary count is at least one. Measurability of the action is an explicit hypothesis rather than a typeclass instance, matching the convention of the whole randomization cluster.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The exact-level property is due to E. L. Lehmann and C. Stein (1949), building on R. A. Fisher (1935) and E. J. G. Pitman (1937); the variant using a random subset of the group is M. Dwass (1957). The reference text states the result for a finite group of transformations under which the null law is invariant, and the formalization proves exactly that, deriving the pointwise orbit identity as a purely combinatorial statement valid for every data point and every statistic, with the distributional hypothesis entering only in the averaging step.

title: Super-Uniformity of the Randomization $p$-Value
informal: With $\mathbf{G}$ a finite group of transformations, $M = |\mathbf{G}|$ and $T$ a real-valued statistic, the randomization $p$-value at a data point $x$ is the proportion of the orbit on which the statistic is at least as large as the observed value, $$ \hat p(x) \;=\; \frac{1}{M}\,\#\{\, g \in \mathbf{G} : T(x) \le T(gx) \,\} . $$ Assume that the statistic is measurable, that each transformation of the sample space is measurable, and that the null law is invariant under every element of the group. Then the $p$-value is super-uniform under the null law, $$ \mathbb{P}\{\hat p(X) \le u\} \;\le\; u \qquad \text{for all } 0 \le u \le 1 , $$ so that the nonrandomized test rejecting when $\hat p(X) \le \alpha$ has level $\alpha$ at every finite sample size, with no boundary randomization.
summary: Under the randomization hypothesis the randomization $p$-value is stochastically at least uniform, so rejecting when it is at most $\alpha$ gives a level-$\alpha$ test.
