formalizationNotes: Stated in the library's super-uniformity form, which quantifies over all thresholds at least $0$; the substantive range is $[0,1]$, and above $1$ the bound is trivial because the law is a probability measure. The proof is a rank argument on each orbit — at most $\lfloor Mt \rfloor$ of the $M$ orbit points can have $p$-value at most $t$ — averaged over the invariant law, so no continuity or tie-breaking assumption on the statistic is used.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The $p$-value formulation of the randomization test goes back to R. A. Fisher (1935); its validity under group invariance is the $p$-value form of the Lehmann–Stein (1949) exactness theorem, and M. Dwass (1957) gives the version based on a random subset of the group. The reference text presents it as the practical form of the test; the formalization proves the super-uniformity inequality directly from a pointwise rank bound on each orbit, without discretizing the level or assuming that ties have probability zero.

title: The Conditional Law Given the Orbit is the Randomization Distribution
informal: The orbits $\mathbf{G}x = \{gx : g \in \mathbf{G}\}$ of a finite transformation group partition the sample space; write $\mathcal{G}$ for the $\sigma$-field of sets that are unions of orbits, and $M = |\mathbf{G}|$. Assume that the statistic $T$ is measurable, that each transformation of the sample space is measurable, and that the null law is invariant under every element of the group. Then, for every threshold $t$, $$ \mathbb{P}\{\, T(X) \le t \mid \mathcal{G} \,\} \;=\; \frac{1}{M}\sum_{g \in \mathbf{G}} \mathbf{1}\{T(gX) \le t\} \qquad \text{almost surely,} $$ that is, the conditional distribution function of the statistic given the orbit of the data is exactly the randomization distribution. Equivalently, given its own orbit the data point is uniformly distributed over the $M$ points of that orbit; when the $M$ orbit values of the statistic are distinct, the conditional law of $T(X)$ is literally the uniform distribution on them. Since this conditional law is the same for every invariant null distribution, a test calibrated conditionally on the orbit is unconditionally exact.
summary: Under the randomization hypothesis the conditional distribution of the statistic given the orbit of the data is the uniform distribution on the orbit values, i.e. the randomization distribution.

hypotheses.label: randomization hypothesis
hypotheses.note: The null law is invariant under every element of the finite group.

formalizationNotes: The orbit $\sigma$-field is realized as the $\sigma$-algebra of measurable sets invariant under every group element. For a finite group this coincides with the $\sigma$-field generated by the orbit partition — a measurable set is a union of orbits precisely when each group element maps it onto itself — and working with the invariant sets directly avoids constructing the generated $\sigma$-field and makes measurability of the orbit average immediate. The general statement is proved for bounded measurable integrands; the displayed distribution-function form is its specialization to indicators of half-lines. Boundedness rather than integrability is the honest hypothesis, since it is what the indicator application supplies.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The conditional-uniformity description of randomization tests is due to E. L. Lehmann and C. Stein (1949), building on R. A. Fisher (1935) and E. J. G. Pitman (1937). The reference text derives it as the structural reason the construction is exact: the conditional law given the orbit does not depend on which invariant null distribution generated the data. The formalization proves the conditional-expectation identity against the $\sigma$-algebra of invariant sets and then specializes to indicators of half-lines to identify the right-hand side with the randomization distribution.

title: Asymptotic Behaviour of the Randomization Distribution
informal: Consider a triangular array: for each sample size $n$ a law $P_n$ on a sample space $\mathcal{X}_n$, a finite group $\mathbf{G}_n$ acting on it, and a real-valued statistic $T_n$. Write $$ \hat R_n(t) \;=\; \frac{1}{|\mathbf{G}_n|}\sum_{g \in \mathbf{G}_n} \mathbf{1}\{T_n(gX^n) \le t\} $$ for the randomization distribution, and let $G_n, G_n'$ be independent and uniformly distributed on $\mathbf{G}_n$, independent of the data $X^n$. Assume that each statistic is measurable, that each group element acts measurably, and that the pair $\bigl(T_n(G_nX^n), T_n(G_n'X^n)\bigr)$ converges in distribution to a pair of independent random variables with common distribution $R$. Then, at every continuity point $t$ of the limiting distribution function, $$ \hat R_n(t) \;\xrightarrow{\;\mathbb{P}\;}\; R(t) . $$ Nothing here assumes the randomization hypothesis: the result describes the behaviour of the randomization distribution even when the null invariance fails, which is exactly what is needed to decide whether a randomization test remains asymptotically level $\alpha$. Under the same joint condition the $(1-\alpha)$-quantile of the randomization distribution — the data-dependent critical value — converges in probability to the corresponding quantile of the limit law, provided the latter is continuous and strictly increasing there.
summary: If the statistic recomputed at two independent uniform group elements is asymptotically independent with a common limit law, the randomization distribution converges in probability to that limit law.

title: Asymptotic Normality of the Sign-Change Randomization Distribution
informal: Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be independent observations on the line with common law $P$, and take as randomization group the group of the $2^n$ sign changes $(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_n)\cdot(x_1,\dots,x_n) = (\varepsilon_1x_1, \dots, \varepsilon_nx_n)$ with $\varepsilon_i \in \{\pm 1\}$. Let $\tilde P$ denote the symmetrization of $P$, the law of $X$ multiplied by an independent random sign, whose distribution function is $\tilde F(t) = \tfrac12\bigl[F(t) + 1 - F(-t)\bigr]$ at continuity points of $F$. Assume that the influence function $\psi$ is odd, that it is measurable, that it is square-integrable under the symmetrized law, that its second moment under the symmetrized law equals $\tau^2$, that each statistic $T_n$ is measurable, and that the statistic is asymptotically linear under the symmetrized law, meaning that $T_n - n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi(X_i)$ tends to $0$ in probability when the data are drawn from $\tilde P$. Then, under the original law $P$, the sign-change randomization distribution satisfies $$ \hat R_n(t) \;\xrightarrow{\;\mathbb{P}\;}\; \Phi(t/\tau) \qquad \text{for every } t , $$ with $\Phi$ the standard normal distribution function; correspondingly the data-dependent critical value converges in probability to $\tau\,z_{1-\alpha}$. Symmetry of $P$ is not required: the randomization distribution still stabilizes, but at the scale of the symmetrized model rather than at the true sampling scale. When $P$ is symmetric about $0$ the randomization hypothesis holds, $\tilde P = P$, and the test is in addition exact at every finite sample size.
summary: For an asymptotically linear statistic with odd influence function the sign-change randomization distribution converges in probability to a normal distribution function whose scale is that of the symmetrized model, even when the sampling law is not symmetric.

title: Two-Sample Permutation Central Limit Theorem
informal: Let $Y_1, \dots, Y_m$ be independent with law $P_Y$ and $Z_1, \dots, Z_n$ independent with law $P_Z$, independent of the first sample, and pool them into a vector of length $N = m + n$ on which the group of all $N!$ coordinate permutations acts. The statistic is the scaled difference of sample means $$ T_{m,n} \;=\; \sqrt{m}\,\bigl(\bar Y_m - \bar Z_n\bigr) . $$ Assume that both sample sizes tend to infinity, that the ratio $m/n$ converges to a limit $\lambda$ which is strictly positive, that both populations have finite second moments, that they share a common mean $\mu$, that both population variances are strictly positive, and write $\tau^2 = \lambda\,\sigma^2(P_Y) + \sigma^2(P_Z)$ for the permutation scale. Let $\pi$ and $\pi'$ be independent uniform random permutations of the pooled sample. Then $$ \bigl(T_{m,n}(\pi X),\; T_{m,n}(\pi' X)\bigr) \;\xrightarrow{\;d\;}\; N(0,\tau^2)\otimes N(0,\tau^2) , $$ the two coordinates being independent in the limit. This is exactly the joint asymptotic-independence condition required by the general theory, so the permutation distribution of $T_{m,n}$ converges in probability to $\Phi(\cdot/\tau)$. The unconditional limit of the same statistic is a different normal law, $N\bigl(0, \sigma^2(P_Y) + \lambda\,\sigma^2(P_Z)\bigr)$, with the roles of $\lambda$ and the two variances interchanged. The two scales agree exactly when $\lambda = 1$ or the two variances are equal; otherwise the unstudentized permutation test does not have asymptotic level $\alpha$ for testing equality of means, which is what makes the studentized version necessary.
summary: The scaled difference of two sample means, evaluated at two independent uniform random permutations of the pooled data, converges jointly to a pair of independent centred normal variables with permutation variance $\lambda\sigma_Y^2 + \sigma_Z^2$.

title: A Slutsky Theorem for Randomization Distributions
informal: Let $T_n$, $A_n$ and $B_n$ be statistics defined on a triangular array with finite groups $\mathbf{G}_n$ acting on the sample spaces, and write $$ \hat R_n^{AT+B}(t) \;=\; \frac{1}{|\mathbf{G}_n|}\sum_{g \in \mathbf{G}_n} \mathbf{1}\bigl\{A_n(gX^n)\,T_n(gX^n) + B_n(gX^n) \le t\bigr\} $$ for the randomization distribution of the affinely transformed statistic. Assume that the base statistic evaluated at two independent uniform group elements converges jointly in law to a pair of independent variables with common law $R$, that the random scaling converges in probability to a constant $a$ when evaluated at randomized data, and that the random shift converges in probability to a constant $b$ at randomized data. Then, at every continuity point $t$ of the law of $aT + b$, $$ \hat R_n^{AT+B}(t) \;\xrightarrow{\;\mathbb{P}\;}\; \mathbb{P}\{aT + b \le t\} . $$ The convergence required of the scaling and shift is at the randomized data $G_nX^n$, with $G_n$ uniform on the group and independent of the data — not at $X^n$ itself; equivalently, the group average of the failure probabilities tends to zero. No invariance of the scaling or shift under the group is assumed, which matters because in the studentized application the scale is a sample variance that is genuinely not invariant.
summary: If a base statistic satisfies the joint asymptotic-independence condition and a random scaling and shift stabilize at constants under a random group element, the randomization distribution of the affine combination converges to the law of the transformed limit.

title: Asymptotic Validity of the Studentized Two-Sample Permutation Test
informal: Pool two independent samples $Y_1, \dots, Y_m \sim P_Y$ and $Z_1, \dots, Z_n \sim P_Z$, and studentize the scaled difference of sample means by $$ \tilde T_{m,n} \;=\; \frac{\sqrt{m}\,(\bar Y_m - \bar Z_n)}{D_{m,n}} , \qquad D_{m,n}^2 \;=\; S_Y^2 + \frac{m}{n}\,S_Z^2 , $$ with $S_Y^2 = m^{-1}\sum_i (Y_i - \bar Y_m)^2$ and $S_Z^2 = n^{-1}\sum_j (Z_j - \bar Z_n)^2$. Let $\varphi_{m,n}$ be the level-$\alpha$ permutation test based on $\tilde T_{m,n}$. Assume that both sample sizes tend to infinity, that the ratio $m/n$ converges to a strictly positive limit $\lambda$, that both populations are square-integrable, that they have equal means, that both population variances are strictly positive, and that the nominal level lies strictly between $0$ and $1$. Then $$ \mathbb{E}_{P_Y^m \times P_Z^n}\bigl[\varphi_{m,n}\bigr] \;\longrightarrow\; \alpha . $$ No equal-variance assumption and no balance condition on the sample sizes appears anywhere — that absence is the content of the theorem. Both the permutation distribution of $\tilde T_{m,n}$ and its unconditional law converge to the standard normal, so the two match. Moreover, dividing numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{m}$ turns $\tilde T_{m,n}$ into the two-sample $t$-statistic with unpooled (Welch) standardization, $(\bar Y_m - \bar Z_n)/\sqrt{S_Y^2/m + S_Z^2/n}$, so the statement applies verbatim to that statistic. Finally, when the two populations coincide the randomization hypothesis holds and the test is in addition exact at every finite sample size, so studentization costs nothing.
summary: The permutation test based on the studentized difference of sample means has rejection probability tending to the nominal level for testing equality of means, with no equal-variance and no balanced-sample-size assumption.

title: Sign-Change Randomization for Hotelling's $T^2$
informal: Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be independent random vectors in $\mathbb{R}^p$ and consider testing that the mean vector is $0$ with Hotelling's statistic $T_n = n\,\bar X_n^{\top}\hat\Sigma_n^{-1}\bar X_n$, where $\hat\Sigma_n$ is the centred sample covariance matrix with divisor $n-1$. The randomization group is the group of the $2^n$ sign changes, replacing $X_i$ by $-X_i$ for an arbitrary subset of indices. Assume that the second-moment matrix $S$ is positive definite, that the observation vector has finite second moments, that the population mean vector vanishes, and that $S$ is the matrix of second moments $\mathbb{E}[X_jX_k]$ — which under the mean-zero assumption is also the covariance. Let $\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon'$ be two independent uniform sign patterns. Then $$ \bigl(T_n(\varepsilon X),\; T_n(\varepsilon' X)\bigr) \;\xrightarrow{\;d\;}\; \chi^2_p \otimes \chi^2_p , $$ a product of two independent chi-squared laws with $p$ degrees of freedom. Since the unconditional limit of $T_n$ is also $\chi^2_p$, the sign-change randomization test based on Hotelling's statistic has rejection probability tending to the nominal level under any law with mean $0$ and finite second moments — while retaining exact level at every finite sample size whenever $X_i$ and $-X_i$ are identically distributed. Classically the exact critical values of $T_n$ require multivariate normality; the randomization test dispenses with that entirely.

title: General Bootstrap Consistency, Uniform Form
informal: Let $J_n(Q)$ denote the sampling distribution function of a root under $n$ observations from a law $Q$, let $\hat P_n$ be an estimate of the unknown law computed from the sample, and let $\mathcal{C}_P$ be a class of sequences of laws. Assume that the constant sequence at the data-generating law $P$ belongs to the class, that along every sequence in the class the sampling distribution functions converge pointwise to one and the same limit $J$, that this common limit is continuous, that every sampling distribution is a genuine distribution function, and that the estimated sequence $n \mapsto \hat P_n$ belongs to the class for almost every sample path. Then, almost surely, $$ \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} \bigl| J_n(P)(x) - J_n(\hat P_n)(x) \bigr| \;\longrightarrow\; 0 . $$ That is, substituting the estimated law for the unknown one inside the sampling distribution is asymptotically harmless, uniformly in the argument. The only stochastic ingredient is the membership of the random sequence of estimated laws in the class; the upgrade from pointwise to uniform convergence is Pólya's theorem, and it is exactly here that continuity of the limit is used.

Then, almost surely, $$ \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} \bigl| J_n(Q)(x) - J_n(\hat Q_n)(x) \bigr| \;\longrightarrow\; 0 . $$ This is the archetypal application of the sequence-class criterion: the relevant class consists of the sequences of square-integrable laws that converge weakly to $Q$ with converging means and variances, along which the sampling distribution functions converge to $\Phi(\cdot/\sigma)$ by a Lindeberg central limit theorem for a triangular array; and the almost-sure membership of the empirical sequence in that class is exactly the Glivenko–Cantelli theorem together with the strong law of large numbers for the empirical means and second moments.

title: Consistency of the Studentized (Bootstrap-$t$) Approximation
informal: In the setting of the nonparametric bootstrap for a mean, replace the centred root by the studentized one and write $$ K_n(F)(x) \;=\; \mathbb{P}_{F^{\,n}}\Bigl\{\, \frac{\sqrt{n}\,(\bar X_n - \mathbb{E}_F X)}{\hat\sigma_n} \le x \,\Bigr\} , $$ with $\hat\sigma_n$ the plug-in sample standard deviation. Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be independent, identically distributed with common law $Q$, let $Q$ be square-integrable and let its variance be strictly positive. Then, almost surely, $$ \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} \bigl| K_n(Q)(x) - K_n(\hat Q_n)(x) \bigr| \;\longrightarrow\; 0 , $$ where $\hat Q_n$ is the empirical measure of the sample. The common limit is now the standard normal distribution function, free of the unknown scale, which is what makes the studentized (bootstrap-$t$) construction the natural one for confidence intervals for a mean.
summary: The bootstrap sampling distribution of the studentized sample mean, computed at the empirical measure, is uniformly close to the true one, almost surely.

title: Consistency of the Multivariate Bootstrap
informal: Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be independent, identically distributed random vectors in $\mathbb{R}^k$ with common law $Q$, and let $\hat Q_n$ be the empirical measure of the first $n$. formalizationNotes: Designed deviation from the reference: closeness of laws is never expressed through a metric metrizing weak convergence. title: Bootstrap Consistency for Smooth Functions of Means
informal: Let each coordinate of the parameter be an expectation $\theta_j = \mathbb{E}_P[h_j(X)]$, estimated by the corresponding sample mean, and let $f$ be a smooth map of the parameter vector. The estimator is $f(\hat\theta_n)$ and the error is $f(\hat\theta_n) - f(\theta)$; the bootstrap replaces it by the resampled error $f(\hat\theta_n^{*}) - f(\hat\theta_n)$, where the resample consists of $n$ independent draws from the empirical measure of the observed sample. Then, almost surely, $$ \sup_{s \in \mathbb{R}} \Bigl| \mathbb{P}\bigl\{\|f(\hat\theta_n) - f(\theta)\| \le s\bigr\} - \mathbb{P}^{*}\bigl\{\|f(\hat\theta_n^{*}) - f(\hat\theta_n)\| \le s\bigr\} \Bigr| \;\longrightarrow\; 0 . $$ Taking the maximum norm on the image space, this is the statement behind simultaneous confidence rectangles for the coordinates of $f(\theta)$. The underlying limit is the delta method: the centred and scaled image converges weakly to the centred multivariate normal law with covariance $D\,\Sigma_h\,D^{\top}$, where $\Sigma_h$ is the covariance matrix of the vector of coordinate functions.
summary: For a parameter obtained by applying a smooth map to a vector of expectations, the resampled distribution of the norm of the estimation error is uniformly close to its true sampling distribution, almost surely.

title: Asymptotic Level of a Bootstrap Test
informal: Let the data be generated by a null law $P$, let $T_n$ be a test statistic with sampling distribution function $G_n(\cdot, Q)$ under $n$ observations from $Q$, and let $\hat Q_n$ be an estimate of the generating law that satisfies the constraints of the null hypothesis. The bootstrap test rejects when $T_n$ exceeds the estimated critical value $G_n(\cdot, \hat Q_n)^{-1}(1-\alpha)$. Assume that the constant sequence at the data-generating law belongs to the null class, that along every sequence of the null class the distribution functions of the statistic converge to one common continuous limit, that the null-restricted estimator lies in the null class in probability, that the nominal level lies strictly between $0$ and $1$, that the limit law is strictly increasing at its $1-\alpha$ quantile, and that at the data-generating law the field really is the distribution function of the statistic. Then $$ \mathbb{P}\bigl\{\, G_n(\cdot, \hat Q_n)^{-1}(1-\alpha) < T_n \,\bigr\} \;\longrightarrow\; \alpha . $$ The essential point is which law is resampled: resampling from the unrestricted empirical measure estimates the distribution of the statistic under the law that actually generated the data, whether or not it satisfies the null, and the resulting test has asymptotic rejection probability $\alpha$ even against alternatives, hence no power. Estimating under the null constraints makes the critical value behave, under an alternative, like the critical value at some null law, against which a divergent statistic rejects with probability tending to one — the accompanying consistency claim, proved separately in the same file.
summary: A test whose critical value is the estimated $1-\alpha$ quantile of the statistic under a null-restricted resampling law has rejection probability tending to the nominal level.

title: Local Power of the Parametric Bootstrap Test
informal: In a parametric model indexed by $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^k$, consider testing $g(\theta) \le 0$ with the statistic $\sqrt{n}\,g(\hat\theta_n)$, calibrated by the estimated $1-\alpha$ quantile of the parametric bootstrap sampling distribution at the estimated parameter. Then, along the local alternatives $\theta + n^{-1/2}h$, $$ \mathbb{P}_{\theta + n^{-1/2}h}\bigl\{\, \text{reject} \,\bigr\} \;\longrightarrow\; 1 - \Phi\Bigl( z_{1-\alpha} - \frac{\langle \nabla g(\theta), h\rangle}{\sigma} \Bigr) . $$ So the bootstrap test attains the same limiting local power as the test that would be used if the limiting normal law were known.
summary: Against contiguous alternatives at distance $n^{-1/2}$ from the boundary of the null hypothesis, the bootstrap test's rejection probability converges to the limiting power of the corresponding normal-theory test.

title: One-Term Edgeworth Expansion for the Centred Mean
informal: Let $F$ be a law on the line with mean $\mu$, variance $\sigma^2$ and skewness $\gamma$, and let $$ J_n(t) \;=\; \mathbb{P}_{F^{\,n}}\bigl\{\, \sqrt{n}\,(\bar X_n - \mu) \le t \,\bigr\} $$ be the sampling distribution function of the centred and scaled sample mean. Assume that $F$ has a finite fourth moment, that its variance is strictly positive, and that $F$ satisfies Cramér's condition, i.e. the modulus of its characteristic function is eventually bounded by a constant strictly below $1$ at infinity. Then there is a constant $C$, depending only on $F$, such that for every sample size $n \ge 1$ and every $t$, $$ \Bigl| J_n(t) - \Bigl[\Phi\!\bigl(\tfrac{t}{\sigma}\bigr) - \tfrac{\gamma}{6}\,\phi\!\bigl(\tfrac{t}{\sigma}\bigr)\Bigl(\tfrac{t^2}{\sigma^2} - 1\Bigr) n^{-1/2} \Bigr] \Bigr| \;\le\; \frac{C}{n} , $$ where $\Phi$ and $\phi$ are the standard normal distribution function and density. Consistency says the bootstrap approximation is asymptotically correct; it says nothing about how fast, and the comparison of competing confidence intervals for a mean is decided at exactly this next order.
summary: Under a finite fourth moment and Cramér's condition, the sampling distribution function of the centred and scaled sample mean equals the normal approximation plus an explicit skewness term of order $n^{-1/2}$, with remainder uniformly $O(1/n)$.

hypotheses.note: The non-lattice requirement behind a one-term Edgeworth expansion; it is implied by absolute continuity of the sampling law.

formalizationNotes: Only the expansion for the centred root is available. The studentized headline and its Cornish–Fisher quantile corollary were deliberately removed from the file (rather than kept as unproved statements), so the studentized analogue — whose $n^{-1/2}$ term differs, and which is the analytic reason the bootstrap-$t$ construction is preferable — is not yet assembled; every piece of supporting analysis built for it is proved and retained in the same file. The constant is existentially quantified with no exposed dependence on the law; a quantitative restatement in terms of explicit moment bounds is available separately. Cramér's condition is used in the form of a single constant strictly below $1$ dominating the modulus of the characteristic function on a whole region away from the origin, which is derived from the eventual bound rather than assumed.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: One-term Edgeworth expansions under a moment condition and the non-lattice condition go back to H. Cramér (1937) and C.-G. Esseen (1945); the systematic use of such expansions to compare bootstrap constructions is P. Hall's (1992), for the bootstrap of B. Efron (1979) whose first-order theory is P. J. Bickel and D. A. Freedman's (1981). The reference text quotes the expansion in its uniform form with an $O(n^{-1})$ remainder; the formalization proves exactly that, via Esseen smoothing against an explicit comparison density whose distribution function is the Edgeworth approximant, splitting the Fourier integral into a window of width of order $\sqrt{n}$ and a Cramér tail.

title: Cornish–Fisher Inversion of an Edgeworth Expansion
informal: Let $S_n$ be a family of distribution functions and $\gamma$ a real constant. Assume that a positive constant $C_0$ is given, that each $S_n$ is a distribution function, and that the family admits the one-term Edgeworth expansion $$ \Bigl| S_n(t) - \Bigl[\Phi(t) + \tfrac{\gamma}{6}\,\phi(t)\,(2t^2 + 1)\,n^{-1/2}\Bigr] \Bigr| \;\le\; \frac{C_0}{n} \qquad \text{for all } t \text{ and all } n \ge 1 . $$ Then, for any margin $\varepsilon \in (0, 1/2)$, there is a constant $C$ such that for every $n \ge 1$ and every level $\alpha \in [\varepsilon, 1-\varepsilon]$ the quantiles satisfy $$ \Bigl| S_n^{-1}(1-\alpha) - \Bigl[ z_{1-\alpha} - \tfrac{\gamma}{6}\,\bigl(2 z_{1-\alpha}^2 + 1\bigr) n^{-1/2} \Bigr] \Bigr| \;\le\; \frac{C}{n} , $$ where $z_{1-\alpha}$ is the standard normal quantile. This is the Cornish–Fisher inversion: an expansion of a distribution function transfers, at the same order, to an expansion of its quantile, which is the form needed to compare the endpoints of competing confidence intervals.
summary: A uniform $O(1/n)$ Edgeworth expansion of a family of distribution functions inverts to a uniform $O(1/n)$ expansion of their quantiles, over levels bounded away from $0$ and $1$.
leanSignature:
theorem cornishFisher_of_edgeworth {S : ℕ → ℝ → ℝ} {γ C₀ : ℝ} (hC₀ : 0 < C₀)
    (hcdf : ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n → IsCDF (S n))
    (hexp : ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n → ∀ t : ℝ,
      |S n t - (stdNormalCDF t
        + 1 / 6 * γ * stdNormalPDF t * (2 * t ^ 2 + 1) * (Real.sqrt n)⁻¹)| ≤ C₀ / n)
    {ε : ℝ} (hε : 0 < ε) (hε' : ε < 1 / 2) :
    ∃ C : ℝ, 0 < C ∧ ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n → ∀ α ∈ Set.Icc ε (1 - ε),
      |cdfPseudoInverse (S n) (1 - α)
        - (stdNormalQuantile (1 - α)
          - 1 / 6 * γ * (2 * stdNormalQuantile (1 - α) ^ 2 + 1) * (Real.sqrt n)⁻¹)| ≤ C / n

hypotheses.label: uniform Edgeworth expansion
hypotheses.note: A one-term expansion with remainder bounded by $C_0/n$ uniformly in the argument.

hypotheses.label: levels bounded away from the extremes
hypotheses.note: The margin keeps the levels inside a compact subinterval of the open unit interval, where the normal quantile and density are bounded and bounded away from zero.

formalizationNotes: Stated abstractly, for an arbitrary family of distribution functions satisfying the displayed expansion, so it applies to any expansion of that shape rather than to one particular root. The correction term is written in the polynomial form $\tfrac{\gamma}{6}(2t^2+1)$ that arises for the studentized root; the theorem is a purely analytic inversion and does not depend on where the expansion comes from. The quantile is the lower generalized inverse. Its intended consumer — the studentized Edgeworth expansion — was removed from the file, so this inversion is currently proved and retained but not applied to a studentized headline.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and J. P. Romano, *Testing Statistical Hypotheses*, 4th ed., Springer Nature Switzerland AG, 2022.
reference.biblio: The inversion of a distribution-function expansion into a quantile expansion is due to E. A. Cornish and R. A. Fisher (1938); its role in comparing bootstrap confidence intervals is developed by P. Hall (1992) for the bootstrap of B. Efron (1979). The reference text uses the inversion to compare the endpoints of competing intervals for a mean; the formalization proves it as a self-contained analytic statement about any family of distribution functions with a uniform one-term expansion, with the constant explicit in the expansion constant and the level margin.

title: Exponential family in canonical form and its natural parameter space
informal:
Let $
u$ be a reference measure on a sample space $\mathcal{X}$ and let $T:\mathcal{X}	o V$ be a measurable statistic taking values in a real inner-product space $V$. The associated **exponential family in canonical form** is the family of probability measures with densities $$ rac{dP_\eta}{d
u}(x)=\exp igl(\langle\eta,T(x)angle-A(\eta) igr),\qquad A(\eta)=\log\int_{\mathcal{X}} e^{\langle\eta,T(x)angle}\,d
u(x),$$ where $T$ is the natural (sufficient) statistic, $\eta$ the natural parameter and $A$ the log-partition, or cumulant, function. The **natural parameter space** is the set of all $\eta\in V$ for which $e^{\langle\eta,T(x)angle}$ is $
u$-integrable, that is, the largest set of parameters for which the normalizing constant is finite and the member $P_\eta$ is defined. The familiar general presentation $p_	heta(x)=\exp igl(\sum_{i=1}^{s}\eta_i(	heta)T_i(x)-B(	heta) igr)h(x)$ relative to a dominating measure $\mu$ is recovered by absorbing the carrier $h$ into the reference measure, $d
u=h\,d\mu$, and reparametrizing through $	heta\mapsto\eta(	heta)$, under which $B(	heta)=A(\eta(	heta))$.
summary: The natural parameter space of a canonical exponential family is the set of parameters at which the exponential tilt of the reference measure has a finite normalizing constant.
leanSignature:
def natSet : Set V :=
  {η : V | Integrable (fun x => Real.exp ⟪η, E.stat x⟫_ℝ) E.base}
formalizationNotes: The family is packaged as the pair (reference measure, measurable natural statistic), with the carrier already absorbed; members are realized as exponential tilts of the reference measure. This fixes a junk convention: for $\eta$ outside the natural parameter space the member is the zero measure rather than being undefined, which removes membership side conditions from downstream statements. No finiteness or $\sigma$-finiteness assumption on the reference measure is built into the definition; individual theorems add it where their proofs need it.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Exponential families were isolated independently by Fisher (1934), Darmois (1935), Koopman (1936) and Pitman (1936) as the families admitting a sufficient statistic of fixed dimension. Lehmann and Casella present the general form (5.1) and the canonical form (5.2) with the natural parameter space; the systematic convex-analytic theory of that space, and of the log-partition function on it, is due to Barndorff-Nielsen (1978) and Brown (1986). The formalization takes the canonical form as primitive — the data of a reference measure and a measurable natural statistic — and recovers the general form as the special case in which a carrier has been absorbed into the reference measure.

title: The natural parameter space is convex
informal: The natural parameter space of an exponential family is a convex subset of the parameter space: if $e^{\langle\eta_0,T(\cdot)\rangle}$ and $e^{\langle\eta_1,T(\cdot)\rangle}$ are both integrable with respect to the reference measure and $\alpha,\beta\ge 0$ satisfy $\alpha+\beta=1$, then $e^{\langle\alpha\eta_0+\beta\eta_1,T(\cdot)\rangle}$ is integrable as well. Equivalently, the set on which the log-partition function is finite is convex. The proof is the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality applied pointwise to $e^{\langle\alpha\eta_0+\beta\eta_1,T(x)\rangle} = \bigl(e^{\langle\eta_0,T(x)\rangle}\bigr)^{\alpha}\bigl(e^{\langle\eta_1,T(x)\rangle}\bigr)^{\beta} \le \alpha e^{\langle\eta_0,T(x)\rangle}+\beta e^{\langle\eta_1,T(x)\rangle}$.
summary: The set of natural parameters at which an exponential family is defined is a convex set.
leanSignature: theorem natSet_convex (E : ExpFamily 𝓧 V) : Convex ℝ E.natSet
formalizationNotes: Holds for an arbitrary reference measure — no finiteness, $\sigma$-finiteness or nondegeneracy assumption is used. The statement is about the parameter set only; convexity of the log-partition function itself is a separate fact and is not part of this declaration.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Convexity of the natural parameter space is stated by Lehmann and Casella immediately after the canonical form (5.2) and is one of the standard structural facts about exponential families; the convex-analytic development around it is due to Barndorff-Nielsen (1978) and Brown (1986). The formalization proves it for an arbitrary reference measure, with no finiteness or nondegeneracy assumption, by the weighted arithmetic–geometric mean inequality rather than by Hölder's inequality in its usual form.

title: Differentiation under the integral sign for exponential integrals
informal: Let $T$ be the natural statistic of an exponential family with reference measure $ u$, let $f$ be a measurable weight function on the sample space, and consider the weighted exponential integral $$I(\eta)=\int f(x)\,e^{\langle\eta,T(x) angle}\,d u(x),$$ defined on the set of parameters at which $|f(x)|e^{\langle\eta,T(x) angle}$ is $ u$-integrable. At every parameter $\eta$ interior to that set the function $I$ is differentiable, and its derivative is obtained by differentiating under the integral sign: the gradient is $$ abla I(\eta)=\int f(x)\,e^{\langle\eta,T(x) angle}\,T(x)\,d u(x),$$ so that the derivative in the direction $u$ equals $\int f(x)\,\langle u,T(x) angle\,e^{\langle\eta,T(x) angle}\,d u(x)$. Taking $f\equiv 1$ this is the differentiability of the normalizing constant of the family, from which $ abla A(\eta)=\mathbb{E}_\eta[T]$ follows.
summary: On the interior of its domain of absolute convergence, a weighted exponential integral is differentiable in the natural parameter and may be differentiated under the integral sign.

hypotheses.label: measurable weight
hypotheses.note: The weight $f$ is a measurable real function on the sample space; it is the arbitrary integrable function of the classical statement.

hypotheses.label: interior parameter
hypotheses.note: The parameter lies in the interior of the set where the weighted integrand is absolutely integrable; interiority is the classical hypothesis licensing differentiation under the integral sign.

formalizationNotes: The parameter space is assumed finite-dimensional. This is a Lean-side requirement, not a restriction of the book: it is what makes the local dominating envelope (built from the finitely many sign vectors of an orthonormal basis) available, and every intended instantiation is a Euclidean parameter space. The derivative is presented as the Riesz vector of the differential — the honest 'integral of the differentiated integrand' — rather than as an abstract linear map. Continuity on the same interior is recorded separately as `continuousOn_integral_exp_inner`, and the derivatives of all orders along a fixed direction as `iteratedDeriv_integral_exp_inner`.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Theorem 5.8 of Lehmann and Casella states that the integral defining the normalizing constant of an exponential family is continuous and has derivatives of all orders on the interior of the natural parameter space, all obtainable by differentiating under the integral sign; the result goes back to Sverdrup (1953), with systematic treatments in Barndorff-Nielsen (1978, §7.1) and Brown (1986, Ch. 2). The formalization proves the differentiability statement for an arbitrary measurable weight $f$ rather than only for $f\equiv 1$, which is what the moment identities need, and represents the differential by the vector of the integral of the differentiated integrand.

title: Analyticity of exponential integrals in the natural parameter
informal: For a measurable weight function $f$ on the sample space, the weighted exponential integral $\eta\mapsto\int f(x)\,e^{\langle\eta,T(x)\rangle}\,d\nu(x)$ is real-analytic on the interior of the set of parameters at which $|f(x)|e^{\langle\eta,T(x)\rangle}$ is integrable: near every such point it is the sum of a convergent power series. In particular it has derivatives of all orders there, and each of them may be computed by repeated differentiation under the integral sign, the $n$-th derivative in the direction $u$ being $\int f(x)\,\langle u,T(x)\rangle^{\,n}\,e^{\langle\eta,T(x)\rangle}\,d\nu(x)$. With $f\equiv 1$ this is the classical statement that the normalizing constant of an exponential family — and hence the log-partition function — is infinitely differentiable, indeed analytic, on the interior of the natural parameter space.
summary: A weighted exponential integral is real-analytic in the natural parameter on the interior of its domain of absolute convergence.
leanSignature:
theorem analyticOnNhd_integral_exp_inner
    [FiniteDimensional ℝ V] (E : ExpFamily 𝓧 V) {f : 𝓧 → ℝ}
    (hf : Measurable f) :
    AnalyticOnNhd ℝ (fun η => ∫ x, f x * Real.exp ⟪η, E.stat x⟫_ℝ ∂E.base)
      (interior (E.weightedNatSet f))

hypotheses.label: measurable weight
hypotheses.note: The weight $f$ is a measurable real function on the sample space.

formalizationNotes: The parameter space is assumed finite-dimensional (as in the differentiability theorem). The Taylor series is exhibited explicitly rather than deduced from a smoothness criterion: its $n$-th coefficient is the symmetric multilinear form obtained by integrating $\prod_i \langle m_i, T(x)\rangle$ against the weighted exponential, and a sign-vector envelope supplies a geometric bound on the coefficients, hence a positive radius of convergence. The one-dimensional case is available separately as `analyticAt_integral_exp_mul`.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The infinite differentiability half of Theorem 5.8 of Lehmann and Casella is here strengthened to the analyticity statement of Barndorff-Nielsen (1978, §7.1) and Brown (1986, Ch. 2), which is what the classical proofs actually deliver; the original differentiation-under-the-integral argument for exponential families is due to Sverdrup (1953). The formalization proves joint analyticity in all coordinates of the natural parameter, for an arbitrary measurable weight.

title: Moment generating function of the natural statistic
informal: Let $X$ follow the member $P_\eta$ of a canonical exponential family with natural statistic $T$, log-partition function $A$ and a reference measure that is not the zero measure. If $\eta$ belongs to the natural parameter space and $\eta+u$ belongs to it as well, then the moment generating function of the natural statistic is a ratio of normalizing constants: $$\mathbb{E}_\eta\bigl[e^{\langle u,\,T(X)\rangle}\bigr]=e^{A(\eta+u)-A(\eta)}.$$ Equivalently, the cumulant generating function of $T(X)$ under $P_\eta$ is $u\mapsto A(\eta+u)-A(\eta)$. In particular it is finite for every $u$ whose shift keeps the parameter inside the natural parameter space, so that the natural statistic has moments of all orders whenever $\eta$ is an interior point.
summary: Under an exponential family member the moment generating function of the natural statistic is the exponential of the increment of the log-partition function.
leanSignature:
theorem integral_exp_inner_P (E : ExpFamily 𝓧 V) {η u : V}
    (hbase : E.base ≠ 0)
    (hη : η ∈ E.natSet)
    (hηu : η + u ∈ E.natSet) :
    ∫ x, Real.exp ⟪u, E.stat x⟫_ℝ ∂(E.P η)
      = Real.exp (E.logPartition (η + u) - E.logPartition η)

hypotheses.label: nonzero reference measure
hypotheses.note: The reference measure is not identically zero; otherwise the member is the zero measure and the left-hand side vanishes while the right-hand side is one.

hypotheses.label: natural parameter
hypotheses.note: The base point lies in the natural parameter space, so that the member is a probability measure.

hypotheses.label: shifted parameter admissible
hypotheses.note: The shifted point also lies in the natural parameter space — exactly the classical requirement that the generating function exist near the origin.

formalizationNotes: The nondegeneracy hypothesis on the reference measure is not cosmetic: for the zero reference measure the left-hand side is $0$ while the right-hand side is $e^{0-0}=1$, both log-partition values having degenerated to $\log 0 = 0$ under the junk convention.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Theorem 5.10 of Lehmann and Casella computes the moment and cumulant generating functions of the natural statistic from the log-partition function; the identification of the derivatives of the log-partition function with the cumulants of $T$ goes back to Fisher (1934), with the modern convex-analytic account in Barndorff-Nielsen (1978, Ch. 7–9) and Brown (1986, Ch. 2). The formalization states the identity in the multivariate canonical form, valid whenever both the base point and the shifted point are natural parameters.

title: Mean of the natural statistic as the derivative of the log-partition function
informal: For a one-parameter canonical exponential family on the line — the natural statistic $T$ being real valued — and a natural parameter $\eta$ interior to the natural parameter space, the expectation of the natural statistic under $P_\eta$ is the derivative of the log-partition function: $$\mathbb{E}_\eta\bigl[T(X)\bigr]=A'(\eta).$$ This is what one obtains by differentiating the normalization identity $\int e^{\eta T(x)-A(\eta)}\,d\nu(x)=1$ under the integral sign.
summary: At an interior natural parameter the mean of the natural statistic equals the first derivative of the log-partition function.

hypotheses.label: interior natural parameter
hypotheses.note: Interiority licenses differentiation under the integral sign and is the classical hypothesis of the moment formulas.

formalizationNotes: The companion declaration `variance_stat_P`, in the same file, gives the second moment identity: at an interior natural parameter the variance of the natural statistic equals the second derivative of the log-partition function. Neither statement needs a nondegeneracy hypothesis on the reference measure — both sides vanish for the zero measure.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: That the successive derivatives of the log-partition function are the cumulants of the natural statistic — the mean being the first derivative and the variance the second — is part of Theorem 5.10 of Lehmann and Casella and goes back to Fisher (1934); see Barndorff-Nielsen (1978) and Brown (1986) for the convex-analytic treatment. The formalization gives the one-dimensional statement; the multivariate gradient and Hessian identities are obtained by combining the generating-function identity with the differentiation-under-the-integral results.

title: The natural statistic is itself exponentially distributed
informal:
If $X$ follows the member $P_\eta$ of a canonical exponential family with natural statistic $T$ and reference measure $
u$, then $T(X)$ again follows an exponential family — the one carried by the statistic's own scale, whose reference measure is the image $
u\circ T^{-1}$ of $
u$ under $T$ and whose natural statistic is the identity: $$ rac{dP^{T}_\eta}{d(
u\circ T^{-1})}(t)=\exp igl(\langle\eta,tangle-A(\eta) igr).$$ The two families share the same natural parameter space and the same log-partition function $A$. Consequently all inference about $\eta$ may be carried out on the scale of the statistic, which is the reduction under which completeness of $T$ is proved.
summary: The law of the natural statistic under an exponential family member is again an exponential family member, with the identity as natural statistic and the same log-partition function.
leanSignature:
theorem map_stat_P (E : ExpFamily 𝓧 V) (η : V) :
    (E.P η).map E.stat = E.statFamily.P η
formalizationNotes: The statement is unconditional — it holds for every $\eta$, not only for natural parameters: off the natural parameter space both sides are the zero measure, since the two families are shown to have the same natural parameter space. Consumers therefore never carry a membership side condition through the push-forward. Combined with the $n$-fold product family (whose natural statistic is $\sum_i T(X_i)$) this gives the classical corollary that a sum of independent natural statistics is again exponentially distributed.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Theorem 5.17 of Lehmann and Casella records that the natural statistic of an exponential family is itself exponentially distributed with the same natural parameter; together with the closure of the class under independent sampling this is part of the classical theory of Fisher (1934), Darmois (1935), Koopman (1936) and Pitman (1936), see also Barndorff-Nielsen (1978, Ch. 8). The formalization proves it as the commutation of exponential tilting with the push-forward along $T$, the tilting density factoring through the statistic.

title: Stein's identity for a one-parameter exponential family on the line
informal: Let $X$ have the one-parameter density $\exp\bigl(\eta\,T(x)-A(\eta)\bigr)h(x)$ with respect to Lebesgue measure on the whole line, the carrier $h$ being a nonnegative weight of the reference measure, and let $\eta$ be a natural parameter. Let $g$ be a differentiable function with $\mathbb{E}_\eta|g'(X)|<\infty$, and assume the boundary term $g(x)\,e^{\eta T(x)}\,h(x)$ tends to zero both as $x\to+\infty$ and as $x\to-\infty$. Then $$\mathbb{E}_\eta\Bigl[\Bigl(\frac{h'(X)}{h(X)}+\eta\,T'(X)\Bigr)g(X)\Bigr]=-\,\mathbb{E}_\eta\bigl[g'(X)\bigr].$$ The bracketed factor is the derivative of the log-density with respect to the sample argument — the score in the sample argument — so the identity states that this score is orthogonal to differentiation. For the normal family with mean $\eta$ and unit variance, where $h(x)=e^{-x^{2}/2}$ and $T(x)=x$, it reduces to Stein's identity $\mathbb{E}\bigl[(X-\eta)g(X)\bigr]=\mathbb{E}\bigl[g'(X)\bigr]$.
summary: Integration by parts on the line turns the expectation of the sample score times a test function into minus the expectation of the test function's derivative.
leanSignature:
theorem stein_identity (E : ExpFamily ℝ ℝ) (densityH g : ℝ → ℝ) (η : ℝ)
    (hbase : E.base = volume.withDensity fun x => ENNReal.ofReal (densityH x))
    (hH0 : ∀ x, 0 ≤ densityH x)
    (hbase0 : E.base ≠ 0)
    (hHdiff : Differentiable ℝ densityH)
    (hTdiff : Differentiable ℝ E.stat)
    (hgdiff : Differentiable ℝ g)
    (hη : η ∈ E.natSet)
    (hg' : Integrable (fun x => deriv g x) (E.P η))
    (hscore : Integrable
      (fun x => (deriv densityH x / densityH x + η * deriv E.stat x) * g x) (E.P η))
    (hTop : Tendsto (fun x => g x * Real.exp ⟪η, E.stat x⟫_ℝ * densityH x) atTop (𝓝 0))
    (hBot : Tendsto (fun x => g x * Real.exp ⟪η, E.stat x⟫_ℝ * densityH x) atBot (𝓝 0)) :
    ∫ x, (deriv densityH x / densityH x + η * deriv E.stat x) * g x ∂(E.P η)
      = -∫ x, deriv g x ∂(E.P η)

hypotheses.label: Lebesgue reference measure
hypotheses.note: The reference measure is Lebesgue measure weighted by the carrier $h$; this is the setting in which the identity is classically stated.

hypotheses.label: natural parameter
hypotheses.note: The parameter lies in the natural parameter space, so that the member is a probability measure.

hypotheses.label: integrable derivative
hypotheses.note: The classical integrability hypothesis on the test function: the derivative of $g$ has a finite expectation under the member.

hypotheses.label: boundary term at $+\infty$
hypotheses.note: The product of the test function with the unnormalized density vanishes at $+\infty$; the classical support condition.

hypotheses.label: boundary term at $-\infty$
hypotheses.note: The same decay at $-\infty$.

formalizationNotes: Three further hypotheses accompany the classical ones: differentiability of the carrier and of the natural statistic (needed for $h'/h$ and $T'$ to exist) and integrability of the left-hand integrand, which the classical statement leaves implicit but without which the left-hand expectation would silently be read as zero. The boundary condition is stated with the factor $g$ included, which is what integration by parts actually needs and is weaker (hence safer) than the classical form asking only for decay of $e^{\eta T}h$. On the set where the carrier vanishes the ratio $h'/h$ takes the value zero by the division convention; that set is null under the member, so the statement is unaffected. The variant with support a bounded interval is not formalized.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The identity for the normal distribution is due to Stein (1981), where it underlies the unbiased estimate of risk; its extension to general exponential families, in the form stated here, is due to Hudson (1978), and it appears as Lemma 5.15 of Lehmann and Casella. The formalization proves the case of support equal to the whole line by integration by parts, with the boundary term stated as decay of the product $g\,e^{\eta T}h$ rather than of $e^{\eta T}h$ alone.

title: The natural statistic of a full-rank exponential family is minimal sufficient
informal: Consider a canonical exponential family $\{P_\eta:\eta\in\Xi\}$ with natural statistic $T$, where the parameter set $\Xi$ is contained in the natural parameter space and the reference measure is not the zero measure. If $\Xi$ contains $s+1$ parameter points lying in no proper affine subspace of the parameter space — which is the case, in particular, when the family has full rank, since a parameter set with nonempty interior in an $s$-dimensional space always contains such a configuration — then $T$ is minimal sufficient: it is sufficient, and every sufficient statistic determines it almost surely. The reason is that the likelihood ratios against a baseline parameter, $$\frac{p_{\eta^{(j)}}(x)}{p_{\eta^{(0)}}(x)}=\exp\bigl(\langle\eta^{(j)}-\eta^{(0)},T(x)\rangle-A(\eta^{(j)})+A(\eta^{(0)})\bigr),$$ are one-to-one functions of the vector $\bigl(\langle\eta^{(j)}-\eta^{(0)},T(x)\rangle\bigr)_j$, and when the differences $\eta^{(j)}-\eta^{(0)}$ span the parameter space this vector recovers $T(x)$.
summary: In a canonical exponential family whose parameter set contains an affinely spanning configuration, the natural statistic is minimal sufficient.
leanSignature:
theorem isMinimalSufficient_stat {s : ℕ} (E : ExpFamily 𝓧 V)
    [SigmaFinite E.base] (Ξ' : Set V)
    (hΞ : Ξ' ⊆ E.natSet)
    (hbase : E.base ≠ 0)
    (hspan : ∃ η' : Fin (s + 1) → V, (∀ i, η' i ∈ Ξ') ∧
      affineSpan ℝ (Set.range η') = (⊤ : AffineSubspace ℝ V)) :
    IsMinimalSufficient (fun θ : Ξ' => E.P (θ : V)) E.stat

hypotheses.label: parameters admissible
hypotheses.note: The parameter set lies inside the natural parameter space, so that every member is a genuine probability measure of the family.

hypotheses.label: nonzero reference measure
hypotheses.note: Nondegeneracy of the reference measure, so that the members are probability measures rather than the zero measure.

hypotheses.label: affinely spanning parameters
hypotheses.note: The parameter set contains $s+1$ points that lie in no proper affine subspace; this is the rank condition the minimality argument actually consumes.

formalizationNotes: Affine independence of the natural statistic — the other half of the classical full-rank condition — is what makes the parametrization identifiable and is not needed here; the companion `fullRank_exists_affineSpan` supplies the span hypothesis from full rank. $\sigma$-finiteness of the reference measure is a Lean-side instance needed to pass from the density factorization to parameter-free conditional determinations; every dominated model supplies it. The classical 'common support' proviso does not appear as a hypothesis because the exponential density is strictly positive, so all members are mutually equivalent.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Minimal sufficiency and the likelihood-ratio construction behind this corollary are due to Lehmann and Scheffé (1950), with the general theory developed by Dynkin (1951) and Bahadur (1954); that exponential structure characterizes families with low-dimensional sufficient statistics goes back to Fisher (1934) and Koopman (1936). The formalization separates the two halves of the classical full-rank condition: the affine-span condition is what the minimality proof consumes and is therefore the hypothesis of the theorem, while a companion result derives it from a parameter set with nonempty interior in a finite-dimensional parameter space.

title: Sufficient statistic
informal: A statistic $T$ is **sufficient** for a family $\{P_\theta\}$ when the conditional distribution of the data given $T$ can be chosen free of the parameter: for every measurable event $A$ of the sample space there is a measurable function $t\mapsto\kappa_A(t)\in[0,1]$, not depending on $\theta$, which is a version of $P_\theta(A\mid T=t)$ for every $\theta$, that is, $$\int_{\{T\in B\}}\kappa_A\bigl(T(x)\bigr)\,dP_\theta(x)=P_\theta\bigl(A\cap\{T\in B\}\bigr)$$ for every measurable set $B$ of values of the statistic and every parameter $\theta$. Informally: once the value of $T$ has been reported, the residual randomness in the data carries no further information about $\theta$, so nothing is lost by discarding the data and keeping only $T$.
summary: A statistic is sufficient when every event admits a version of its conditional probability given the statistic that does not depend on the parameter.

The formalization records three carriers of the notion: this per-event definition, a regular-conditional (Markov kernel) form, and the Fisher–Neyman factorization of densities, together with the theorems relating them.

title: Fisher–Neyman factorization: a factorized density makes the statistic sufficient
informal: Suppose the model is dominated by a $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$, with densities $p_\theta=dP_\theta/d\mu$, and let $T$ be a measurable statistic. If the densities split into a factor that sees the data only through $T$ and a factor that does not see the parameter at all, $$p_\theta(x)=g_\theta\bigl(T(x)\bigr)\,h(x)\qquad\text{for $\mu$-almost every }x,\ \text{for every }\theta,$$ then $T$ is sufficient for the family.
summary: If the densities of a dominated family factor as a function of the statistic times a parameter-free function, the statistic is sufficient.

hypotheses.label: dominated model
hypotheses.note: The members are the given densities against a $\sigma$-finite dominating measure; this is the classical setup of the factorization criterion.

hypotheses.label: measurable statistic
hypotheses.note: The statistic is measurable into its value space.

hypotheses.label: Fisher–Neyman factorization
hypotheses.note: The densities factor almost everywhere as a function of the statistic times a parameter-free carrier.

formalizationNotes: Densities are extended-nonnegative-real valued, so no positivity or finiteness side conditions appear; measurability of the densities and of the two factors is what the change-of-variables steps consume. The proof runs through an equivalent countable mixture of members (the Halmos–Savage device), so this direction consumes the existence of such a mixture for a dominated family.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The factorization criterion is due to Neyman (1935), following Fisher's (1922) introduction of sufficiency; its measure-theoretic form for arbitrary dominated families — which is what is formalized here — is due to Halmos and Savage (1949) and appears as Corollary 2.6.1 of Lehmann and Romano (2022). The formalization states the criterion relative to an arbitrary $\sigma$-finite dominating measure and fixed densities, with the factorization holding almost everywhere rather than pointwise.

title: Fisher–Neyman factorization: a sufficient statistic factorizes the densities
informal: Conversely, suppose the model is dominated by a $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$ with densities $p_\theta$ and that the measurable statistic $T$ is sufficient. Then the densities admit a factorization: there are measurable functions $g_\theta$ on the value space of the statistic and a measurable function $h$ on the sample space, the latter not depending on the parameter, such that $$p_\theta(x)=g_\theta\bigl(T(x)\bigr)\,h(x)\qquad\text{for $\mu$-almost every }x,\ \text{for every }\theta.$$ Together with the previous direction this is the Fisher–Neyman factorization theorem: for a dominated family, sufficiency of $T$ is exactly the factorization of the densities through $T$.
summary: A sufficient statistic for a dominated family produces a Fisher–Neyman factorization of the densities.

title: Halmos–Savage criterion for sufficiency
informal: Let $\{P_ heta\}$ be a family of probability measures and let $ u=\sum_i c_i P_{ heta_i}$ be a finite countable mixture of members of the family which dominates every member. Then a measurable statistic $T$ is sufficient if and only if every member has a density with respect to $ u$ that is a function of $T$ alone: for every $ heta$ there is a measurable $g_ heta$ with $$ rac{dP_ heta}{d u}(x)=g_ heta igl(T(x) igr)\qquad u ext{-almost everywhere.}$$

hypotheses.note: The statistic is measurable into its value space.

formalizationNotes: No positivity of the mixture weights is assumed: it is not needed, because domination is required for every parameter, not only for those appearing in the mixture. Densities are extended-nonnegative-real valued Radon–Nikodym derivatives, so no finiteness or positivity side conditions appear. The forward direction is the substantive one: a parameter-free version of the conditional probability of an event given the statistic is also a version for the mixture, which identifies the density on the sub-$\sigma$-field generated by the statistic.

title: Existence of a parameter-free regular conditional distribution
informal: On a standard Borel sample space, let $T$ be a measurable statistic which is sufficient in the per-event sense — each event admits a version of its conditional probability given $T$ that is free of the parameter. Then there is a *single* parameter-free Markov kernel $Q$, from the value space of the statistic to the sample space, which is a regular conditional distribution of the data given $T$ simultaneously under every member: for every $\theta$ the joint law of $\bigl(T(X),X\bigr)$ under $P_\theta$ is the law of $T(X)$ followed by $Q$. In particular the data may be regenerated from the reported value of the statistic by a random mechanism that does not involve the parameter, and $Q$ puts all of its mass on the fibre $\{x: T(x)=t\}$ for almost every $t$.
summary: A sufficient statistic on a standard Borel sample space admits a single parameter-free Markov kernel that disintegrates the joint law of the statistic and the data under every member.

hypotheses.label: sufficiency (per-event)

The general version genuinely needs a gluing argument, since for an uncountable parameter set no single member's disintegration can serve; the kernel is built from the parameter-free determinations of the half-lines of a Borel embedding of the sample space into the line. Nonemptiness of the sample space is a technical requirement of the disintegration machinery and is no restriction.

reference.biblio: The existence of parameter-free conditional distributions given a sufficient statistic on Euclidean sample spaces is classical; the measure-theoretic treatment for dominated families is due to Halmos and Savage (1949), and the decision-theoretic formulation, in which the reconstruction kernel is the object of interest, to Bahadur (1954). The formalization delivers the joint-law (graph) form of the disintegration rather than the bare reconstruction identity, which additionally pins the kernel to the fibres of the statistic — a property the risk-equality theorem and Basu's theorem both use.

title: The likelihood-ratio vector is minimal sufficient
informal: Let $P_0,\dots,P_k$ be a finite family of probability measures dominated by a $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$, with densities $p_0,\dots,p_k$ that are almost everywhere strictly positive, so that the members share a common support and almost everywhere finite. Then the vector of likelihood ratios against the baseline member, $$T(x)=\Bigl(\frac{p_1(x)}{p_0(x)},\dots,\frac{p_k(x)}{p_0(x)}\Bigr),$$ is minimal sufficient: it is sufficient, and it reduces the data as far as any sufficient statistic can, in the sense that for every sufficient statistic $U$ there is a measurable map $H$ with $T=H\circ U$ almost surely under every member.
summary: For a finite dominated family with common support, the vector of likelihood ratios against a fixed baseline member is a minimal sufficient statistic.

hypotheses.note: Every density is almost everywhere strictly positive; this is how the classical common-support proviso is formalized.

hypotheses.label: finite densities
hypotheses.note: Every density is almost everywhere finite — a Lean-side hypothesis with no classical counterpart, keeping the ratio algebra free of case analysis.

hypotheses.label: dominated family
hypotheses.note: The members are the given densities against a $\sigma$-finite dominating measure.

formalizationNotes: Ratios are formed in the extended nonnegative reals, where division is total, so the statistic is a genuine total function; the common-support hypothesis is what makes the ratios meaningful almost everywhere. Almost-everywhere finiteness of the densities is an addition without classical counterpart, used only to keep the ratio algebra free of case distinctions. The companion `isSufficient_iff_ratio_factors` (Corollary 6.13) characterizes sufficiency of an arbitrary statistic by the requirement that every density ratio of the family factor through it.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Minimal sufficiency and the likelihood-ratio construction are due to Lehmann and Scheffé (1950), with the general existence theory developed by Dynkin (1951) and Bahadur (1954, 1955); the underlying factorization criterion is due to Neyman (1935) and Halmos and Savage (1949). The formalization proves the finite-family statement of Theorem 6.12 of Lehmann and Casella; the subfamily route from finite families to general ones — minimal for a subfamily plus sufficient for the whole family implies minimal for the whole family — is not part of this development.

title: Sufficiency costs nothing: risk-equal estimators based on a sufficient statistic
informal: Let $T$ be sufficient for the model in the regular-conditional sense, let $L(\theta,d)$ be a loss function that is measurable in the decision argument, and let $\delta$ be any measurable estimator of the data. Then there exists a randomized estimator $\delta'$ that reads the data only through $T$ and has exactly the same risk function: $$\mathbb{E}_\theta\bigl[L\bigl(\theta,\delta'(T(X))\bigr)\bigr]=\mathbb{E}_\theta\bigl[L\bigl(\theta,\delta(X)\bigr)\bigr]\qquad\text{for every }\theta.$$ It is obtained by reporting the value of $T(X)$, regenerating an observation from the parameter-free reconstruction kernel attached to the sufficient statistic, and then applying $\delta$ to the regenerated observation. Consequently the class of risk functions attainable by arbitrary procedures coincides with the class attainable by procedures depending on the data only through a sufficient statistic.
summary: Every estimator is matched, risk function for risk function, by a randomized estimator that depends on the data only through a sufficient statistic.

hypotheses.label: measurable loss

hypotheses.label: measurable estimator
hypotheses.note: The estimator being matched is measurable, so that it defines a decision kernel.

formalizationNotes: Risks are extended-nonnegative-real lower integrals, so the identity is an honest equality even when both sides are infinite and no integrability hypothesis is needed anywhere. No convexity of the loss is used: this is the risk-*equality* statement, not the Rao–Blackwell improvement statement. The decision-theoretic form proved here — the attainable risk functions are the same whether or not procedures are restricted to depend on a sufficient statistic — is due to Bahadur (1954), building on Blackwell (1947). The formalization states it for arbitrary losses and gives both the randomized and the nonrandomized version.

title: Complete family of distributions; complete and ancillary statistics
informal: A family of probability measures $\{Q_\theta\}$ is **complete** when the only integrable functions whose expectation vanishes identically in the parameter are those that vanish almost surely: if $f$ is measurable and integrable under every $Q_\theta$ and $\int f\,dQ_\theta=0$ for every $\theta$, then $f=0$ almost everywhere under every $Q_\theta$. A statistic $T$ is complete for a model when the family of its laws is complete; equivalently, an unbiased estimator of zero based on $T$ must be zero, which is what makes an unbiased estimator based on a complete sufficient statistic unique. Restricting the test to uniformly bounded $f$ gives the weaker notion of **bounded completeness**, and a statistic whose distribution is the same under every parameter value is called **ancillary** (**first-order ancillary** when only its mean is parameter-free).
summary: A family is complete when no nonzero integrable function has expectation zero under every member.
formalizationNotes: The full (unbounded) variant quantifies over measurable functions that are integrable under every member, and concludes almost-everywhere vanishing under every member — the classical 'almost everywhere with respect to the family' conclusion. Completeness and bounded completeness are kept as independent predicates; the implication from the former to the latter is proved separately for families of probability measures, where bounded implies integrable.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Completeness, and its use for unbiased estimation and for similar tests, is due to Lehmann and Scheffé (1950, 1955). Ancillarity goes back to Fisher, and the theorem linking the two notions — a complete sufficient statistic is independent of every ancillary statistic — to Basu (1955). The formalization states completeness family-first, so that the same predicate applies to laws of statistics, to exponential families on the natural-statistic scale, and to the bounded variant used in the theory of similar tests.

title: Basu's theorem
informal: Let $T$ be a sufficient statistic in the parameter-free regular-conditional sense which is moreover boundedly complete, and let $V$ be ancillary, that is, a statistic whose distribution is the same under every parameter value. Then $T$ and $V$ are independent under every member of the family. The argument is short: for a measurable set $A$ the conditional probability $\eta_A(t)=P(V\in A\mid T=t)$ does not depend on the parameter by sufficiency, its mean $\mathbb{E}_\theta[\eta_A(T)]=P_\theta(V\in A)$ does not depend on the parameter by ancillarity, and bounded completeness applied to $\eta_A-P(V\in A)$ — a function bounded by one — forces $\eta_A$ to be constant almost everywhere. Constancy of the conditional probability is exactly independence.
summary: A boundedly complete sufficient statistic is independent of every ancillary statistic under every member of the family.

title: The natural statistic of a full-rank exponential family is complete
informal: Consider a canonical exponential family with an $s$-dimensional natural parameter and natural statistic $T$, and a parameter set $\Xi$ that is contained in the natural parameter space and whose interior is nonempty — the rank condition of the classical statement. Then the family of laws of $T$ is complete: if $f$ is integrable with $\mathbb{E}_\eta\bigl[f(T)\bigr]=0$ for every $\eta\in\Xi$, then $f=0$ almost surely under every member. Indeed, on the scale of the statistic the hypothesis reads $$\int f(t)\,e^{\langle\eta,t\rangle}\,d\nu_T(t)=0\qquad\text{for all }\eta\in\Xi,$$ so the two finite measures obtained by weighting $\nu_T$ with the positive and the negative part of $f$ have the same Laplace transform on a set with nonempty interior; uniqueness of Laplace transforms on an open set forces them to coincide, that is, $f=0$ almost everywhere.

title: Risk function of an estimator
informal: In a decision problem given by a model $\{P_\theta\}$ and a loss function $L(\theta,d)$, the **risk function** of an estimator $\delta$ is its average loss under the parameter, $$R(\theta,\delta)=\mathbb{E}_\theta\bigl[L\bigl(\theta,\delta(X)\bigr)\bigr]=\int L\bigl(\theta,\delta(x)\bigr)\,dP_\theta(x),$$ the function of $\theta$ by which estimators are compared: one estimator is at least as good as another when its risk function is nowhere larger. It is the diagonal of the two-parameter cross risk $\int L\bigl(\theta',\delta(x)\bigr)\,dP_\theta(x)$ — the expected loss of estimating the value at $\theta'$ when the data are generated at $\theta$ — whose off-diagonal values are what risk-unbiasedness is stated in terms of.
summary: The risk function of an estimator is its expected loss as a function of the parameter.
