title: Unbiasedness and the UMVU Property
informal: Let $\{P_\theta : \theta \in \Theta\}$ be a family of probability measures on the sample space and let $g$ be a real-valued function of the parameter, the estimand. A statistic $\delta$ is an **unbiased** estimator of $g$ when its expectation reproduces the estimand at every parameter, $\mathbb{E}_\theta[\delta(X)] = g(\theta)$ for all $\theta$, and it belongs to the estimator class $\Delta$ when it has a finite second moment under every member of the family. Such a $\delta$ is **uniformly minimum variance unbiased (UMVU)** for $g$ if in addition every unbiased estimator $\delta'$ of $g$ in the class $\Delta$ satisfies $\operatorname{var}_\theta(\delta) \le \operatorname{var}_\theta(\delta')$ at every parameter $\theta$. Minimality is demanded simultaneously at all parameter values; demanding it at a single $\theta_0$ only gives the weaker notion of a locally minimum variance unbiased estimator at $\theta_0$.
summary: An estimator is UMVU when it is unbiased, square-integrable, and has the smallest variance at every parameter among all square-integrable unbiased estimators of the same estimand.
leanSignature:
def IsUMVU (P : Θ → Measure 𝓧) (g : Θ → ℝ) (δ : 𝓧 → ℝ) : Prop :=
  IsUnbiased P g δ ∧ MemEstL2 P δ ∧
    ∀ δ', IsUnbiased P g δ' → MemEstL2 P δ' →
      ∀ θ, variance δ (P θ) ≤ variance δ' (P θ)
formalizationNotes: The auxiliary notions used throughout the area are declared in the same file: unbiased estimators of zero (the space $\mathcal{U}$ of the covariance characterization), the square-integrable estimator class $\Delta$, and the local variant at a single parameter. Variance is Mathlib's, whose junk convention returns $0$ for a variable with infinite second moment; this never bites, since the definition quantifies only over the class $\Delta$, where second moments are finite by definition. UMVU here is variance-based; the stronger convex-loss optimality of the estimator built from a complete sufficient statistic is a separate statement.

hypotheses.label: unbiasedness
hypotheses.note: The expectation of the estimator equals the estimand at every parameter.

hypotheses.label: estimator class $\Delta$
hypotheses.note: The estimator has a finite second moment under every member of the model.

hypotheses.leanToken: variance δ (P θ) ≤ variance δ' (P θ)
hypotheses.label: uniform minimality
hypotheses.note: Its variance is no larger than that of any competing unbiased square-integrable estimator, at every parameter simultaneously.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Unbiasedness as a systematic requirement descends from Gauss's theory of least squares (1821/1823) and its refinement by Markov. The modern minimum-variance theory is due to Rao (1945), Blackwell (1947) and Lehmann and Scheffé (1950); the reading of the unbiased class as an affine subspace, with the optimal element obtained by projecting onto the space of unbiased estimators of zero, is developed by Bahadur (1957). The formalization states the definition for an arbitrary parameter set, with variance taken under each member of the model and the competitor class restricted to square-integrable unbiased estimators.

title: Structure of the Class of Unbiased Estimators
informal: Let $\{P_\theta\}$ be a family of probability measures and $g$ an estimand. Suppose $\delta_0$ is an unbiased estimator of $g$ and that $\delta_0$ is integrable under every member of the family, and let $\delta$ be a statistic that is likewise integrable under every member. Then $\delta$ is unbiased for $g$ if and only if the difference $\delta_0 - \delta$ is an unbiased estimator of zero, that is $\mathbb{E}_\theta[\delta_0(X) - \delta(X)] = 0$ for every $\theta$. Equivalently, the unbiased estimators of $g$ form the affine class $\{\delta_0 - U : U \in \mathcal{U}\}$, where $\mathcal{U}$ is the linear space of unbiased estimators of zero. Finding the best unbiased estimator of $g$ is therefore the same problem as best approximating $\delta_0$ by elements of $\mathcal{U}$, which is what makes the covariance criterion and its projection reading possible.
summary: Once one unbiased estimator of an estimand is available, the unbiased estimators are exactly the differences of it with unbiased estimators of zero.
leanSignature:
theorem isUnbiased_iff_sub_unbiasedZero (P : Θ → Measure 𝓧) [∀ θ, IsProbabilityMeasure (P θ)]
    (g : Θ → ℝ) {δ₀ δ : 𝓧 → ℝ}
    (hδ₀ : IsUnbiased P g δ₀)
    (hδ₀i : ∀ θ, Integrable δ₀ (P θ))
    (hδi : ∀ θ, Integrable δ (P θ)) :
    IsUnbiased P g δ ↔ IsUnbiasedZero P (fun x => δ₀ x - δ x)
formalizationNotes: The equivalence is stated in the difference form, that $\delta_0 - \delta$ is an unbiased estimator of zero, rather than as an existential over that space; the two are trivially interchangeable and the difference form is what every downstream argument uses. Integrability of both estimators under every member is needed in both directions: means split additively only for integrable functions, and Lean's Bochner integral returns the junk value $0$ for non-integrable ones, so without integrability the two sides of the equivalence can disagree rather than the equivalence merely being unprovable.

hypotheses.label: reference unbiased estimator
hypotheses.note: One unbiased estimator of the estimand is given; the classical starting point.

hypotheses.label: integrability of the reference
hypotheses.note: The reference estimator is integrable under every member of the model.

hypotheses.label: integrability of the candidate
hypotheses.note: The candidate statistic is integrable under every member of the model.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The systematic theory of minimum-variance unbiased estimation is due to Rao (1945, 1949), Blackwell (1947) and Lehmann and Scheffé (1950). The identification of the unbiased class as an affine subspace parallel to the space of unbiased estimators of zero, and the resulting projection picture of minimum-variance estimation, is developed by Bahadur (1957). The formalization adds only the integrability required for expectations to subtract.

title: Uniqueness of the UMVU Estimator
informal: Let $\{P_\theta\}$ be a family of probability measures and $g$ an estimand. If $\delta_1$ is uniformly minimum variance unbiased for $g$ and $\delta_2$ is uniformly minimum variance unbiased for the same estimand $g$, then $\delta_1 = \delta_2$ almost surely under $P_\theta$, for every parameter $\theta$. This is why one speaks of *the* UMVU estimator of an estimable function.
summary: Two uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimators of the same estimand agree almost surely under every member of the model.
leanSignature:
theorem isUMVU_unique (P : Θ → Measure 𝓧) [∀ θ, IsProbabilityMeasure (P θ)] (g : Θ → ℝ)
    {δ₁ δ₂ : 𝓧 → ℝ}
    (h₁ : IsUMVU P g δ₁)
    (h₂ : IsUMVU P g δ₂) (θ : Θ) :
    δ₁ =ᵐ[P θ] δ₂
formalizationNotes: Uniqueness is proved parameter by parameter and uses only local minimality at that parameter: the two variances agree by mutual minimality, the average of the two estimators is again an unbiased square-integrable competitor, and comparing its variance with the common value forces equality in the Cauchy–Schwarz bound for the covariance, hence an affine relation between the centered estimators; equal variances and equal means then give almost sure equality. The degenerate case of zero variance is the statement that both are almost surely constant, equal to the estimand. No measurability hypothesis is needed: square-integrability already carries an almost-everywhere strongly measurable representative under each member.

hypotheses.label: first UMVU estimator
hypotheses.note: The first estimator is unbiased, square-integrable and of minimal variance at every parameter.

hypotheses.label: second UMVU estimator
hypotheses.note: The second estimator is UMVU for the same estimand.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Uniqueness of the minimum-variance unbiased estimator is part of the foundational treatment of Rao (1945, 1949) and Lehmann and Scheffé (1950); Bahadur (1957) gives the projection-theoretic account in which uniqueness is the uniqueness of a projection onto a closed subspace. The formalization states almost sure equality under each member separately, which is the strongest form available without a dominating measure.

title: UMVU Characterization by Zero Correlation
informal: Let $\{P_\theta\}$ be a family of probability measures and $g$ an estimand, and let $\delta$ be a statistic that is unbiased for $g$ and has a finite second moment under every member of the family. Then $\delta$ is uniformly minimum variance unbiased for $g$ if and only if it is uncorrelated with every unbiased estimator of zero: for every square-integrable statistic $U$ with $\mathbb{E}_\theta[U(X)] = 0$ at all parameters, and every $\theta$, one has $\operatorname{cov}_\theta(\delta, U) = 0$. Because $U$ is centered this is the classical condition $\mathbb{E}_\theta[\delta(X) U(X)] = 0$. Geometrically, the UMVU estimator is the member of the affine class of unbiased estimators of $g$ that is orthogonal, at every parameter, to the linear space $\mathcal{U}$ of unbiased estimators of zero: adding $\lambda U$ to $\delta$ preserves unbiasedness and changes the variance by $\lambda^2 \operatorname{var}_\theta(U) + 2\lambda \operatorname{cov}_\theta(\delta, U)$, which is negative for some $\lambda$ unless the covariance vanishes.
summary: A square-integrable unbiased estimator is UMVU exactly when it is uncorrelated with every square-integrable unbiased estimator of zero, at every parameter.
leanSignature:
theorem isUMVU_iff_uncorrelated_unbiasedZero (P : Θ → Measure 𝓧)
    [∀ θ, IsProbabilityMeasure (P θ)] (g : Θ → ℝ) {δ : 𝓧 → ℝ}
    (hδu : IsUnbiased P g δ)
    (hδ2 : MemEstL2 P δ) :
    IsUMVU P g δ ↔
      ∀ U : 𝓧 → ℝ, IsUnbiasedZero P U → MemEstL2 P U → ∀ θ, covariance δ U (P θ) = 0
formalizationNotes: The classical statement is phrased as $\mathbb{E}_\theta[\delta U] = 0$; since the estimator of zero is centered this is the same as a vanishing covariance, and the covariance form is used because it is what Mathlib's bilinearity interface consumes directly. Both directions quantify over the square-integrable class, exactly as the source does: outside it the variance-minimization problem is vacuous, and the sufficiency direction is proved by discarding competitors of infinite variance. A companion theorem in the same file records when a covariance lower bound applies to *all* unbiased estimators of a given estimand — the covariance of an estimator with a reference statistic depends on the estimator only through its mean function exactly when that reference statistic is uncorrelated with every unbiased estimator of zero.

hypotheses.label: unbiasedness
hypotheses.note: The candidate estimator is unbiased for the estimand.

hypotheses.label: estimator class $\Delta$
hypotheses.note: The candidate has a finite second moment under every member of the model.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The covariance characterization of minimum-variance unbiased estimators is due to Lehmann and Scheffé (1950, 1955) and Rao (1949), with the projection-theoretic account given by Bahadur (1957). The condition under which a covariance inequality yields a genuine lower bound valid for every unbiased estimator of a given estimand is due to Blyth (1974); the underlying inequality goes back to Rao (1945). The formalization proves both directions, the necessity by minimizing the perturbed variance as a quadratic in the perturbation size.

title: Rao–Blackwell Theorem for Convex Losses
informal: Let $T$ be a sufficient statistic for the family $\{P_\theta\}$, sufficiency being witnessed by a parameter-free Markov kernel $Q$ that reconstructs the data from the statistic: under every $P_\theta$ the joint law of $(T(X), X)$ is the law of $T(X)$ followed by $Q$. Let $\delta$ be a statistic that is integrable under every member of the family, and let $$\eta(t) \;=\; \int \delta(x)\, dQ_t(x)$$ be its average over the reconstruction fibre at $t$, so that the Rao–Blackwellized estimator $\eta(T(X))$ reads the data only through $T$. If the loss $L(\theta, d)$ is convex in the decision $d$ at every parameter and nonnegative, and $\delta$ has finite risk at every parameter, then $$R\bigl(\theta, \eta \circ T\bigr) \;\le\; R(\theta, \delta) \qquad \text{for every } \theta .$$ Conditioning on a sufficient statistic therefore never increases the risk. Averaging also preserves unbiasedness, so the Rao–Blackwellization of an unbiased estimator is again unbiased, and for squared error the inequality is the familiar reduction of variance.
summary: Averaging an estimator over the fibres of a sufficient statistic does not increase its risk, for any loss convex in the decision.
leanSignature:
theorem risk_rbEstimator_le (P : Θ → Measure 𝓧) [∀ θ, IsProbabilityMeasure (P θ)]
    {T : 𝓧 → S}
    (hT : Measurable T) {Q : Kernel S 𝓧} [IsMarkovKernel Q]
    (hgraph : ∀ θ, (P θ).map (fun x => (T x, x)) = (statLaw P T θ) ⊗ₘ Q) {δ : 𝓧 → ℝ}
    (hδm : Measurable δ)
    (hδi : ∀ θ, Integrable δ (P θ)) (ρ : Θ → ℝ → ℝ)
    (hconv : ∀ θ, ConvexOn ℝ Set.univ (ρ θ))
    (hcont : ∀ θ, Continuous (ρ θ))
    (hnn : ∀ θ y, 0 ≤ ρ θ y)
    (hρi : ∀ θ, Integrable (fun x => ρ θ (δ x)) (P θ)) (θ : Θ) :
    risk P (fun θ' d => ENNReal.ofReal (ρ θ' d)) (fun x => rbEstimator Q δ (T x)) θ ≤
      risk P (fun θ' d => ENNReal.ofReal (ρ θ' d)) δ θ
formalizationNotes: Sufficiency is carried by an explicit parameter-free reconstruction kernel rather than by a sub-σ-field, so the risk bound is ordinary Jensen applied fibrewise and then integrated against the law of the statistic: no conditional expectation, no conditional Jensen, no filtration bookkeeping. Integrability of the estimator along the fibres is *derived* from the reconstruction identity rather than assumed, since assuming it would be laundering a consequence of the setup into a hypothesis. Continuity of the loss is an extra hypothesis, automatic for a convex function on the whole line, kept only to avoid importing the convex-continuity machinery. Risks are extended-nonnegative-real valued and losses enter through the nonnegative-real embedding. The squared-error case, and the conditional-expectation form of the variance reduction (the law of total variance, which needs no measurable representative), are separate declarations in the same area.

hypotheses.label: sufficiency kernel
hypotheses.note: The joint law of the statistic and the data disintegrates through a Markov kernel that does not depend on the parameter.

hypotheses.label: integrability
hypotheses.note: The estimator is integrable under every member; integrability along the fibres is derived from this, not assumed.

hypotheses.label: convex loss
hypotheses.note: The loss is convex in the decision argument at every parameter.

hypotheses.label: nonnegative loss
hypotheses.note: The loss takes nonnegative values.

hypotheses.label: finite risk
hypotheses.note: The risk of the original estimator is finite (otherwise the inequality is trivial).

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The theorem is due to Rao (1945) and Blackwell (1947); its extension from squared error to arbitrary convex losses, via Jensen's inequality, appears in Lehmann and Scheffé (1950). The formulation through a reconstruction kernel rather than a conditional expectation follows Bahadur (1954). The formalization proves the inequality for an arbitrary nonnegative convex loss and derives the fibrewise integrability that the classical proof assumes implicitly.

title: At Most One Unbiased Function of a Complete Statistic
informal: Let $T$ be a statistic for the family $\{P_\theta\}$ which is complete: the only integrable function of $T$ whose expectation vanishes at every parameter is zero almost surely. If $u_1$ and $u_2$ are measurable functions of the statistic such that $u_1(T(X))$ is unbiased for the estimand $g$ and $u_2(T(X))$ is unbiased for the same estimand, then $u_1 = u_2$ almost surely under the law of $T$ at every parameter. There is therefore at most one unbiased function of a complete statistic, which is what makes the Rao–Blackwellization of an unbiased estimator along such a statistic canonical: it does not depend on which unbiased estimator one starts from.
summary: Two unbiased functions of a complete statistic agree almost surely under every law of the statistic.
leanSignature:
theorem unique_unbiased_function_of_complete (P : Θ → Measure 𝓧)
    [∀ θ, IsProbabilityMeasure (P θ)] (g : Θ → ℝ) {T : 𝓧 → S}
    (hT : Measurable T)
    (hcomp : IsCompleteStat P T) {η₁ η₂ : S → ℝ}
    (hη₁ : Measurable η₁) (hη₂ : Measurable η₂)
    (hi₁ : ∀ θ, Integrable η₁ (statLaw P T θ)) (hi₂ : ∀ θ, Integrable η₂ (statLaw P T θ))
    (hu₁ : IsUnbiased P g fun x => η₁ (T x)) (hu₂ : IsUnbiased P g fun x => η₂ (T x))
    (θ : Θ) :
    η₁ =ᵐ[statLaw P T θ] η₂
formalizationNotes: Only completeness is used: the classical statement additionally assumes sufficiency, which is what guarantees that unbiased functions of the statistic *exist* but is not needed for uniqueness. Dropping it strengthens the lemma and is recorded as a deliberate deviation. Measurability of the statistic and of the two candidate functions, and their integrability under the laws of the statistic, are Lean-side requirements so that the change of variables applies and the expectations subtract.

hypotheses.label: completeness
hypotheses.note: No nonzero integrable function of the statistic has identically vanishing expectation.

hypotheses.label: first unbiased function
hypotheses.note: The first function of the statistic is unbiased for the estimand.

hypotheses.label: second unbiased function
hypotheses.note: The second function of the statistic is unbiased for the same estimand.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Completeness was introduced by Lehmann and Scheffé (1950, 1955) precisely to obtain this uniqueness, and with it the passage from Rao–Blackwellization to optimality. Bahadur (1957) showed conversely that, under mild conditions, the existence of a complete sufficient statistic is also necessary for every estimable function to admit a uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator. The formalization states almost sure equality under the law of the statistic at each parameter.

title: Lehmann–Scheffé Theorem
informal: Let $\{P_\theta\}$ be a family of probability measures dominated by a $\sigma$-finite measure, and let $T$ be a statistic which is sufficient — witnessed by a parameter-free Markov kernel $Q$ reconstructing the data from the statistic — and complete. Suppose the estimand $g$ is estimable, in the sense that some statistic $\delta$ is unbiased for $g$ and has a finite second moment under every member of the family. Then the Rao–Blackwellized estimator $$\eta(t) = \int \delta(x)\, dQ_t(x), \qquad x \mapsto \eta(T(x)),$$ is the uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator of $g$. By the uniqueness of unbiased functions of a complete statistic it does not matter which unbiased estimator one starts from, and by the uniqueness of the UMVU estimator it is the only one.
summary: Averaging an unbiased square-integrable estimator over the fibres of a complete sufficient statistic produces the UMVU estimator of the estimand.
leanSignature:
theorem isUMVU_of_complete_sufficient (P : Θ → Measure 𝓧) [∀ θ, IsProbabilityMeasure (P θ)]
    (g : Θ → ℝ) {T : 𝓧 → S}
    (hT : Measurable T)
    (μ : Measure 𝓧) [SigmaFinite μ] (hdom : ∀ θ, P θ ≪ μ) {Q : Kernel S 𝓧} [IsMarkovKernel Q]
    (hgraph : ∀ θ, (P θ).map (fun x => (T x, x)) = (statLaw P T θ) ⊗ₘ Q)
    (hcomp : IsCompleteStat P T) {δ : 𝓧 → ℝ}
    (hδm : Measurable δ)
    (hδu : IsUnbiased P g δ)
    (hδ2 : MemEstL2 P δ) :
    IsUMVU P g (fun x => rbEstimator Q δ (T x))
formalizationNotes: Domination of the family by a σ-finite measure is an added hypothesis, not present in the printed statement. It is used only to glue a competitor's per-parameter almost-everywhere versions into a single measurable representative — the completeness test and the fibrewise average both need a genuine measurable function — and without it these versions need not glue: for a family of Dirac measures each parameter constrains the competitor at a single point, so no one measurable function need represent all of them at once. It is the standing hypothesis of the dominated theory of sufficiency and completeness, and it is discharged for free by the only consumer of the theorem, the exponential-family corollary. A companion theorem in the same file gives the convex-loss form of Lehmann–Scheffé: the same estimator minimizes the risk among all unbiased estimators, simultaneously for every nonnegative convex loss, so its optimality is not tied to squared error. Optimality is proved by transport rather than by a fresh variational argument: a competitor's Rao–Blackwellization is an unbiased function of the complete statistic, hence almost everywhere equal to the given one.

hypotheses.label: dominated model
hypotheses.note: The members of the family are absolutely continuous with respect to one σ-finite measure.

hypotheses.label: sufficiency kernel
hypotheses.note: The joint law of the statistic and the data disintegrates through a parameter-free Markov kernel.

hypotheses.label: completeness
hypotheses.note: No nonzero integrable function of the statistic has identically vanishing expectation.

hypotheses.label: unbiased witness
hypotheses.note: Some unbiased estimator of the estimand exists, witnessing estimability.

hypotheses.label: estimator class $\Delta$
hypotheses.note: That witness has a finite second moment under every member of the model.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The theorem is due to Lehmann and Scheffé (1950, 1955), building on the conditioning theorem of Rao (1945) and Blackwell (1947). Bahadur (1957) proved the converse direction, that under mild conditions a complete sufficient statistic must exist if every estimable function is to admit a uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator. The formalization states the variance form here and the all-convex-losses form alongside it, and it makes explicit the domination hypothesis that the classical proof uses tacitly when it replaces a competitor by a measurable version.

title: UMVU Estimation in Full-Rank Exponential Families
informal: Let $\{P_\theta\}$ be a family of probability measures which is a reparametrization of a canonical exponential family, with densities $\exp\bigl(\langle \eta, T(x)\rangle - A(\eta)\bigr)$ relative to a reference measure and natural statistic $T$. Suppose the parametrization covers a set $\Xi$ of natural parameters on which the family is of full rank, that is $\Xi$ has nonempty interior and the natural statistic is affinely independent. If an estimand $g$ admits an unbiased estimator $\delta$ which has a finite second moment under every member, then there is a measurable function $u$ of the natural statistic such that $u(T(X))$ is the uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator of $g$. The natural statistic of a full-rank exponential family is complete and sufficient, so this is the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem applied to it.
summary: In a full-rank exponential family every estimable function has a UMVU estimator, and it is a function of the natural statistic.
leanSignature:
theorem isUMVU_of_fullRank_expFamily {s : ℕ} (E : ExpFamily 𝓧 (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin s)))
    [SigmaFinite E.base] (Ξ : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin s))) (P : Θ → Measure 𝓧)
    [∀ θ, IsProbabilityMeasure (P θ)]
    [StandardBorelSpace 𝓧] [Nonempty 𝓧] (ηmap : Θ → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin s))
    (hrepr : IsCanonicalRepr P E ηmap)
    (hcover : Ξ ⊆ Set.range ηmap)
    (hFR : E.FullRank Ξ) (g : Θ → ℝ) {δ : 𝓧 → ℝ}
    (hδm : Measurable δ)
    (hδu : IsUnbiased P g δ)
    (hδ2 : MemEstL2 P δ) :
    ∃ η : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin s) → ℝ, Measurable η ∧
      IsUMVU P g (fun x => η (E.stat x))
formalizationNotes: Two authorized deviations from the printed statement. First, the natural statistic is valued in $\mathbb{R}^s$ rather than in an abstract inner-product space: the completeness theorem for the natural statistic rests on a finite-dimensional Laplace-transform uniqueness argument, and no completeness statement is available for an abstract space. Second, the reference measure is assumed σ-finite, which is what turns the Fisher–Neyman factorization of the densities into sufficiency and then into a reconstruction kernel; the sample space is assumed standard Borel for the same reason, as everywhere in this area's sufficiency theory. Nothing else is added: neither the nonvanishing of the reference measure nor membership of the parameters in the natural parameter set is assumed, both being derived from the members' being probability measures. The conclusion is existential because the optimal function of the natural statistic is determined only almost everywhere.

hypotheses.label: canonical exponential family
hypotheses.note: The model is a reparametrization of a canonical exponential family.

hypotheses.label: parametrization covers $\Xi$
hypotheses.note: Every natural parameter in the distinguished set is attained by the parametrization.

hypotheses.label: full rank
hypotheses.note: The natural parameter set has nonempty interior and the natural statistic is affinely independent.

hypotheses.label: estimability
hypotheses.note: Some unbiased estimator of the estimand exists.

hypotheses.label: estimator class $\Delta$
hypotheses.note: That witness has a finite second moment under every member of the model.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Completeness of the natural statistic of a full-rank exponential family is established by Lehmann and Scheffé (1955), on the basis of the characterizations of exponential families by Darmois (1935), Koopman (1936) and Pitman (1936); the convex-analytic theory of the natural parameter set and its interior is that of Brown (1986). The corollary combines that completeness with the conditioning theorem of Rao (1945) and Blackwell (1947). The formalization derives completeness of the natural statistic from nonempty interior of the natural parameter set and transports it from the distinguished parameter subfamily to the whole model by mutual absolute continuity.

title: Score Function and Fisher Information
informal: Let $\{p_\theta\}$ be a family of densities relative to a dominating measure $\mu$, indexed by a real parameter $\theta$. The **score** at $\theta$ is the logarithmic derivative of the density in the parameter, $$\dot\ell_\theta(x) \;=\; \frac{\partial_\theta\, p_\theta(x)}{p_\theta(x)},$$ and the **Fisher information** at $\theta$ is the second moment of the score taken under the model, that is with the density as weight: $$I(\theta) \;=\; \int \dot\ell_\theta(x)^2\, p_\theta(x)\, d\mu(x) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_\theta\bigl[\dot\ell_\theta(X)^2\bigr].$$ Under the regularity conditions of the theory the score has mean zero, so the information is exactly the variance of the score, and with one more derivative it is also the expected negative curvature of the log-likelihood. For a parameter ranging in $\mathbb{R}^s$ the same construction gives the score vector of partial logarithmic derivatives and the Fisher information matrix of their second moments.
summary: The score is the logarithmic derivative of the density in the parameter, and the Fisher information is its second moment under the model.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def fisherInfo (M : ParametricFamily 𝓧 ℝ) (μ : Measure 𝓧) (θ : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∫ x, score M θ x ^ 2 * M.density θ x ∂μ
formalizationNotes: The score is *derived from the densities* as a derivative in the parameter, unlike the free candidate-score functionals of the asymptotic-statistics part of the library; a bridge lemma identifies this information with that area's bilinear Fisher-information form evaluated on the derived score. Both definitions are junk-safe: division by a vanishing density returns zero under Lean's total real division, and a derivative that fails to exist returns a junk value, so regularity — differentiability in the parameter for almost every observation, and differentiation under the integral sign — enters only through the hypotheses of the theorems, never through the definitions. The score vector and the information matrix for an $\mathbb{R}^s$-valued parameter are declared in the same file, with partial derivatives taken along the coordinate directions; positive definiteness of the matrix is always a hypothesis, never built in.

hypotheses.label: squared score
hypotheses.note: The integrand is the square of the logarithmic derivative of the density in the parameter.

hypotheses.label: model weight
hypotheses.note: The second moment is taken under the member of the family at that parameter, i.e. weighted by its density.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.pointer: Chapter 2, §2.5 (the score function and the Fisher information)
reference.biblio: The score and the information it carries were introduced by Fisher (1925), building on his foundations paper (1922). The information lower bound for variances is due independently to Rao (1945) and Cramér (1946), with earlier forms in Fréchet (1943) and Darmois (1945); the multiparameter matrix form is due to Rao (1945). The formalization takes the density-based definition, so that the information of a concrete dominated family can be computed rather than posited.

title: The Information Is the Variance of the Score
informal: Let $\{p_\theta\}$ be a family of densities relative to $\mu$ which are probability densities, each integrating to one and integrable, and which have a common support, the set where the density is positive not depending on the parameter. Assume that the normalization identity $\int p_t \, d\mu = 1$ may be differentiated under the integral sign at $\theta$ and that the Fisher information is finite. Then the score is centered, $$\mathbb{E}_\theta\bigl[\dot\ell_\theta(X)\bigr] \;=\; 0,$$ and consequently the Fisher information is exactly the variance of the score under the model: $$I(\theta) \;=\; \operatorname{var}_\theta\bigl(\dot\ell_\theta(X)\bigr).$$ With one further derivative the information is also the expected negative curvature of the log-likelihood, $I(\theta) = -\mathbb{E}_\theta[\partial_\theta^2 \log p_\theta(X)]$.
summary: Under differentiation under the integral sign the score has mean zero, so the Fisher information is exactly its variance.
leanSignature:
theorem fisherInfo_eq_variance_score (M : ParametricFamily 𝓧 ℝ) (μ : Measure 𝓧)
    (hpdf : IsPDFOf M μ)
    (hsupp : HasCommonSupport M)
    (θ : ℝ)
    (hswap : HasDerivAt (fun t => ∫ x, M.density t x ∂μ)
      (∫ x, deriv (fun t => M.density t x) θ ∂μ) θ)
    (hmeas : AEStronglyMeasurable (score M θ) μ)
    (hint : Integrable (fun x => score M θ x ^ 2 * M.density θ x) μ) :
    fisherInfo M μ θ = variance (score M θ) (M.toMeasure μ θ)
formalizationNotes: Differentiation under the integral sign is never derived here: it is an explicit hypothesis about the normalization identity, which is exactly the classical regularity condition; sufficient conditions on the family alone are supplied by the density-regularity companion file. The common-support condition is what allows the junk-safe score to be traded against the derivative of the density — off the support the score times the density is zero while the derivative of the density need not be — and it is a genuine condition of the classical theory, failing precisely for families whose support moves with the parameter, which is where the information inequality itself fails. Measurability of the score is an extra hypothesis in this shape: built from a derivative in the parameter, the score carries no measurability in the observation by construction. The mean-zero property and the negated-curvature expression are separate named theorems in the same file, as is the transformation rule $I^{*}(\xi) = I(h(\xi)) h'(\xi)^2$ under reparametrization, which shows that the information is not parametrization invariant.

title: Additivity of the Fisher Information over a Sample
informal: Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be an independent identically distributed sample from a family of densities relative to $\mu$ which are probability densities, have a common support and are differentiable in the parameter at every point of that support, and assume the score of one observation has mean zero. Then the information carried by the sample is $n$ times the information carried by a single observation: $$I_{X_1,\dots,X_n}(\theta) \;=\; n\, I(\theta).$$ The joint density is the product of the coordinate densities, so the joint score is the sum $\sum_i \dot\ell_\theta(x_i)$ of the coordinate scores; squaring and integrating, the diagonal terms contribute $I(\theta)$ each and the cross terms factorize by Fubini into products of two vanishing mean scores. The same computation gives additivity over two independent, not necessarily identically distributed, observations: $I_{(X,Y)}(\theta) = I_X(\theta) + I_Y(\theta)$.
summary: An independent identically distributed sample of size n carries n times the Fisher information of one observation.
leanSignature:
theorem fisherInfo_pi (M : ParametricFamily 𝓧 ℝ) (μ : Measure 𝓧)
    [SigmaFinite μ]
    (n : ℕ) (θ : ℝ)
    (hM : IsPDFOf M μ)
    (hsupp : HasCommonSupport M)
    (hdiff : ∀ x, 0 < M.density θ x → DifferentiableAt ℝ (fun t => M.density t x) θ)
    (hmean0 : ∫ x, score M θ x * M.density θ x ∂μ = 0)
    (hint : Integrable (fun x => score M θ x ^ 2 * M.density θ x) μ)
    (hint1 : Integrable (fun x => score M θ x * M.density θ x) μ) :
    fisherInfo (piFamily M n) (Measure.pi fun _ : Fin n => μ) θ = (n : ℝ) * fisherInfo M μ θ

The families are built at the level of densities, so the dominating measure of the sample is the product measure and the joint score is literally the sum of the coordinate scores on the common support. σ-finiteness of the dominating measure and integrability of the mean score are Lean-side requirements of the product-measure and Fubini machinery, not conditions of the classical statement. For $n = 0$ the empty product convention gives density one and information zero, which is the correct degenerate value.

title: Cramér–Rao Information Inequality
informal: Let $\{p_\theta\}$ be a family of probability densities relative to $\mu$ with a common support, and let $\delta$ be a statistic with a finite second moment at $\theta$. Assume that the Fisher information at $\theta$ is positive, that the expectation $t \mapsto \mathbb{E}_t[\delta(X)]$ is differentiable at $\theta$, with derivative $g'$, that this derivative is obtained by differentiating under the integral sign, and that the score has mean zero. Then $$\operatorname{var}_\theta(\delta) \;\ge\; \frac{(g')^2}{I(\theta)} .$$ For an unbiased estimator of an estimand $g$ the numerator is $g'(\theta)^2$, the familiar bound. No unbiasedness is needed: writing $\mathbb{E}_t[\delta(X)] = g(t) + b(t)$ for a bias $b$, the same inequality reads $\operatorname{var}_\theta(\delta) \ge (g'(\theta) + b'(\theta))^2 / I(\theta)$, so a biased estimator can beat the unbiased bound only through a nonconstant bias.
summary: The variance of a statistic is at least the squared derivative of its expectation divided by the Fisher information.
leanSignature:
theorem cramer_rao (M : ParametricFamily 𝓧 ℝ) (μ : Measure 𝓧)
    (hpdf : IsPDFOf M μ)
    (hsupp : HasCommonSupport M)
    (θ : ℝ) (δ : 𝓧 → ℝ) (g' : ℝ)
    (hmeas : AEStronglyMeasurable (score M θ) μ)
    (hδ2 : MemLp δ 2 (M.toMeasure μ θ))
    (hscore_int : Integrable (fun x => score M θ x ^ 2 * M.density θ x) μ)
    (hI : 0 < fisherInfo M μ θ)
    (hdiff : HasDerivAt (fun t => ∫ x, δ x * M.density t x ∂μ) g' θ)
    (hswap : g' = ∫ x, δ x * deriv (fun t => M.density t x) θ ∂μ)
    (hmean0 : ∫ x, score M θ x * M.density θ x ∂μ = 0) :
    g' ^ 2 / fisherInfo M μ θ ≤ variance δ (M.toMeasure μ θ)
formalizationNotes: The proof is the covariance inequality $\operatorname{var}(\delta) \ge \operatorname{cov}(\delta,\psi)^2/\operatorname{var}(\psi)$ — Cauchy–Schwarz for the centered variables — applied with the score in place of $\psi$: the mean-zero property turns its variance into the information and its covariance with the statistic into the integral of the statistic against the derivative of the density, which the exchange hypothesis identifies with the derivative of the expectation. The bound is written with the division on the smaller side so that a vanishing information falls back harmlessly on Lean's convention that division by zero is zero; positivity of the information is nonetheless kept as a hypothesis, as in the source. The common-support condition is what lets the junk-safe score be traded for the derivative of the density; without it the two integrals differ by the contribution of the set where the density vanishes, and the bound need not hold. Measurability of the score and finiteness of the information as a Bochner integral are extra hypotheses of this estimator-side shape; both are consequences of the family-side regularity used in the companion theorem. The bias form is a separate declaration in the same file.

title: Information Inequality under Family-Side Regularity
informal: Let $\{p_\theta\}$ be a family of probability densities relative to $\mu$ with a common support, differentiable in the parameter at every point of that support, with positive Fisher information at $\theta$, and satisfying the dominated-difference-quotient condition at $\theta$: there are $\varepsilon > 0$ and an envelope $b$ with $\mathbb{E}_\theta[b(X)^2] < \infty$ such that the normalized difference quotients satisfy $\bigl|(p_{\theta+\Delta}(x) - p_\theta(x)) / (\Delta\, p_\theta(x))\bigr| \le b(x)$, almost surely under the model, for every increment with $0 < |\Delta| < \varepsilon$. Then for **every** statistic $\delta$ with a finite second moment at $\theta$ the expectation $t \mapsto \mathbb{E}_t[\delta(X)]$ is differentiable at $\theta$, its derivative equals the covariance of the statistic with the score, and $$\operatorname{var}_\theta(\delta) \;\ge\; \frac{\bigl(\partial_\theta\, \mathbb{E}_\theta[\delta(X)]\bigr)^2}{I(\theta)} .$$ Every condition is on the family: nothing is required of the estimator beyond square-integrability. For an independent identically distributed sample the same bound holds with $n I(\theta)$ in the denominator.
summary: Under a dominated-difference-quotient condition on the densities alone, the information inequality holds for every square-integrable statistic.
leanSignature:
theorem cramer_rao_of_density_regular (M : ParametricFamily 𝓧 ℝ) (μ : Measure 𝓧)
    (hpdf : IsPDFOf M μ)
    (hsupp : HasCommonSupport M)
    (θ : ℝ)
    (hdiff : ∀ x, 0 < M.density θ x → DifferentiableAt ℝ (fun t => M.density t x) θ)
    (hI : 0 < fisherInfo M μ θ)
    (hreg : HasDominatedDifferenceQuotient M μ θ)
    (δ : 𝓧 → ℝ)
    (hδ2 : MemLp δ 2 (M.toMeasure μ θ)) :
    HasDerivAt (fun t => ∫ x, δ x * M.density t x ∂μ)
        (∫ x, δ x * score M θ x * M.density θ x ∂μ) θ ∧
      (∫ x, δ x * score M θ x * M.density θ x ∂μ) ^ 2 / fisherInfo M μ θ
        ≤ variance δ (M.toMeasure μ θ)

The mean-zero property of the score is likewise derived, by applying the differentiation step to the constant statistic one, and measurability of the score is derived as an almost-everywhere limit of measurable difference quotients. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the integrand by the product of the statistic with the envelope, which is integrable because both factors are square-integrable, and dominated convergence then exchanges limit and integral; that dominated-convergence core is the single sanctioned analytic step of the file, and everything downstream — including the sample-size-$n$ form with $n I(\theta)$ in the denominator — is a genuine reduction to it. The domination is imposed almost everywhere under the model and is local at the parameter: no uniformity in the parameter is assumed.

title: Attainment of the Information Bound
informal: Let $\{p_\theta\}$ be a family of probability densities relative to $\mu$, and fix a parameter $\theta$ at which the Fisher information is positive and the score has mean zero. If the statistic is almost surely an affine function of the score at $\theta$, $\delta(x) = a\,\dot\ell_\theta(x) + b$ for constants $a$ and $b$, then the information bound is attained with equality: $$\operatorname{var}_\theta(\delta) \;=\; \frac{\mathbb{E}_\theta[\delta(X)\,\dot\ell_\theta(X)]^2}{I(\theta)} .$$ This is the equality case of Cauchy–Schwarz, and it needs no regularity of the family beyond a centered score and a positive information at that parameter. The constants are allowed to depend on $\theta$; if they genuinely do, the affine function of the score is not an estimator and no estimator attains the bound, which is why the classical converse quantifies over all parameter values with one fixed statistic. When the representation does hold at every parameter with the estimator fixed, the density takes the exponential form $\exp\bigl(\eta(\theta)\delta(x) - B(\theta)\bigr) h(x)$, so the family is exponential with the estimator as natural statistic.
summary: A statistic that is an affine function of the score attains the Cramér–Rao bound with equality.
leanSignature:
theorem cramer_rao_attained_of_affine (M : ParametricFamily 𝓧 ℝ) (μ : Measure 𝓧)
    (hpdf : IsPDFOf M μ)
    (θ : ℝ) (δ : 𝓧 → ℝ) (a b : ℝ)
    (hmeas : AEStronglyMeasurable (score M θ) μ)
    (hI : 0 < fisherInfo M μ θ)
    (hmean0 : ∫ x, score M θ x * M.density θ x ∂μ = 0)
    (haffine : ∀ᵐ x ∂(M.toMeasure μ θ), δ x = a * score M θ x + b) :
    variance δ (M.toMeasure μ θ)
      = (∫ x, δ x * score M θ x * M.density θ x ∂μ) ^ 2 / fisherInfo M μ θ

The converse printed in the source — attainment at every parameter forces an exponential family with the estimator as natural statistic — is not included here; formalizing it would require adding the nondegeneracy assumption that the derivative of the estimand never vanishes. Without that assumption the attainment identity is vacuous wherever the derivative of the estimand and the variance both vanish, so the printed hypotheses are met by the Gaussian location family with the identically zero estimator, which is not an exponential family in that estimator. The source carries the missing assumption implicitly, through the companion identity relating the information to the product of the derivatives of the natural parameter and the estimand. The Cauchy–Schwarz equality step that the converse would consume is available in the same file: attainment at a parameter, together with a nonzero derivative, forces the score to be almost surely an affine function of the statistic.

title: Fisher Information of an Exponential Family
informal: Let the canonical one-parameter exponential family have densities $p_\eta(x) = \exp\bigl(\eta\, T(x) - A(\eta)\bigr)$ relative to a reference measure, where $T$ is the natural statistic and $A$ the log-partition (cumulant) function. If the natural parameter $\eta$ lies in the interior of the natural parameter set, then the Fisher information in the natural parametrization is the curvature of the log-partition function, $$I(\eta) \;=\; A''(\eta) \;=\; \operatorname{var}_\eta\bigl(T(X)\bigr).$$ Indeed the log-density is $\eta T(x) - A(\eta)$, so the score is the centered natural statistic $T(x) - A'(\eta)$ and the information is its variance. In the mean-value parametrization $\tau = A'(\eta)$ the information is instead the reciprocal $1/\operatorname{var}_\eta(T(X))$, by the transformation rule for the information under reparametrization.
summary: In the natural parametrization the Fisher information of an exponential family is the second derivative of its log-partition function.
leanSignature:
theorem fisherInfo_expFamily (E : ExpFamily 𝓧 ℝ) (η : ℝ)
    (hη : η ∈ interior E.natSet) :

The density presentation used here agrees with the member measure built by exponential tilting; where the reference measure is the zero measure both sides degenerate to zero and the identity still holds. The mean-value parametrization statement is a deliberate change of presentation, obtained from the reparametrization rule for the information, not a separate theorem.

The formalization proves it in the natural parametrization, deriving analyticity of the cumulant function on the interior of the natural parameter set rather than assuming smoothness.

title: Information Matrix of an Exponential Family
informal: Let the canonical exponential family on an $s$-dimensional natural parameter have densities $p_\eta(x) = \exp\bigl(\langle \eta, T(x)\rangle - A(\eta)\bigr)$ relative to a reference measure, with natural statistic $T = (T_1,\dots,T_s)$. If the natural parameter $\eta$ lies in the interior of the natural parameter set, then the Fisher information matrix is the covariance matrix of the natural statistic, $$I(\eta)_{ij} \;=\; \operatorname{cov}_\eta\bigl(T_i(X),\, T_j(X)\bigr) \;=\; \frac{\partial^2 A}{\partial \eta_i \partial \eta_j}(\eta),$$ equivalently the Hessian of the log-partition function. Each coordinate score is the centered coordinate statistic $T_i - \partial_i A(\eta)$, so the entries of the information matrix are exactly the second central moments of the natural statistic. In the mean-value parametrization the information matrix is the inverse of this covariance matrix.
summary: The Fisher information matrix of a canonical exponential family is the covariance matrix of its natural statistic.

The degenerate case of a zero reference measure is covered explicitly: both sides vanish.

title: Covariance Inequality in Quadratic Form
informal: Fix a probability measure and a statistic $\delta$ with a finite second moment, together with auxiliary functions $\psi_1,\dots,\psi_r$ each with a finite second moment. Let $C$ be their covariance matrix, $C_{ij} = \operatorname{cov}(\psi_i,\psi_j)$, and let $\gamma$ be the vector of covariances of the statistic with the auxiliary functions, $\gamma_i = \operatorname{cov}(\delta,\psi_i)$. If the covariance matrix is positive definite, then $$\operatorname{var}(\delta) \;\ge\; \gamma^{\mathsf{T}} C^{-1} \gamma .$$ The right-hand side is exactly the best one-dimensional covariance bound available from linear combinations of the auxiliary functions: maximizing $\operatorname{cov}(\delta, \sum_i a_i \psi_i)^2 / \operatorname{var}(\sum_i a_i \psi_i)$ over the coefficient vector $a$ gives $\gamma^{\mathsf{T}} C^{-1}\gamma$, the maximum being attained at $a = C^{-1}\gamma$. Taking the auxiliary functions to be the coordinate scores turns $C$ into the Fisher information matrix and $\gamma$ into the gradient of the expectation of $\delta$.
summary: The variance of a statistic is at least the quadratic form of its covariance vector against the inverse covariance matrix of any square-integrable auxiliary family.

theorem covariance_matrix_inequality {r : ℕ} (P : Measure 𝓧)
    [IsProbabilityMeasure P]
    (δ : 𝓧 → ℝ) (ψ : Fin r → 𝓧 → ℝ)
    (hδ : MemLp δ 2 P)
    (hψ : ∀ i, MemLp (ψ i) 2 P)
    (C : Matrix (Fin r) (Fin r) ℝ)
    (hC : ∀ i j, C i j = covariance (ψ i) (ψ j) P)
    (hCpos : C.PosDef)
    (γ : Fin r → ℝ)
    (hγ : ∀ i, γ i = covariance δ (ψ i) P) :
    γ ⬝ᵥ (C⁻¹ *ᵥ γ) ≤ variance δ P

Unbiasedness of the statistic plays no role in the proof and is therefore not assumed, a deliberate strengthening of the classical phrasing — unbiasedness matters only for the *use* of the bound, where one wants the right-hand side to depend on the statistic through its expectation alone, which happens exactly when each auxiliary function is uncorrelated with every unbiased estimator of zero. The covariance matrix and covariance vector are supplied as data together with their defining identities, rather than inlined, so the statement reads as the classical quadratic form and consumers may substitute a matrix they have already computed. Positive definiteness is a genuine hypothesis: without it the inverse is a junk value and the bound carries no content.

title: Multiparameter Cramér–Rao Bound
informal: Let $\{p_ heta\}$ be a family of probability densities on an $s$-dimensional parameter with a common support, differentiable in the parameter along each coordinate direction on that support, and let $\delta$ be a statistic with a finite second moment at $ heta$. Assume that every coordinate score has mean zero, that the Fisher information matrix $I( heta)$, whose entries are the expectations of products of coordinate scores, is positive definite, that the expectation $t \mapsto \mathbb{E}_t[\delta(X)]$ has a partial derivative $\alpha_i$ in each coordinate direction at $ heta$, and that those derivatives are obtained by differentiating under the integral sign. Then $$\operatorname{var}_ heta(\delta) \;\ge\; \alpha^{\mathsf{T}}\, I( heta)^{-1}\, \alpha .$$ For an unbiased estimator of an estimand $g$ the vector $\alpha$ is the gradient $ abla g( heta)$, giving the familiar bound $ abla g( heta)^{\mathsf{T}} I( heta)^{-1} abla g( heta)$; in general it is the gradient of the expectation of the statistic, so a bias contributes through its gradient.
summary: For a vector parameter the variance of a statistic is at least the gradient of its expectation contracted with the inverse Fisher information matrix.

The formalization states the bound with the gradient of the expectation, so that no unbiasedness is assumed and a bias enters only through its gradient.

title: Minimum Risk Equivariant Location Estimator
informal: Let $X = (X_1,\dots,X_n)$ have joint density $f(x_1-\xi,\dots,x_n-\xi)$, where $\xi \in \mathbb{R}$ is an unknown location parameter, and let the loss be of the form $L(\xi,d) = \rho(d-\xi)$. An estimator $\delta$ is location equivariant when $$\delta(x_1+a,\dots,x_n+a) = \delta(x_1,\dots,x_n) + a \qquad \text{for every } a \in \mathbb{R}.$$ The risk of a location-equivariant estimator does not depend on $\xi$, so it equals its value at $\xi = 0$, namely $R(\delta) = \mathbb{E}_0[\rho(\delta(X))]$. The estimator $\delta$ is minimum risk equivariant when it is measurable, location equivariant, and satisfies $R(\delta) \le R(\delta')$ for every measurable location-equivariant $\delta'$.
summary: An estimator of a location parameter is minimum risk equivariant when it is measurable, location equivariant, and has the smallest risk in that class.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Equivariant (“invariant”) estimation of a location parameter, and the reduction of the risk of an equivariant estimator to a single number, are due to Pitman (1939). The general group-theoretic formulation was developed by Hunt and Stein (1946, unpublished) and first reported in print by Girshick and Savage (1951). The formalization fixes the concrete additive translation group on $\mathbb{R}^n$, defines the risk at the base parameter $\xi = 0$, and bundles measurability, equivariance and minimality into one predicate.

formalizationNotes: Risk is a lower Lebesgue integral of the nonnegative part of the loss, so the definition needs no integrability side condition: a divergent risk simply records $+\infty$. Measurability of the estimator is an explicit clause of the predicate, whereas the book leaves it implicit.

title: The Pitman Estimator of Location
informal: For a location family with joint density $f(x_1-\xi,\dots,x_n-\xi)$, the Pitman estimator is $$\delta^*(x) \;=\; \frac{\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} u\, f(x_1-u,\dots,x_n-u)\,du}{\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x_1-u,\dots,x_n-u)\,du}.$$ Equivalently, it is the mean of the posterior distribution of $\xi$ obtained from the improper uniform prior on the line. It is the minimum risk equivariant estimator of $\xi$ under squared error.
summary: The Pitman estimator is the ratio of the first moment to the mass of the density slice through the sample point along the diagonal direction.
leanSignature:

  (∫ u : ℝ, u * f (x - u • (1 : Fin n → ℝ))) / (∫ u : ℝ, f (x - u • (1 : Fin n → ℝ)))

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The estimator and its derivation by conditioning on the differences are due to Pitman (1939). Stein (1959) proved that it is admissible for a single location parameter under squared error. The formalization takes the closed-form ratio as the definition and proves separately that it is equivariant and that it coincides with the conditional-mean form $x_n - \mathbb{E}_0[X_n \mid Y]$.

formalizationNotes: Being a quotient of two Bochner integrals, the definition returns the junk value $0$ wherever the denominator vanishes or either integral fails to converge; every theorem about it carries explicit convergence and non-vanishing hypotheses.

title: Invariance of the Risk Function under the Induced Group
informal: Let a group $G$ act on the sample space, on the parameter space and on the space of decisions. Assume the model is invariant: transporting the data by $g$ turns the law $P_\theta$ into $P_{g\theta}$, and the loss is invariant under the simultaneous action, $L(g\theta, g d) = L(\theta, d)$. Then for any equivariant estimator, that is one satisfying $\delta(g x) = g\,\delta(x)$, $$R(g\theta, \delta) \;=\; R(\theta, \delta) \qquad \text{for every } g \in G \text{ and every } \theta.$$ The argument is a change of variables, for which the estimator and each loss slice $d \mapsto L(\theta,d)$ are required to be measurable. This is the structural reason the equivariance principle turns a risk function into a risk number: when the induced action is transitive the risk is a constant, and it is constant on each orbit in general.
summary: In an invariant estimation problem the risk of an equivariant estimator is unchanged when the parameter is moved by the induced group action.

theorem risk_smul {P : Θ → Measure 𝓧} {L : Θ → D → ℝ≥0∞} {δ : 𝓧 → D}
    (hP : IsInvariantModel (G := G) P)
    (hL : IsInvariantLoss (G := G) L)
    (hLmeas : ∀ θ, Measurable (L θ))
    (hδ : Measurable δ)
    (hδeq : IsEquivariant (G := G) δ)
    (g : G) (θ : Θ) :
    risk P L δ (g • θ) = risk P L δ θ

hypotheses.note: The push-forward of $P_\theta$ under the action of $g$ on the sample space is $P_{g\theta}$.

hypotheses.label: invariant loss
hypotheses.note: The loss is unchanged when the parameter and the decision are moved by the same group element.

hypotheses.label: equivariant estimator
hypotheses.note: The estimator intertwines the actions on the sample space and on the decision space.

hypotheses.label: measurable estimator
hypotheses.note: Needed only to run the change of variables under the push-forward measure.

hypotheses.label: measurable loss slices
hypotheses.note: Each map $d \mapsto L(\theta,d)$ is measurable; the classical statement leaves this implicit.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The group-theoretic (“invariance”) reduction of a decision problem originates with Hunt and Stein (1946, unpublished manuscript), whose argument first reached print through Girshick and Savage (1951); the location and scale cases go back to Pitman (1939). The formalization states the invariance of the risk function itself, from which the book's constant-risk corollaries follow by transitivity or by restriction to an orbit; the only additions to the book's hypotheses are the two measurability clauses that make the change of variables meaningful.

formalizationNotes: The group is only required to act by measurable maps on the sample space (a constant-scalar-multiplication measurability class), not to carry a measurable structure itself, since nothing here integrates over the group. Transitivity of the induced action is Mathlib's pretransitivity and orbits are Mathlib orbits; the two classical corollaries — constant risk under transitivity, constant risk on orbits — are separate declarations in the same file.

title: Equivariance Implies Constant Risk (Location Case)
informal: Let the observations have joint density $f(x_1-\xi,\dots,x_n-\xi)$ and let the loss be $\rho(d-\xi)$. If the estimator is location equivariant, $\delta(x_1+a,\dots,x_n+a) = \delta(x)+a$ for every real $a$, then its risk is free of the parameter: $$\mathbb{E}_\xi\big[\rho(\delta(X)-\xi)\big] \;=\; \mathbb{E}_0\big[\rho(\delta(X))\big] \qquad \text{for every } \xi \in \mathbb{R}.$$ Uniform minimization of the risk over the equivariant class is therefore the minimization of a single number, which is what makes a minimum risk equivariant estimator a sensible target. The proof is the substitution $x \mapsto x + a\mathbf{1}$, so it needs only that the loss and the estimator be measurable.
summary: The risk of a location-equivariant estimator is the same at every value of the location parameter, hence equals its value at the origin.

    (hδ : Measurable δ)
    (hδeq : IsLocEquivariant δ)
    (ξ : ℝ) :
    ∫⁻ x, ENNReal.ofReal (ρ (δ x - ξ)) ∂(locationFamily f ξ) = locRisk f ρ δ

hypotheses.label: location equivariance
hypotheses.note: A common shift of all coordinates shifts the estimate by the same amount.

hypotheses.label: measurable loss
hypotheses.note: Required for the change-of-variables step, not by the classical argument.

hypotheses.label: measurable estimator
hypotheses.note: Same role; no statistical content is added.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The reduction of equivariant location estimation to a constant-risk problem is due to Pitman (1939); the general group version is Hunt and Stein (1946, unpublished), reported by Girshick and Savage (1951). The formalization proves the identity as a pure change of variables under the push-forward that defines the location family, so the density enters nowhere.

formalizationNotes: The book states the constancy for the bias, the risk and the variance of an equivariant estimator and assumes a density throughout; the formalization proves the risk clause only (the other two follow by the identical substitution and are not used downstream) and needs no regularity of the density beyond what the location family already encodes, so the hypotheses are weaker than the book's.

title: Structure of the Location-Equivariant Class
informal: Fix a reference location-equivariant estimator $\delta_0$, and for $n = m+1$ observations write $$y \;=\; (x_1 - x_n,\; \dots,\; x_{n-1} - x_n)$$ for the vector of differences, the maximal invariant of the group of common translations. Then an estimator $\delta$ is location equivariant if and only if $$\delta(x) \;=\; \delta_0(x) - v(y)$$ for some function $v$ of the differences alone. Consequently, selecting an equivariant estimator amounts to selecting one real number $v(y)$ for each value of the maximal invariant — the step that turns “minimize the risk over the equivariant class” into a fibrewise minimization. For a single observation the difference vector is empty and the statement reads: the equivariant estimators are exactly $\delta_0$ minus a constant.
summary: Relative to any fixed equivariant estimator, the location-equivariant estimators are exactly those obtained by subtracting a function of the differences of the observations.
leanSignature:
theorem isLocEquivariant_iff_exists_diffs_rep {δ₀ : (Fin (m + 1) → ℝ) → ℝ}
    (h₀ : IsLocEquivariant δ₀)
    (δ : (Fin (m + 1) → ℝ) → ℝ) :
    IsLocEquivariant δ ↔ ∃ v : (Fin m → ℝ) → ℝ, ∀ x, δ x = δ₀ x - v (diffs x)

hypotheses.label: reference equivariant estimator
hypotheses.note: Any fixed measurable location-equivariant estimator; the caller's free choice.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The description of the location-equivariant class through the differences as maximal invariant is due to Pitman (1939); the general group formulation is Hunt and Stein (1946, unpublished), reported by Girshick and Savage (1951). The formalization proves the equivalence for arbitrary functions and, separately, a measurable version obtained from a measurable section of the difference map, which is what the conditional-minimization argument consumes.

formalizationNotes: The book splits the statement into the cases $n \ge 2$ (a function of the differences) and $n = 1$ (a constant); indexing the differences by $m$ with $n = m+1$ makes the empty difference vector a one-point space, so a single statement covers both with no case analysis. A measurable refinement, in which measurable equivariant estimators correspond to measurable functions of the differences, is proved alongside it using the explicit section that appends a zero last coordinate.

title: The MRE Location Estimator by Conditional Minimization
informal: Let the observations have joint density $f(x_1-\xi,\dots,x_n-\xi)$ with $n = m+1$, let the loss be $\rho(d-\xi)$, and let $Y = (X_1-X_n,\dots,X_{n-1}-X_n)$ be the vector of differences. Let $\delta_0$ be a location-equivariant estimator with finite risk. Suppose $v^*$ is a measurable function of the differences which minimizes, for almost every value $y$ of $Y$, the conditional expected loss $\mathbb{E}_0\big[\rho(\delta_0(X) - v)\,\big|\, Y = y\big]$ over all real numbers $v$. Then $$\delta^*(x) \;=\; \delta_0(x) - v^*(y)$$ is a minimum risk equivariant estimator of $\xi$. The two ingredients are the representation of the equivariant class as $\delta_0$ minus a function of the differences, and the fact that an integral is minimized by minimizing its integrand inside each fibre of the maximal invariant.
summary: If a function of the differences minimizes the conditional expected loss in almost every fibre, subtracting it from a reference equivariant estimator produces a minimum risk equivariant estimator.

    (ρ : ℝ → ℝ)

    {δ₀ : (Fin (m + 1) → ℝ) → ℝ}

    (heq₀ : IsLocEquivariant δ₀)
    (hfin : locRisk f ρ δ₀ ≠ ∞)
    {vStar : (Fin m → ℝ) → ℝ}
    (hvStar : Measurable vStar)
    (hmin : ∀ᵐ y ∂((locationBase f).map diffs), ∀ w : ℝ,
      ∫⁻ x, ENNReal.ofReal (ρ (δ₀ x - vStar y))
          ∂(orbitCondKernel (locationBase f) diffs y) ≤
        ∫⁻ x, ENNReal.ofReal (ρ (δ₀ x - w))
          ∂(orbitCondKernel (locationBase f) diffs y)) :
    IsLocMRE f ρ (fun x => δ₀ x - vStar (diffs x))

hypotheses.note: A fixed location-equivariant estimator against which the class is parametrized.

hypotheses.label: finite reference risk
hypotheses.note: Its risk is finite, so the fibrewise minimization is meaningful.

hypotheses.label: measurable minimizer
hypotheses.note: The fibrewise minimizer must be measurable for the resulting estimator to be one.

hypotheses.label: fibrewise minimality
hypotheses.note: In almost every fibre of the differences, no constant beats $v^*(y)$ in conditional expected loss.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The reduction of best equivariant location estimation to a minimization of the conditional expected loss given the differences is due to Pitman (1939); admissibility of the resulting estimator for a single location parameter was established by Stein (1959). The formalization routes the reduction through a general disintegration engine — a conditional distribution of the data given the maximal invariant — which is instantiated identically in the scale case.

(i) The book asks for a minimizer in every fibre; the proof only ever uses one on a set of full measure, so the hypothesis is stated almost everywhere, which strengthens the theorem. (ii) Measurability of the fibrewise minimizer has no classical counterpart but is genuinely needed, since without it the resulting object is not an estimator; for convex non-monotone losses a measurable selection is produced separately, giving an unconditional existence theorem.

title: The Pitman Estimator Is Minimum Risk Equivariant
informal: Let $X$ have joint density $f(x_1-\xi,\dots,x_n-\xi)$ with $n = m+1$, where $f$ is a nonnegative probability density, and let the loss be squared error $\rho(t) = t^2$. Assume that at every sample point the first-moment integral $\int u\,f(x_1-u,\dots,x_n-u)\,du$ converges, the normalizing integral $\int f(x_1-u,\dots,x_n-u)\,du$ converges and does not vanish, and that the last coordinate $X_n$ — itself an equivariant estimator — has finite squared-error risk. Then the Pitman estimator $$\delta^*(x) \;=\; \frac{\int u\,f(x_1-u,\dots,x_n-u)\,du}{\int f(x_1-u,\dots,x_n-u)\,du}$$ is the minimum risk equivariant estimator of $\xi$. Equivalently, $\delta^*(X) = X_n - \mathbb{E}_0[X_n \mid Y]$, where $Y$ is the vector of differences.
summary: Under squared error the Pitman ratio of integrals is the minimum risk equivariant estimator of a location parameter.

reference.biblio: Both the estimator and the derivation are due to Pitman (1939); Stein (1959) proved its admissibility for a single location parameter. The formalization proves the closed form directly minimum risk equivariant, going through the conditional-minimization engine with the last coordinate as reference estimator, and thereby avoids any every-fibre integrability hypothesis on that reference.

formalizationNotes: The convergence and non-vanishing conditions are implicit in the classical development and explicit here, because dividing Bochner integrals otherwise silently returns zero. Measurability of the closed form is not assumed but derived from measurability of the density. The identification of the ratio with $X_n - \mathbb{E}_0[X_n \mid Y]$ is stated almost everywhere rather than pointwise, since a conditional distribution is only determined up to a null set; the unit-Jacobian shear $(x_1-x_n,\dots,x_{n-1}-x_n,\,x_n)$ carries the change of variables.

title: Minimum Risk Equivariant Estimators Are Risk-Unbiased
informal: An estimator is risk-unbiased when, on the average, it is at least as close to the true parameter value as to any other one: $$\mathbb{E}_\theta\, L(\theta, \delta(X)) \;\le\; \mathbb{E}_\theta\, L(\theta', \delta(X)) \qquad \text{for all } \theta, \theta'.$$ This is the decision-theoretic extension of unbiasedness: under squared error it reduces to ordinary unbiasedness, under absolute error to median-unbiasedness. Suppose a group $G$ acts transitively on the parameter space through the induced action, the loss is invariant under the simultaneous action on parameters and decisions, the induced action on the decision space is commutative, and $\delta$ is an equivariant estimator, measurable, which minimizes the risk among all measurable equivariant estimators. Then $\delta$ is risk-unbiased. Transitivity supplies a group element carrying the competing value onto the true one; invariance of the loss converts the cross risk into the risk of the transported estimator, which commutativity keeps equivariant.
summary: Under a transitive parameter action and a commutative decision action, an equivariant estimator of minimal risk is risk-unbiased.

    (hδeq : IsEquivariant (G := G) δ)

    (hmin : ∀ δ', Measurable δ' → IsEquivariant (G := G) δ' →

hypotheses.note: The loss is unchanged when parameter and decision are moved by the same group element.

hypotheses.label: commutative decision action
hypotheses.note: Any two group elements act on decisions in either order with the same effect.

hypotheses.label: equivariant estimator
hypotheses.note: The estimator intertwines the sample-space and decision-space actions.

hypotheses.label: measurable estimator
hypotheses.note: Needed so that the transported estimator qualifies as a competitor in the minimality clause.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Risk-unbiasedness as the decision-theoretic generalization of unbiasedness is due to Lehmann (1951). The equivariance framework in which it is proved here originates with Hunt and Stein (1946, unpublished), first reported by Girshick and Savage (1951), with the location case going back to Pitman (1939). The formalization also records the location specialization, where the proof is a one-line application of minimality to the translate $\delta - a$, and the squared-error refinement that a finite-risk minimum risk equivariant estimator is unbiased.

formalizationNotes: The formalization is sharper than the book in two ways. First, the invariant-model hypothesis is omitted: it is what makes minimality the right notion of “minimum risk equivariant” in the first place, but it is never used in the implication. Second, minimality is taken as an explicit hypothesis rather than through a bundled predicate, because in the general setting there is no canonical constant risk to minimize until transitivity has been used. In the location specialization both extra conditions hold automatically and no convexity, symmetry or boundedness of the loss is needed.

title: The Sample Mean Is MRE in the Normal Location Family
informal: Suppose the base member of the location family is an independent sample of $n$ normal observations with mean $0$ and common variance $\sigma^2$, where the variance is known and nonzero; that is, the model is $X_1,\dots,X_n$ independent and $N(\xi,\sigma^2)$-distributed with $\xi$ unknown. Then, under squared error, the sample mean $$\bar X \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i$$ is the minimum risk equivariant estimator of $\xi$. The proof identifies the Pitman estimator of the product normal density with $\bar X$ by completing the square: the slice $u \mapsto \prod_i \varphi_{\sigma^2}(x_i - u)$ is a constant multiple of the $N(\bar x, \sigma^2/n)$ density, whose mean is $\bar x$.

The formalization proves the positive statement by explicitly computing the Pitman ratio for the product normal density.

formalizationNotes: The sampling structure is supplied as an identity between the base member of the family and the product of normal laws, rather than by writing out a joint density: only the law is ever used, and this keeps the product structure available as a rewrite. The converse — that for $n \ge 3$ the normal is the only unit-variance sampling law for which the minimum risk equivariant risk attains $1/n$ — is a characterization result of Kagan, Linnik and Rao that the book quotes but does not prove, and it is deliberately not formalized.

title: Power Series Families Admit No Nontrivial Invariance
informal: Consider the power series family on $\{0,1,2,\dots\}$, $$P_\theta\{X = k\} \;=\; \frac{c_k\,\theta^k}{\sum_{j\ge 0} c_j\,\theta^j}, \qquad k = 0,1,2,\dots,$$ and assume every coefficient $c_k$ is strictly positive and the series converges for every $\theta$ in an interval $(0,R)$. If a bijection $g$ of the sample space leaves the family invariant — that is, for each $\theta$ in the interval the law of $g(X)$ under $P_\theta$ is $P_{\theta'}$ for some $\theta'$ in the same interval, then $g$ is the identity. The invariance group is therefore trivial and the equivariance principle has no content for such a family. Strict positivity of the coefficients is essential rather than cosmetic: the binomial family, whose coefficients vanish beyond $n$, is invariant under $k \mapsto n-k$, with induced parameter map $p \mapsto 1-p$.
summary: A power series family with all coefficients strictly positive is left invariant only by the identity transformation of the sample space, so the equivariance principle is vacuous for it.

theorem powerSeriesFamily_invariant_perm_eq_one {a : ℕ → ℝ≥0∞}
    (ha₀ : ∀ k, a k ≠ 0)
    (ha : ∀ k, a k ≠ ∞)
    {R : ℝ}
    (hR : 0 < R)
    (hconv : ∀ θ ∈ Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ) R, (∑' j, a j * (ENNReal.ofReal θ) ^ j) ≠ ∞)
    (g : Equiv.Perm ℕ)
    (hg : ∀ θ ∈ Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ) R, ∃ θ' ∈ Set.Ioo (0 : ℝ) R,
      (powerSeriesFamily a θ).map (g : ℕ → ℕ) = powerSeriesFamily a θ') :
    g = 1

hypotheses.label: strictly positive coefficients
hypotheses.note: Every coefficient is nonzero, so the family has full support on the nonnegative integers.

hypotheses.label: convergence on an interval
hypotheses.note: The normalizing series is finite throughout an interval of parameter values.

hypotheses.label: invariance-preserving bijection
hypotheses.note: The transformation maps each member of the family to another member.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The framework in which “the model admits no nontrivial symmetry” is the relevant negative statement is due to Hunt and Stein (1946, unpublished), first reported by Girshick and Savage (1951). The formalization proves the full classical conclusion — the transformation is the identity, not merely that two points cannot be interchanged — by matching point masses, taking logarithms, and using that a linear relation in $\log\theta$ holding on an interval forces the coefficient to vanish.

formalizationNotes: The exponent-matching step needs the parameter to range over an interval, so the parameter set is the interval $(0,R)$ on which the series converges rather than the informal “all $\theta > 0$”. Increments of the transformation are recorded as integers, since natural subtraction would truncate before their sign is known. A finiteness hypothesis on the coefficients is carried so that the densities are genuine real numbers. The intermediate structural step — an invariance-preserving bijection has constant successive increments, hence is affine — is available as a separate declaration, as is the packaging “the set of invariance-preserving permutations is a singleton”.

title: Structure of the Scale-Equivariant Class
informal: In the scale model the data have joint density $\tau^{-n} f(x/\tau)$, the estimand is $\tau^{r}$, and an estimator is scale equivariant of degree $r$ when $\delta(bx) = b^{r}\delta(x)$ for every $b > 0$. Fix a reference scale-equivariant estimator $\delta_0$ of degree $r$ which is nowhere zero, and let $$z \;=\; \Big(\frac{x_1}{x_n},\dots,\frac{x_{n-1}}{x_n},\ \operatorname{sgn} x_n\Big)$$ be the maximal invariant of the multiplicative group. Then, on the set where $x_n \ne 0$, an estimator $\delta$ is scale equivariant of degree $r$ if and only if $$\delta(x) \;=\; \frac{\delta_0(x)}{w(z)}$$ for some function $w$ of the maximal invariant. This is the multiplicative analogue of the additive decomposition of the location-equivariant class, with division replacing subtraction and the coordinate ratios replacing the differences.
summary: Relative to a nowhere-vanishing reference estimator, the scale-equivariant estimators are exactly those obtained by dividing it by a function of the coordinate ratios.
leanSignature:
theorem isScaleEquivariant_iff_div_scaleZ {r : ℕ} {δ₀ : (Fin (m + 1) → ℝ) → ℝ}
    (h₀ : IsScaleEquivariant r δ₀)
    (h₀ne : ∀ x, δ₀ x ≠ 0)
    (δ : (Fin (m + 1) → ℝ) → ℝ) :
    (∀ ⦃b : ℝ⦄, 0 < b → ∀ x, x (Fin.last m) ≠ 0 → δ (b • x) = b ^ r * δ x) ↔
      ∃ w : (Fin m → ℝ) × ℝ → ℝ,
        ∀ x, x (Fin.last m) ≠ 0 → δ x = δ₀ x / w (scaleZ x)

hypotheses.note: A fixed scale-equivariant estimator of the same degree; the caller's free choice.

hypotheses.label: nowhere vanishing
hypotheses.note: The classical argument divides by the reference estimator without comment; here the non-vanishing is explicit, and it is harmless because the estimand is positive.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Equivariant estimation of scale and location-scale parameters is due to Pitman (1939); the general group-theoretic formulation is Hunt and Stein (1946, unpublished), first reported by Girshick and Savage (1951). The formalization proves the abstract equivalence and a measurable refinement built from an explicit measurable section of the ratio map, which is what the fibrewise minimization consumes.

formalizationNotes: The maximal invariant is only meaningful off the null set where the last coordinate vanishes, which the book records in a parenthesis; here both sides of the equivalence are explicitly restricted to that set. The restriction on both sides is needed because the factorization imposes no constraint at all on the null set, so were only the right-hand side restricted an estimator agreeing with the representation off that set could still violate equivariance on it. The maximal invariant records the coordinate ratios together with the sign of the last coordinate, which is the full maximal invariant of the positive scale group.

title: The MRE Scale Estimator by Conditional Minimization
informal: Let the data have joint density $\tau^{-n} f(x/\tau)$, the estimand be $\tau^{r}$ and the loss be $\gamma(d/\tau^{r})$, and let $z$ be the maximal invariant consisting of the coordinate ratios and the sign of the last coordinate. Let $\delta_0$ be a scale-equivariant estimator of degree $r$ which is nowhere zero, and assume the last coordinate vanishes with probability zero, so that the maximal invariant is defined almost surely. If a measurable positive function $w^*$ of the maximal invariant minimizes, in almost every fibre, the conditional expected loss $\mathbb{E}_1\big[\gamma\big(\delta_0(X)/w\big)\,\big|\,z\big]$ over all real $w$, then $$\delta^*(x) \;=\; \frac{\delta_0(x)}{w^*(z)}$$ is minimum risk equivariant for $\tau^{r}$. This is the exact multiplicative counterpart of the location construction, obtained from the same disintegration engine with the template $\delta_0(x)/w$ in place of $\delta_0(x) - w$.
summary: A fibrewise minimizer of the conditional expected loss given the coordinate ratios turns a reference scale-equivariant estimator into a minimum risk equivariant one.
