hypotheses.label: reference scale-equivariant estimator
hypotheses.note: A fixed scale-equivariant estimator of degree $r$ with finite risk.

hypotheses.label: nowhere vanishing
hypotheses.note: Needed for the representation of the equivariant class as $\delta_0$ divided by an invariant function.

hypotheses.label: maximal invariant defined a.s.
hypotheses.note: The set where the last coordinate vanishes is null, so the ratios are well defined almost surely.

hypotheses.label: fibrewise minimality
hypotheses.note: In almost every fibre no constant divisor beats $w^*(z)$ in conditional expected loss.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Equivariant estimation of a scale parameter is due to Pitman (1939), with the general group formulation of Hunt and Stein (1946, unpublished) reported by Girshick and Savage (1951); the entropy (Stein) loss used in the accompanying explicit corollaries was introduced by James and Stein (1961). The formalization shares a single conditional-risk engine with the location theory, so the scale construction differs from the location one only in the template family.

formalizationNotes: Three honest deviations. (i) As in the location case, fibrewise minimality is assumed almost everywhere rather than in every fibre, and measurability of the minimizer is a genuine requirement with no classical counterpart. (ii) The minimality hypothesis quantifies over all real divisors $w$, including $w = 0$ and negative values. The full range is needed because the equivariant class contains opposite-signed competitors and, through the convention that division by zero returns zero, the identically zero estimator; a hypothesis restricted to positive or merely nonzero $w$ would therefore not dominate every equivariant competitor. (iii) The null-set hypothesis is used only for the minimality half; equivariance of the constructed estimator holds without restriction.

title: Least Squares as an Orthogonal Projection
informal: In the linear model the observation $Y$ has mean vector $\xi$ constrained to a linear subspace $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$. The least-squares estimator of $\xi$ is the orthogonal projection of the observation onto that subspace, $$\hat\xi(y) \;=\; P_W\,y \;=\; \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\zeta \in W} \|y - \zeta\|^2 ,$$ and the associated residual sum of squares is $S^2 = \|y - \hat\xi(y)\|^2$. Because the projection is self-adjoint, every least-squares functional is a linear statistic: $\langle \gamma, \hat\xi(y)\rangle = \langle P_W\gamma,\, y\rangle$.
summary: The least-squares estimator of the mean vector of a linear model is the orthogonal projection of the observation onto the mean subspace.
leanSignature:
noncomputable def lse (W : Submodule ℝ (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)))
    [W.HasOrthogonalProjection] (y : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)) :
    EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n) :=
  W.starProjection y

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.pointer: Chapter 3, §3.4 (canonical and subspace forms of the normal linear model)
reference.biblio: Least squares and the optimality of its linear functionals are due to Gauss (1821/1823) and Markov (1912); the coordinate-free treatment used here, in which the estimator is literally the orthogonal projection onto the mean subspace, follows Kruskal (1965) and Scheffé (1959). The formalization takes the projection as the definition and derives the classical normal equations as identities of inner products.

formalizationNotes: The observation space is Euclidean space so that projection geometry and measure theory coexist; the product normal law lives naturally on the coordinate space and is transported to the Euclidean space along a measurable linear isometry. Finite-dimensional subspaces automatically carry the orthogonal-projection instance, so the definition is total and needs no side condition.

title: UMVU Estimation of Linear Functionals in the Canonical Model
informal: In the canonical normal linear model the observations $Y_1,\dots,Y_{s+m}$ are independent with common unknown variance $\sigma^2$: the first $s$ have free means $\eta_1,\dots,\eta_s$ and the remaining $m$ have mean zero. If there is at least one residual coordinate, that is $s < n$, then for known coefficients $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_s$ the statistic $$\sum_{i=1}^{s} \lambda_i\,Y_i$$ is the uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator of $\sum_{i=1}^{s} \lambda_i\,\eta_i$. In particular each $Y_i$ is UMVU for $\eta_i$. The proof is the Lehmann–Scheffé route: the pair consisting of the signal block and the residual sum of squares is complete and sufficient for $(\eta,\sigma^2)$, and the estimator is a function of it.
summary: In the canonical normal linear model every linear combination of the signal coordinates is the UMVU estimator of the corresponding linear combination of the means.
leanSignature:
theorem isUMVU_linear_combination
    (hm : 0 < m)
    (lam : Fin s → ℝ) :
    IsUMVU (canonicalModel (s := s) (m := m)) (fun p => ∑ i, lam i * p.1 i)
      (fun y => ∑ i, lam i * canonicalHead y i)

hypotheses.label: at least one residual coordinate
hypotheses.note: The standing dimension condition of the model: the mean subspace is proper, so the variance is estimable.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The canonical reduction of the normal linear model by an orthogonal transformation goes back to Gauss (1821/1823) and Markov (1912), with the modern treatment in Scheffé (1959) and Rao (1973); the minimum-variance property rests on the completeness theory of Lehmann and Scheffé (1950). The formalization proves completeness and sufficiency of the canonical statistic and derives the optimality of each linear combination from them.

formalizationNotes: The observation dimension is written as $s + m$ rather than through an inequality $s \le n$, so “the first $s$” and “the last $m$” coordinates carry no arithmetic side conditions and the standing assumption $s < n$ becomes positivity of $m$. The variance is restricted to be strictly positive, the degenerate member being outside the classical statements. Completeness goes through the full-rank exponential-family theorem with natural statistic the signal block together with the residual sum of squares.

title: Optimality of the Least-Squares Functional
informal: Let the observation be normal with mean vector $\xi$ ranging over a subspace $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and unknown common variance $\sigma^2 > 0$, and let $\hat\xi(y) = P_W y$ be the least-squares estimator. If the mean subspace is proper, $\dim W < n$, then for a known coefficient vector $\gamma$ lying in the mean subspace the statistic $$y \;\longmapsto\; \langle \gamma,\ \hat\xi(y)\rangle$$ is the uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator of $\xi \mapsto \langle\gamma,\xi\rangle$. Since $\langle\gamma,\xi\rangle = \langle P_W\gamma,\xi\rangle$ for $\xi \in W$, restricting the coefficient vector to the subspace is no restriction: a general one is replaced by its projection without changing either the estimand or the estimator.
summary: With the mean vector confined to a subspace and the variance unknown, the least-squares functional is the UMVU estimator of the corresponding linear functional of the mean.
leanSignature:
theorem isUMVU_lse_functional (W : Submodule ℝ (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)))
    [W.HasOrthogonalProjection]
    (hW : Module.finrank ℝ W < n)

hypotheses.label: proper mean subspace
hypotheses.note: The dimension of the mean subspace is strictly less than the number of observations, so the variance is estimable.

hypotheses.label: coefficient vector in the subspace
hypotheses.note: A normalization, not a restriction: a general coefficient vector is replaced by its orthogonal projection.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Least squares and the optimality of its linear functionals are due to Gauss (1821/1823) and Markov (1912); the coordinate-free formulation follows Kruskal (1965), Scheffé (1959) and Rao (1973), while the minimum-variance property in the normal model rests on Lehmann and Scheffé (1950). The formalization proves Gaussian isometry invariance from scratch and uses it to pull the canonical-model optimality back to the original coordinates.

title: Optimality of the Residual Variance Estimator
informal: Let the observation be normal with mean vector confined to a subspace $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and unknown common variance $\sigma^2 > 0$. If the mean subspace is proper, $\dim W < n$, then $$\frac{\|y - \hat\xi(y)\|^2}{n - \dim W}$$ is the uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator of $\sigma^2$, where $\hat\xi(y) = P_W y$ is the least-squares estimator of the mean vector. The numerator is the residual sum of squares and the denominator is the number of residual degrees of freedom.
summary: The residual sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom is the UMVU estimator of the variance in the normal linear model.

hypotheses.note: Without it there are no residual degrees of freedom and the variance is not estimable.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The optimality of the residual variance estimator in the normal linear model is classical, going back to Gauss (1821/1823) and Markov (1912) for least squares and to Lehmann and Scheffé (1950) for the completeness argument that upgrades unbiasedness to minimum variance; see Scheffé (1959) and Rao (1973). The formalization derives it from completeness of the pair consisting of the signal block and the residual sum of squares in the canonical model.

The result is obtained by transporting the canonical-model statement — the residual sum of squares divided by the number of residual coordinates — along the adapted-basis rotation, using that the rotation carries the residual sum of squares to itself.

title: Least Squares Is Minimum Risk Equivariant
informal: Consider the normal linear model with mean vector in a subspace $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and known variance, and the group of translations $y \mapsto y + b$ with $b \in W$, under which the estimand $\langle\gamma,\xi\rangle$ shifts by $\langle\gamma,b\rangle$. An estimator is equivariant for this group when $\delta(y+b) = \delta(y) + \langle\gamma,b\rangle$ for every $b \in W$. Assume the mean subspace is proper, $\dim W < n$, the coefficient vector lies in the mean subspace, and the loss $\rho(d - \langle\gamma,\xi\rangle)$ is convex and even. Then the least-squares functional $$y \;\longmapsto\; \langle \gamma,\ P_W\,y\rangle$$ is minimum risk equivariant: its (constant) risk is smallest among all measurable equivariant estimators. The argument is the reflection symmetry of the centred normal law together with midpoint convexity of the loss.
summary: Under translations by the mean subspace, the least-squares functional is minimum risk equivariant for every convex even loss.

hypotheses.note: A normalization: a general coefficient vector is replaced by its projection.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Equivariant estimation of location parameters is due to Pitman (1939); its use in the linear model follows Scheffé (1959) and Rao (1973), with the coordinate-free viewpoint of Kruskal (1965). Because the risk of an equivariant estimator is constant in the parameter, minimality is stated at the single base parameter $\xi = 0$, and the loss enters the risk through its nonnegative part so that no integrability hypothesis is needed.

title: MRE Estimation of the Variance in the Linear Model
informal: In the canonical normal linear model with $m = n - s$ residual coordinates, consider the group generated by the translations of the signal block together with the scale changes $y \mapsto c\,y$ for $c > 0$, under which $\sigma^2 \mapsto c^2\sigma^2$, and the standardized squared-error loss $$L(\sigma^2, d) \;=\; \frac{(d - \sigma^2)^2}{\sigma^4}.$$ If there is at least one residual coordinate, then the minimum risk equivariant estimator of $\sigma^2$ is $$\frac{S^2}{n - s + 2},$$ where $S^2$ is the residual sum of squares. The denominator is larger than the $n-s$ of the unbiased estimator: the optimal multiplier is the ratio $\mathbb{E}[V]/\mathbb{E}[V^2]$ of chi-square moments with $n-s$ degrees of freedom, and $\mathbb{E}[V] = m$, $\mathbb{E}[V^2] = m(m+2)$.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: Equivariant estimation of a scale parameter is due to Pitman (1939); its use in the linear model follows Scheffé (1959) and Rao (1973). The distribution of the residual sum of squares goes back to Helmert (1876). The formalization computes the chi-square moments from a Gamma-moment brick, so the classical constant $1/(n-s+2)$ is derived rather than assumed.

The general power case, in which the minimum risk equivariant estimator of $(\sigma^2)^r$ is the chi-square moment ratio times $(S^2)^r$, is proved first and this is its case $r = 1$, with the moment ratio evaluated explicitly.

title: The Gauss–Markov Theorem
informal: Drop both normality and independence and retain only the first two moments: the mean vector lies in the subspace $W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, and the coordinates of the observation are uncorrelated with common variance $\sigma^2$ and square-integrable. Let $\gamma$ be a known coefficient vector, and let $y \mapsto \langle c, y\rangle$ be a competing linear estimator which is unbiased throughout the mean subspace, that is $\langle c,\zeta\rangle = \langle \gamma,\zeta\rangle$ for every $\zeta \in W$. Then $$\operatorname{Var}\big(\langle \gamma,\ P_W\,Y\rangle\big) \;\le\; \operatorname{Var}\big(\langle c,\ Y\rangle\big).$$ The least-squares functional therefore has the smallest variance among all linear estimators unbiased on the mean subspace. Geometrically, unbiasedness forces $P_W c = P_W\gamma$, so $\|c\|^2 = \|P_W\gamma\|^2 + \|c - P_W c\|^2$, and both variances are $\sigma^2$ times the respective squared norms.
summary: Among linear estimators unbiased throughout the mean subspace, the least-squares functional has the smallest variance, assuming only uncorrelated coordinates with a common variance.

reference.biblio: The theorem is due to Gauss (1821/1823), with the formulation for linear unbiased estimators associated with Markov (1912); see Kruskal (1965) for the coordinate-free treatment and Scheffé (1959) and Rao (1973) for the standard developments. title: Uniqueness of the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator
informal: Assume the observation is nondegenerate, $\sigma^2 > 0$, its coordinates are uncorrelated with common variance $\sigma^2$ and square-integrable, and let $y \mapsto \langle c, y\rangle$ be a linear estimator that is unbiased throughout the mean subspace and whose variance attains the least-squares minimum. Then its coefficient vector is forced: $$c \;=\; P_W\,\gamma,$$ so the estimator is the least-squares functional $y \mapsto \langle\gamma, P_W y\rangle$. The best linear unbiased estimator of $\langle\gamma,\xi\rangle$ is therefore unique. Nondegeneracy is needed: with $\sigma^2 = 0$ every coefficient vector ties.
summary: A linear estimator unbiased on the mean subspace and of minimal variance must be the least-squares functional.
leanSignature:
theorem blue_lse {W : Submodule ℝ (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n))}
    [W.HasOrthogonalProjection] {σ2 : ℝ} {γ c : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)}
    {P : Measure (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n))} [IsProbabilityMeasure P]
    (hσ2 : 0 < σ2)
    (hcov : ∀ i j, covariance (fun y => y i) (fun y => y j) P = if i = j then σ2 else 0)
    (hL2 : ∀ i, MemLp (fun y => y i) 2 P)
    (hc : ∀ ζ ∈ W, ⟪c, ζ⟫_ℝ = ⟪γ, ζ⟫_ℝ)
    (hbest : variance (fun y => ⟪c, y⟫_ℝ) P ≤ variance (fun y => ⟪γ, lse W y⟫_ℝ) P) :
    c = W.starProjection γ

hypotheses.label: nondegenerate variance
hypotheses.note: With zero variance all linear estimators have zero variance and uniqueness fails.

hypotheses.label: uncorrelated, common variance
hypotheses.note: The same second-moment assumption as in the Gauss–Markov comparison.

hypotheses.label: unbiased on the subspace
hypotheses.note: The estimator has the right expectation for every admissible mean vector.

hypotheses.label: attains the minimum
hypotheses.note: This is the equality case of the Gauss–Markov inequality, not an extra modelling assumption.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The uniqueness clause accompanies the Gauss (1821/1823) and Markov (1912) theorem; see Scheffé (1959), Kruskal (1965) and Rao (1973). The formalization derives it from the norm decomposition used in the comparison, so no separate argument is needed, and the conclusion is the exact identification of the optimal coefficient vector rather than an almost-sure equality of estimators.

formalizationNotes: Uniqueness is the equality case of the variance comparison: minimality forces the component of the coefficient vector orthogonal to the mean subspace to vanish, and unbiasedness has already pinned its projection. Square-integrability of the coordinates is carried as a separate hypothesis, as in the comparison itself, because the variance is junk-valued outside $L^2$.

title: Optimality of the Regression Coefficient Estimator
informal: In the regression form of the normal linear model the mean vector is $\xi = \theta A$ for a known $s \times n$ design matrix $A$, and the least-squares estimator of the coefficient vector is $$\hat\theta(y) \;=\; y\,A^{\mathsf T}\,(A A^{\mathsf T})^{-1}.$$ If the design has full row rank $s$ and there are more observations than coefficients, $s < n$, then for known coefficients $c_1,\dots,c_s$ the statistic $\sum_i c_i\,\hat\theta_i(y)$ is the uniformly minimum variance unbiased estimator of $\sum_i c_i\,\theta_i$. Moreover the covariance matrix of the least-squares coefficients is $\sigma^2 (A A^{\mathsf T})^{-1}$.
summary: For a design of full row rank, every linear function of the least-squares coefficients is UMVU for the corresponding linear function of the regression coefficients.
leanSignature:
theorem isUMVU_regression_coeff {A : Matrix (Fin s) (Fin n) ℝ}
    (hA : A.rank = s)
    (hsn : s < n)
    (c : Fin s → ℝ) :
    IsUMVU (regressionModel A) (fun p => ∑ i, c i * p.1 i)
      (fun y => ∑ i, c i * lseCoeff A y i)

hypotheses.label: full row rank design
hypotheses.note: The rows of the design are linearly independent, so the coefficient vector is identified by the mean vector.

hypotheses.label: more observations than coefficients
hypotheses.note: The standing dimension condition, without which the variance is not estimable.

reference.formal: E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, *Theory of Point Estimation*, 2nd ed., Springer Texts in Statistics, Springer-Verlag New York, 1998.
reference.biblio: The regression form of the linear model and the covariance formula $\sigma^2 (A A^{\mathsf T})^{-1}$ are classical, going back to Gauss (1821/1823) and Markov (1912); see Scheffé (1959), Kruskal (1965) and Rao (1973). The failure of best linear unbiased estimation for random regressors with known second moment is due to Shaffer (1991); the formalization records that the printed hypothesis for that clause is too weak and does not state it.

formalizationNotes: Coefficient vectors multiply the design on the left, matching the row convention; the coefficient estimator is a total function that returns zero exactly when the design does not have full row rank, so every statement carries the rank hypothesis. The proof is a reparametrization of the subspace statement along the span of the rows of the design, using that applying the design to the coefficient estimator returns the orthogonal projection of the observation. The source's companion claim that no best linear unbiased estimator exists when the design is random with a known second moment is not included here; formalizing it would require replacing the printed non-degeneracy hypothesis by non-constancy of the design information. Under the printed hypothesis alone a symmetric two-point design law is admissible, and for such a law the design information is constant, so a best linear unbiased estimator does exist.
